text: Wren wrote a short report for the council and took it to the office herself. She described the decline, the weather checks, the notice on the board and the sentence about June. She did not blame anyone. "The mowing was for safety, I understand," she wrote. "People walk through the meadow, and long grass hides holes. But there are ways to do both."

She listed three proposals at the bottom. The first was to stop mowing altogether. The second was to mow the whole meadow only in September, after the butterfly season, as before. The third was to mow the paths and the edges near the road in June, for safety, and to leave the middle two thirds of the meadow standing until September.

The chief of the council's gardening department read the three lines. "The first would make the paths impossible to use," he said. "The second is cheap but leaves the sides messy for the summer. The third solves both problems." Wren nodded. "It protects the caterpillars, and it keeps the paths clear for walkers."
The council agreed to try the third. Wren spent the next summer counting. In the first week of July, her clicker made a hundred and four clicks.
ch.clue: leave the middle two thirds of the meadow standing until September
ch.q: Which proposal protects the butterflies without making the paths unsafe?
o: Stop mowing the whole meadow for the next ten years
Mow the whole meadow twice in the month of June
Move the walking paths out of the meadow
Mow only the paths and edges in June, the rest in September
Plant new trees in the middle of the meadow
ch.hint: Hem kelebekleri hem de yürüyüş yollarının güvenliğini korumak için hangi öneri iki ihtiyacı birden karşılar?
ch.why: Yolları ve kenarları Haziran'da biçip ortadaki bölümü Eylül'e kadar bırakmak hem tırtılları koruyor hem yolları açık tutuyordu.

outro: Çayırın orta kısmı kesilmeden bırakıldı ve ertesi yaz kelebekler geri döndü. Wren şunu yazdı: doğada bir azalmanın nedeni çoğu zaman en uzak değil, en yakın şeydir.

title: The Fading Colours
hero: Küratör Hugo Laurent ve güvenlik görevlisi Mina
intro: Müzenin 3. salonundaki resimlerin renkleri, altı ayda yan salondakilerden çok daha fazla soldu. Küratör Hugo Laurent ile güvenlik görevlisi Mina, ışığın ölçümünü yaparak nedenini ve çözümünü araştırıyor.

text: Six months earlier, Hugo Laurent had taken photographs of twelve watercolours in the City Museum, six in Room 3 and six in Room 4, as part of the yearly inspection. Now he laid the new photographs beside the old ones on the table in his office. Mina stood beside him with her arms crossed.

The six watercolours of Room 4 looked exactly as they had a half-year earlier, the blues still deep, the reds warm. But those of Room 3 were different. The blue of a harbour scene had turned a pale grey-green. A red coat in a portrait had become pink. The yellow flowers in a still life had almost disappeared into the paper.

"Same artist, same year, same kind of paper and paint," said Hugo. "They were purchased together from the same collector. They were hanging side by side in the same corridor until last winter, when we divided them. So the pictures themselves cannot be the difference."

Mina looked at the plan of the building. "Room 3 and Room 4 are identical in size," she said. "They have the same walls, the same temperature, and the same kind of air-conditioning. The only difference is in the ceilings."
"Then the difference must be in what reaches them from above," said Hugo. "It is time to measure the light."
ch.clue: the pictures themselves cannot be the difference
ch.q: Why does Hugo think the paintings themselves are not the cause?
o: They were all repaired at the same time last year
They were painted by different artists in different years
They are less valuable than the other paintings
They are the same kind, bought together and hung together
They were never photographed before this inspection
ch.hint: On iki suluboya aynı sanatçıdan, aynı yıl, aynı kâğıt ve boyayla yapılmış ve birlikte satın alınmış. Bu benzerlik, soruna yol açan şeyin resimlerin kendisi olmadığını nasıl gösterir?
ch.why: Suluboyalar aynı sanatçıdan, aynı malzemeyle yapılmış ve birlikte satın alınmıştı; fark resimlerde değil, ortamdaydı.

text: The curator's light meter was a small grey box with a round white sensor on one side. It measured the brightness of light in units called lux. Hugo explained to Mina that museums keep watercolours in dim light, at no more than fifty lux, because their colours are fragile. "A bright room for people is about five hundred lux," he said. "A museum's watercolour room is as dim as a restaurant in the evening."

They measured each of the twelve paintings, one by one, holding the sensor in front of the paper, at about the height of the observer's eyes. In Room 4, the readings were between forty and forty-eight lux. In Room 3, they were between forty-five and fifty-two. Mina wrote the numbers in a table. "The readings in Room 3 are a little higher," she said, "but only by a few lux. It is almost the same."

Hugo looked at the table and frowned. "It does not explain such a big difference in fading," he said. "If fading were only caused by the brightness we can see, then Room 3's pictures should be only a few percent worse. But they are twice as pale. Something else reaches the paper, something that our meter cannot measure."
"What kind of light is invisible?" asked Mina.
"The kind that does the most damage," said Hugo, and he opened a drawer.
ch.clue: Something else reaches the paper
ch.q: What do the lux readings tell Hugo and Mina?
o: The visible light is nearly equal, so it cannot explain the fading
The light meter was broken during the measurement
The light in both rooms is much too dim to be seen
The light in Room 3 is dangerously bright for visitors
The paintings in Room 4 are in complete darkness
ch.hint: Salon 3 ve 4'ün lüks değerleri birbirine çok yakın. Görünür ışık farkı bu kadar küçükken, soldurma farkının bu kadar büyük olması neyi gösterir?
ch.why: Görünür ışık değerleri neredeyse eşitti; solmadaki büyük farkı açıklamak için görünmeyen başka bir şey olmalıydı.

text: From the drawer, Hugo took a second meter, a larger black one, with a small label: UV. "Ultraviolet," he explained. "It is the same invisible light that gives people sunburn. It has more energy than visible light, and it breaks the chemical bonds in paints and paper. Museums keep it below ten microwatts for every lumen of visible light, because even a tiny amount, over many months, destroys colours."

They went first to Room 4. The meter showed 4. Then they walked into Room 3, and Hugo held the sensor in front of the harbour watercolour. The number on the screen jumped immediately: 38. He moved the meter slowly along the wall, and the numbers changed. Near the corner, close to the glass roof, it showed 52. At the other end of the room, farther from the roof, it showed 21.
"Nearly ten times more than in Room 4," said Mina. "And the highest numbers are right under the glass roof."

Hugo looked up. Above them, the ceiling of Room 3 had a wide skylight, a rectangle of glass, covered by a thin transparent film that was meant to block the invisible light. He climbed a stepladder, and at the corner he stopped. The film had peeled from the glass, and a small triangular patch was open. Through that opening, the sun was shining straight into the room.
ch.clue: a small triangular patch was open
ch.q: What caused the extra fading in Room 3?
o: A faulty lamp that was left on all night
The paper of the watercolours was too old to survive
Ultraviolet light entering through a peeled patch of the skylight film
Too many visitors breathing in the room each day
Too much humidity from the room's air-conditioning
ch.hint: UV ölçer Salon 4'te 4, Salon 3'te ise 38 gösteriyor ve en yüksek değerler tavan camının altında. Camı kaplayan filmin durumu ne?
ch.why: Salon 3'ün tavan camındaki koruyucu film bir yerde sıyrılmıştı; oradan giren ultraviyole ışığı resimleri soldurmuştu.

text: The skylight film was replaced the following week by two technicians on a platform. It was a long job. They removed the old film from the whole glass, cleaned it, and applied a new one, a clear, thin, expensive material that blocks more than ninety-nine percent of ultraviolet light. When they finished, Hugo and Mina went up with the meter to check the work. The corner that had read 52 showed 2. The other end of the room, which had been 21, was now 1.

"It looks good," said Mina. "But how do we know that the paintings are safe?" Hugo smiled. "We will measure the light every week for a month, and then every month for the rest of the year. And we will photograph the watercolours exactly as we did before and compare them to the old photographs. If the colours do not change, the repair was successful."

He opened a small notebook and wrote a plan with dates. Then he stopped. "There is another thing," he said, almost to himself. "We have eleven other rooms with skylights. Nobody has ever measured their UV."
"Then that is our task for the winter," said Mina, and wrote it on the whiteboard in big green letters: Check every skylight.
ch.clue: blocks more than ninety-nine percent of ultraviolet light
ch.q: How will Hugo know that the repair has worked?
o: The new film is more expensive than the old one
The skylight looks clean and new from the outside
The museum has more visitors in the following month
The technicians say that the job was finished well
The UV readings are low and the colours stop changing
ch.hint: Onarımdan sonra hem ölçümler hem de resimler izlenecek. Çözümün işe yaradığını gösteren iki gözlem nedir?
ch.why: Ölçümlerde UV değerlerinin düşük kalması ve renklerin fotoğraflara göre değişmemesi onarımın başarılı olduğunu gösterirdi.

outro: Çatı penceresine yeni bir film yapıştırıldı ve resimlerin solması durdu. Hugo şöyle dedi: bir resmin düşmanı çoğu zaman görmediğimiz ışıktır.

title: The Puzzle Library
hero: Oyun testçileri Zoe ve Max
intro: Zoe ve Max bu kez eski bir kütüphane gibi görünen bir odada. Dört kişinin oturma düzeni, şifreli bir mesaj, bir sayı dizisi ve renkli ampuller; her bulmaca bir sonrakinin anahtarı. Süre bir saat.

text: The door closed with a deep thud, and the digital clock above it began to run: 60:00. Zoe and Max stood in a round room full of old books. In the middle, around a low table, four chairs were arranged in a row, numbered 1 to 4 from left to right. On the back of each chair hung a name card: Ann, Ben, Cara, Dan.

A piece of paper lay on the table. Max picked it up. "The four characters are sitting in the wrong order," he read. "Put them in the correct order, and the right chair will tell you the first digit. Here are the clues. One: Ann does not sit at either end. Two: Ben sits somewhere to the left of Cara, but not next to her. Three: Dan sits at one of the ends. Four: Cara does not sit next to Dan."

Zoe took a pencil and drew four boxes in her notebook. "Let us think," she said. "Ann is not at an end, so she is in chair 2 or 3. Dan is at an end, so chair 1 or chair 4. And Ben is to the left of Cara, with at least one person between them."

Max leaned over her shoulder, counting under his breath. "We can try them, one by one," he said. "There are not so many possibilities when you have four rules. The first digit of the code is the number of the chair where Cara sits."
ch.clue: Ben sits somewhere to the left of Cara, but not next to her
ch.q: In which chair does Cara sit?
o: Chair 2
It cannot be decided
Chair 3
Chair 1
Chair 4
ch.hint: Ann uçta değil, Dan uçta; Ben, Cara'nın solunda ama yanında değil; Cara, Dan'in yanında oturmuyor. Dört kuralı birlikte sağlayan tek dizilişi bul.
ch.why: Dört kuralı birlikte sağlayan tek dizilim Dan–Ben–Ann–Cara'dır; diğer olasılıkta (Ben–Ann–Cara–Dan) Cara, Dan'in yanında oturur ve bu yasaktı.

text: The number 4 opened a small drawer in the table, and inside there was a tiny brass key and a folded card. The card said: To read the book, step back three letters. Below it, in neat capitals, a message had been printed: IURP WKH EOXH ERRN. And on the next line: The code word is the last word of the message.

"Step back three letters," said Zoe. "A shifted alphabet. It is a cipher that Julius Caesar used to write to his generals. Each letter of the message has been moved forward by three places. To read it, we move each letter back by three."

She wrote the alphabet in a row in her notebook, and under it, in a second row, the same alphabet moved three places to the right. Max looked at the first word. "I, U, R, P," he said. "If I step back three from I, I get F. From U, I get R. Then O and M. F, R, O, M." He stopped and laughed. "It is a word."

Zoe did the rest slowly, working on each word with her finger on the alphabet. They had eleven minutes before the clock would pass forty-five, and she did not want to make a mistake. When she had written the last word, she looked at Max. "The last word is the code word. We only have to say it."
ch.clue: step back three letters
ch.q: What is the code word, the last word of the message?
o: FROM
BOOK
THE
BOLD
BLUE
ch.hint: Şifreli mesajın son kelimesi ERRN. Her harfi alfabede üç adım geri götür: E, R, R, N hangi harflere dönüşüyor?
ch.why: ERRN, her harf üç adım geri gidince BOOK olur; mesaj "FROM THE BLUE BOOK" idi ve son kelime BOOK'tu.

text: The code word BOOK made one of the old books on the shelf light up from the inside, a thick blue volume with the name Fibonacci on its spine. When Max pulled it out, the book opened itself, and a small drawing of a spiral appeared on the first page, with a row of numbers next to it: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and then a question mark. A short sentence was written underneath: The next step is a sum.

"Fibonacci," said Zoe. "A man from Italy in the thirteenth century, who invented a famous sequence. He asked a question about a family of rabbits, and the answer was a row of numbers where each number is the sum of the two before it. Start with one and one. The next is two. Then three. Then five. Then eight."

Max pointed at the page. "So the sentence 'The next step is a sum' means that the next number is a sum of the last two. I think I see." He wrote 5 and 8 on his hand with a pen, and drew a plus sign between them. "The spiral on the page is made from squares of those sizes, you see, one after another, each bigger than the last."
On the wall, the clock showed 27:30. Zoe took a deep breath. "That is the second digit pair of the code. Let us not rush."
ch.clue: each number is the sum of the two before it
ch.q: What number comes after 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8?
ch.hint: Dizide her sayı kendinden önceki iki sayının toplamı. Son iki sayı 5 ve 8 ise bir sonraki sayı kaç olur?
ch.why: Her sayı önceki iki sayının toplamıdır; 5 + 8 = 13.

text: The numbers of the sequence, 13 followed by another that Zoe typed in, made the lower part of the bookshelf slide open, and behind it was a small round chamber with a single lamp on the ceiling, and twelve coloured bulbs in a ring around the door. A note was pinned to the wall: One third of the bulbs are blue. One quarter are red. All the others are white. The final digit is the number of white bulbs.

Max looked at the ring of bulbs, and he started to count them, but Zoe stopped him. "No need to count the colours," she said. "The note gives us a rule, and the number of bulbs is twelve. A third of twelve is easy. A quarter of twelve is easy, too. We only need to take them away from the total."
"If I subtract the blue and the red from twelve," said Max slowly, "what remains is white. But there is a catch, isn't there? You have to be careful that a bulb is not counted in both groups."
"No bulb is both blue and red," said Zoe. "A bulb can only be one colour. So the groups do not overlap."
The clock now showed only 04:55. Max put his hand on the cold steel handle of the exit door, and Zoe looked at the keypad with a single empty box.
ch.clue: One third of the bulbs are blue
ch.q: How many white bulbs are there?
ch.hint: On iki ampulün üçte biri mavi, dörtte biri kırmızı. Kalan beyaz ampullerin sayısını bulmak için mavi ve kırmızıları toplamdan çıkar.
ch.why: 12'nin üçte biri 4, dörtte biri 3'tür; 12 − 4 − 3 = 5 beyaz ampul vardı.

outro: Kütüphanenin kapısı açıldı ve Zoe ile Max, sayı kodlarını hâlâ gülerek tekrarlayarak çıktı. Oda sahibi onlara, en güzel bulmacanın ipucunun en baştan orada olan olduğunu söyledi.

title: The Wrong Terminal
hero: Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ve stajyer Sam
intro: Bir öğrenci olan Jun, pasaportunu kaybetti ve uçağı birkaç saat sonra kalkıyor. Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ile stajyer Sam, banka fişleri, taksi makbuzu ve kayıp eşya kaydından yararlanarak pasaportu bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: At half past twelve, a young man ran up to the information desk of Heathfield Airport, with his jacket open and his hair in his eyes. "Please help me," he said, in a mixture of English and his own language. "My name is Jun Park. My flight to Seoul leaves at three o'clock. I have my ticket and my suitcase, but my passport is gone. It was in my jacket this morning, and now it is not."

Dara Mills, who had been in the airport for twelve years, asked him to sit down and to breathe. Her young trainee Sam gave him a glass of water. "We will find it," said Dara. "But I need you to remember very carefully where you have been today. Start from the beginning, and do not leave anything out."

Jun closed his eyes. "I woke up at eight in my friend's flat in the city," he said. "I took the train to the airport station, and I arrived at about eleven. In the hall, I went to a bank machine because I wanted to take some cash. Then I took a taxi..." He stopped. "A taxi, from the station to the airport terminal. The station is not at the terminal, you see, it is a few kilometres away."
"Good," said Dara. "That is already three places: the bank machine, the taxi, and the terminal. Let us find out which one is the right one."
ch.clue: I took the train to the airport station
ch.q: What is the best way to find the missing passport?
o: Follow Jun's movements step by step, from the morning
Close the airport until the passport is found
Wait until the end of the day for someone to call
Ask all the passengers to open their bags
Print a new passport at the information desk
ch.hint: Jun'un gün boyunca durakları: arkadaşın evi, tren, banka makinesi, taksi, terminal. Kaybolan bir şeyi bulmak için bu zinciri hangi sırayla incelemek mantıklı?
ch.why: Dara, Jun'dan günün başından itibaren gittiği yerleri sırayla hatırlamasını istedi; bu zincir pasaportun kaybolduğu yeri gösterecekti.

text: Jun emptied his pockets on the desk. There was a crumpled tissue, a pencil, a tram ticket, and two small slips of paper. Sam smoothed them out and read them aloud. The first was a receipt from the bank machine, printed with the time of the withdrawal: 11:34. The second was a receipt from a taxi company: Pick-up 11:48, Station. Drop-off 11:59, Terminal 2. Fare: £11.50.

Dara looked at the second slip more carefully. "Terminal 2," she said. "Jun, your boarding pass. What terminal does your flight leave from?" Jun handed it to her. She turned it to the light and read: Gate 17. Terminal 1. Departure 15:00.
"Terminal 1," said Sam. "But the taxi took you to Terminal 2."

Jun looked confused. "I did not look at the number," he said. "I told the driver 'to the airport', and he took me to the first door he saw. I walked through the building, and when I saw the departure boards, I thought I was in the right place. I took the free shuttle to Terminal 1. I did not understand it was two buildings."

"So the passport fell out of your pocket either at the bank, in the taxi, or at Terminal 2, before you took the shuttle," said Dara. "The bank was before the taxi, so the passport must have been in your jacket when you got into the taxi. Let us start by phoning Terminal 2."
ch.clue: Drop-off 11:59, Terminal 2
ch.q: What do the two receipts show about Jun's journey?
o: The bank machine kept his passport by mistake
He withdrew money after the taxi dropped him off
The taxi took him to a different terminal from his flight
He took the taxi from the wrong railway station
He arrived at the airport before eleven o'clock
ch.hint: Taksi makbuzu hangi terminalde indiğini, biniş kartı ise uçuşun hangi terminalden kalktığını söylüyor. İkisini karşılaştır.
ch.why: Taksi onu 2. terminale bırakmıştı ama uçuşu 1. terminaldendi; Jun ücretsiz servisle terminaller arasında geçmişti.

text: Sam phoned the lost property office at Terminal 2 and talked for about two minutes, with the receiver pressed to his ear, nodding. When he put the phone down, his face was unreadable. "They have a number of things," he said. "A blue umbrella, a laptop charger, two children's gloves, a set of keys and a red passport cover. No passport."
"A cover?" said Dara. "Jun, what colour was your passport?" Jun's eyes lit up. "Dark red. With a gold lion on the front. But I did not know that it had a cover..."

"They say it was handed in at 12:20," said Sam, reading from his notes. "By a cleaner, who found it under a bench in the waiting area near the shuttle bus stop. The cover was empty, but the cleaner remembers that there was a small card in a plastic pocket, and the card said 'Park'. Is that your name?"
"Yes!" said Jun. He jumped up. "Then the passport must be inside something else. A bag? A card holder?"

Dara shook her head slowly. "The cover and the passport have been separated. The cleaner put the cover in lost property, but the passport... Sam, ask them if the cleaner remembers who else was near the bench."
ch.clue: a red passport cover
ch.q: What do Sam's phone call and the lost property list suggest?
o: The whole passport was found by a cleaner at 12:20
The passport is lying in the taxi that Jun took
Jun's passport was stolen by someone at the bank
The passport was found in the umbrella at the office
Jun's passport cover was found, but the passport itself is missing
ch.hint: Kayıp eşya listesinde ne var ve Sam'e göre "pasaport" bunlar arasında mı? Pasaport kılıfıyla pasaportun kendisi arasındaki farka dikkat et.
ch.why: Terminal 2'de pasaport kılıfı bulunmuştu ama pasaportun kendisi yoktu; ikisi birbirinden ayrılmıştı.

text: A minute later, Sam's phone rang. It was the supervisor at Terminal 2, a woman with a brisk, kind voice. "I have news," she said. "The cleaner has just remembered. Just after twelve, the shuttle bus driver found a passport on the floor of the bus, between the seats. He is a careful man. He gave it to the driver's office in Terminal 1, and it was sent to our lost property by the internal mail. It will arrive in the afternoon, but we have a second possibility. The office at Terminal 1 still has it in a drawer."

Dara looked at the clock on the wall. "Quarter to one," she said. "Jun, your flight leaves at three. Check-in closes at two. Terminal 1 is where you need to be anyway. The driver's office is on the ground floor, near the main entrance. It will take you five minutes to walk there, and ten to get your passport."
"So I can check in at ten past one," Jun said, smiling for the first time. "And we have seven minutes for a coffee."
"We have a rule here at the desk," said Dara. "No coffee until the passport is in the hand." They walked together to the driver's office, and the officer opened a drawer.
ch.clue: Terminal 1 still has it in a drawer
ch.q: Where is the passport, and when will Jun be able to check in?
o: In the taxi company's office on the station road
In the Terminal 1 driver's office, well before check-in closes
On the shuttle bus that left for the city
In the lost property office of Terminal 2 until evening
At the bank machine where Jun took his money
ch.hint: Şoför pasaportu nerede bulmuş ve nereye teslim etmiş? Check-in saat kaçta kapanıyor ve şu an saat kaç?
ch.why: Pasaport, otobüs şoförü tarafından Terminal 1'deki ofise teslim edilmişti; şu an 12:45'ti ve check-in 14:00'te kapanacaktı.

outro: Pasaport, uçağın kalkmasına kırk dakika kala Jun'un elindeydi ve o, yeni bir çanta fermuarı satın aldı. Dara şunu dedi: kayıp bir şey çoğu zaman gittiğimiz yolun üzerinde durur; yeter ki sırayla geriye bakalım.

title: The Wet Umbrella
hero: Dedektif Edmund Crane ve asistanı Tess
intro: Bir bankada çalışan Mr. Hale, ofisinden önemli bir sözleşmenin kaybolduğunu söylüyor ve temizlikçiyi suçluyor. Edmund Crane ile Tess, ofiste gözlem yaparak olayın gerçekte nasıl geliştiğini anlamaya çalışıyor.

text: It was a grey Monday morning when Mr. Hale, a heavy man with a loud voice, walked into Edmund Crane's office with an umbrella in his hand. He placed it on the stand and began to speak before he had even sat down. "A contract has disappeared from my desk at the bank," he said. "A very important one, worth two million pounds. It was there at six o'clock on Friday evening, and this morning it was gone. Only one person has been in my room since then: the cleaner, Mrs. Doyle, who comes on Saturday mornings. I want her dismissed."

Edmund asked him to describe Friday evening. "I worked until six," said Mr. Hale. "I put the contract in the top drawer, but I did not lock it. I went home by taxi, because it was raining hard. I did not come back until this morning." Tess, who was writing in her notebook, looked up. "The bank has cameras?" she asked. "Only at the entrance," Mr. Hale said. "They show that nobody came in on Saturday except the cleaner, and she left at eleven."
Edmund said nothing for a while, his eyes on the umbrella on the stand. Then he asked in a soft voice, "Mr. Hale, did you go back to the office at any time over the weekend?"
"Of course not," the man replied sharply. "Why should I?"
ch.clue: I went home by taxi, because it was raining hard
ch.q: What does Mr. Hale say about his Friday evening?
o: He stayed in the bank until the cleaner arrived
He left at six by taxi because of the heavy rain
He locked the contract in the top drawer of the desk
He walked home in the rain with the umbrella
He took the contract home with him for the weekend
ch.hint: Mr. Hale cuma akşamı nasıl eve gittiğini ve neden öyle gittiğini söylüyor. Bu ayrıntıyı aklında tut; çünkü ileride şemsiyeyle ilgili önemli olacak.
ch.why: Mr. Hale cuma günü saat altıda, yağmur çok yağdığı için taksiyle eve gittiğini söylüyordu.

text: An hour later, Edmund and Tess stood in Mr. Hale's office at the bank. It was a large, tidy room on the third floor, with a big window that looked over the street. The desk was empty except for a lamp and a telephone. Tess opened the top drawer. It contained paper clips, a calendar, and a few blank folders. The contract was nowhere.

"Cameras only at the entrance," said Edmund, looking round. "So we cannot see the corridor. But we can see other things." He pointed at the floor near the door. "Mrs. Doyle cleans on Saturday morning. The carpet is vacuumed. Look: the vacuum lines are clean, regular, and run parallel to the wall. Nobody has walked on them, except along the path between the door and the desk." He walked slowly along the path, then stopped near the chair.

Tess bent down. "There is a small mark on the carpet," she said. "A dark, round patch, about the size of a coin." She touched it. "It is slightly damp, still." Edmund crouched beside her. "Near the chair, and on a vacuumed carpet," he said. "Mrs. Doyle left on Saturday at eleven. Something wet fell here after that, on a floor that was already clean."
"A drip," said Tess. "From what?"
Edmund looked at the stand by the door, where Mr. Hale's umbrella had been standing an hour earlier. It was gone. Mr. Hale had taken it with him when he went to the meeting room.
ch.clue: slightly damp, still
ch.q: What is strange about the wet mark on the carpet?
o: It was left by the rain that came through the window
It was made by the cleaner's wet cloth on Saturday
It had been there for several weeks already
It was made after Mrs. Doyle had cleaned the carpet
It was made by a coffee cup that someone dropped
ch.hint: Halı Cumartesi sabahı süpürülmüş ve temizlikçi saat 11'de gitmiş. Hâlâ nemli olan bir leke, bu zamana göre ne zaman oluşmuş olabilir?
ch.why: Halı temizlikçi tarafından süpürülmüş ve o gittikten sonra temizdi; leke hâlâ nemliydi, yani temizlikten sonra birisi içeri girmişti.

text: Back in the office, Tess opened her laptop and found the weather records for the weekend. She read them aloud. "On Friday evening, it rained heavily from four until ten. On Saturday, the sky was clear all day. On Sunday, it rained again from about two o'clock in the afternoon, a light, steady rain. On Monday morning, it is dry."

Edmund, with his hands behind his back, was walking up and down. "Let me put it in order," he said. "If Mr. Hale left on Friday at six, a wet umbrella would have dripped at once in the hall, on the carpet of the third floor, not near his chair. But the cleaner came on Saturday and vacuumed the whole floor. So the carpet was dry on Saturday afternoon. The drop that we found fell after that. It was still damp this morning, which means it fell not long before. Rain fell on Sunday afternoon, and only then."
"So Mr. Hale came back to the office on Sunday," said Tess slowly. "With an umbrella that was dripping. He told us that he did not return all weekend."
"He told us two things that cannot both be true," said Edmund. "That he did not return, and that only the cleaner had been in the room. I think we should ask him about Sunday afternoon."
ch.clue: Rain fell on Sunday afternoon, and only then
ch.q: What can Edmund conclude from the weather records and the damp mark?
o: Mr. Hale returned to his office on Sunday afternoon
Mrs. Doyle returned to the office on Sunday morning
The cleaner brought the wet umbrella on Saturday
The carpet was wet because of a leak in the roof
A thief climbed in through the window on Friday
ch.hint: Cumartesi hava açıktı, pazar öğleden sonra yağmur yağdı. Halıdaki nemli leke nem hâlâ kuru olmayacak kadar yeni. Bu bilgilerle, o lekeyi bırakan kişi ofise ne zaman gelmiş?
ch.why: Cumartesi hava açık, pazar öğleden sonra yağmurluydu; leke yağmurlu bir günde bir ıslak şemsiyeden düşmüş olmalıydı, yani Mr. Hale pazar günü ofise gelmişti.

text: Mr. Hale came into the room at noon, his face red. Edmund asked him calmly to sit down. "Mr. Hale," he said, "we believe you came back to the office on Sunday afternoon. There is a damp mark on the carpet from your umbrella. It was not Mrs. Doyle."

The big man was silent for a long moment, then he put his hands over his face. "I came on Sunday," he said, in a very different voice. "I wanted to check the contract once more. I took it out, and I read it, and then I put it in my bag, intending to read it at home. I did not tell the police because... I was embarrassed. And then on Monday morning, I could not find it, and I was frightened."

Tess looked at the black leather bag beside his chair. "May I?" she asked. He nodded weakly. She opened it. Inside, among a diary and a pair of gloves, there was a thick blue folder. In the folder, under a sheet marked Annual Report, lay the contract.
"I picked up the wrong folder in a hurry," murmured Mr. Hale. "I thought it was the annual report."
"I suggest that you phone Mrs. Doyle," said Edmund quietly, "and apologise to her."
ch.clue: I picked up the wrong folder in a hurry
ch.q: What happened to the contract?
o: Mrs. Doyle hid it in her cleaning cupboard
It was destroyed by the rain on Sunday afternoon
Mr. Hale took it home by mistake inside the wrong folder
A thief took it out of the drawer on Saturday
The bank's manager removed it for a meeting
ch.hint: Mr. Hale pazar günü ofise gelip sözleşmeyi aldığını itiraf ediyor. Sözleşme nerede ve hangi klasörün içinde çıkıyor?
ch.why: Mr. Hale sözleşmeyi pazar günü acele içinde yanlış klasöre koyup çantasında eve götürmüştü; sözleşme o çantadaki klasörün içinde bulundu.

outro: Sözleşme, Mr. Hale'in kendi çantasında, yanlış klasörün içinde bulundu. Edmund şunu söyledi: bir suçlamayı kabul etmeden önce, suçlayanın anlattığı zamanın doğru olup olmadığına bakmak gerekir.

title: The Pale Child
hero: Dr. Mara Quinn ve hemşire Joe
intro: Sekiz yaşında bir çocuk, haftalardır solgun ve yorgun. Aile ilk başta sadece büyüdüğünü düşünüyor. Dr. Mara Quinn ile hemşire Joe, çocuğun beslenmesini, kan sonuçlarını ve günlük alışkanlıklarını sorarak nedeni arıyor.

text: Eight-year-old Theo came into Dr. Quinn's room slowly, holding his mother's hand. He was a thin child with big brown eyes and very pale cheeks. His mother, Mrs. Bell, sat on the edge of the chair and spoke in a low, worried voice. "He used to run around all day," she said. "Now he comes home from school and falls asleep on the sofa at four o'clock. His teacher says that he cannot concentrate. He has no energy for football any more, and it was his favourite thing."

Nurse Joe measured the boy's height and weight. "He is growing normally," he said. "A little under the average weight, but not worrying." Dr. Quinn looked at Theo's fingernails and then, gently, pulled down the lower edge of his eyelid. Normally the inside is a deep pink. Theo's was almost white.

"How long has he been like this?" she asked. "About two months," said Mrs. Bell. "At first I thought it was just a growth spurt, or a cold." Dr. Quinn smiled kindly at the boy. "Theo, can you tell me what you eat on a normal day?"
"Pasta," said Theo, thinking hard. "And bread. And cereal with milk. And crisps." He paused. "I do not like meat. Or beans. Or green things."
Dr. Quinn wrote a few words on her notes, and underlined one of them twice.
ch.clue: almost white
ch.q: Which sign makes Dr. Quinn suspect a problem with Theo's blood?
o: He is thin and has big brown eyes
He does not like to play football
The inside of his lower eyelid is almost white
He has grown more slowly than other boys
He sleeps for a short time after school
ch.hint: Normalde göz kapağının iç yüzü koyu pembedir. Dr. Quinn kapağı çektiğinde ne görüyor ve bu kan hakkında ne düşündürür?
ch.why: Theo'nun alt göz kapağının içi neredeyse beyazdı; bu, kanda bir sorun, örneğin kansızlık olabileceğini düşündürüyordu.

text: Nurse Joe took a small sample of blood from Theo's finger. The boy watched the tiny red drop with great interest, and Joe told him that it was a secret mission for the laboratory. "It will take about fifteen minutes," he said. "We have a machine that counts everything."

While they waited, Dr. Quinn asked Mrs. Bell some more questions. Did Theo have any stomach pain? No. Was there blood in his stool? No. Had he been ill recently, with fever or a long cold? No. Did anybody in the family have anaemia? "My sister did," said Mrs. Bell, "when she was young."

The printed results arrived on a thin white strip. Dr. Quinn read them in silence. Theo's haemoglobin, the substance that carries oxygen in red blood cells, was 9.8 grams per decilitre. For a boy of his age, the normal value is at least eleven and a half. His red cells were also smaller and paler than normal. A third value, called ferritin, which shows how much iron the body has stored, was very low.

"It is a mild anaemia," she told his mother. "His blood cannot carry enough oxygen, which is why he feels tired and looks so pale. But it is not dangerous, and it can be treated. The question is why it happened."
ch.clue: ferritin
ch.q: What do the blood results show?
o: A serious infection which needs hospital treatment
Normal blood values and a mistake in the test
A high level of sugar which suggests diabetes
Too many red cells, which makes the blood thick
Low haemoglobin and low iron stores: a mild anaemia
ch.hint: Hemoglobin normalin altında ve ferritin çok düşük. Hemoglobin oksijen taşır, ferritin depo demiri gösterir. Bu iki değer birlikte hangi sorunu gösterir?
ch.why: Düşük hemoglobin ve çok düşük ferritin, çocukta demir yetersizliğine bağlı hafif bir kansızlık olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: "Iron comes mostly from our food," said Dr. Quinn, "so let us look at what Theo eats." She took a sheet of paper and drew two columns. In the first, she wrote the foods that Theo had listed: pasta, white bread, cereal, milk, crisps. "Milk is excellent for bones, but it contains almost no iron, and drinking a lot of it can even make it harder for the body to take iron from other foods. Pasta and white bread have only a little. Crisps have none."

In the second column she wrote the foods rich in iron: red meat, chicken, fish, beans, lentils, spinach, eggs, and breakfast cereals with added iron. "He does not like meat, beans, or green vegetables," said Mrs. Bell, "and he drinks about three glasses of milk a day, because he refuses to eat anything else when he is full."

Dr. Quinn nodded. "It is very common," she said. "A child who fills up on milk and bread, and who avoids red meat and green vegetables, can easily lack iron. It is nobody's fault. Children's tastes are very strong at this age."
"What can I do?" asked Mrs. Bell. "I have tried everything. He pushes the spinach to the side of the plate."
ch.clue: it can even make it harder for the body to take iron
ch.q: What is the most likely cause of Theo's anaemia?
o: He has caught a serious infection at school
His diet has very little iron and a lot of milk
He inherited an illness from his aunt
He is growing too quickly for his age
He is losing blood slowly from his stomach
ch.hint: Theo'nun yediği besinlerin çoğunda demir yok ve günde üç bardak süt içiyor, bu da demir emilimini zorlaştırabilir. Bu beslenme düzeni neye yol açabilir?
ch.why: Theo demirden fakir yiyecekler yiyor ve çok süt içiyordu; bu, demir eksikliğine ve kansızlığa yol açmıştı.

text: Dr. Quinn and Nurse Joe made a plan together with Mrs. Bell, and they wrote it down on a card so that nobody would forget. First, Theo would take an iron syrup every morning for three months, a small spoonful, which Joe explained could turn his stool dark and was harmless. Second, he would drink no more than two glasses of milk a day, and not at the same time as the iron.

Third, and most important, they would change the menu in small steps. Joe, who had two children of his own, had practical suggestions. "Do not hide the vegetables," he said. "Let him help you cook. Make little meatballs with lentils inside. Put raisins and a few slices of orange next to his cereal. Vitamin C, which is in oranges and strawberries, helps the body take in iron. If he drinks orange juice with his meal, he will absorb more from the same food."
Mrs. Bell wrote everything on the card. Then Dr. Quinn smiled at Theo. "In six weeks I would like to measure your blood again," she said, "and we will see whether the secret mission was a success."
Six weeks later, the paper strip showed a haemoglobin of 11.9. When Theo came into the room, he ran.
ch.clue: Vitamin C
ch.q: Why does Joe suggest that Theo drinks orange juice with his meal?
o: The juice hides the taste of the vegetables
Oranges contain much more iron than red meat
It makes the boy drink less milk during the day
Vitamin C helps the body absorb the iron from the food
Orange juice replaces the iron syrup completely
ch.hint: Joe portakal suyunu yemekle birlikte öneriyor. C vitamininin vücutta demirle ilgili ne işlevi olduğunu hatırla.
ch.why: C vitamini, vücudun yiyeceklerdeki demiri daha iyi emmesine yardım eder; bu yüzden Joe yemekle birlikte portakal suyu önerdi.

outro: Çocuğun demir eksiği vardı; menüsüne demirden zengin yiyecekler ve C vitamini eklendi, birkaç haftada rengi geri geldi. Mara şunu yazdı: bir belirti, sorunun kendisi değil, onu gösteren işarettir.

title: The Silent Radio
hero: Komutan Noor Hale ve mühendis Pip
intro: Ay üssünün Dünya ile bağlantısı sessizce kesiliyor. Komutan Noor Hale ile mühendis Pip, sinyali, anteni ve güneş aktivitesini inceleyerek sorunun üssün kendisinde mi, yoksa dışarıda mı olduğunu bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: At 14:20 base time, the main radio of Moonbase Selene went silent. There was no warning, no alarm, no error message on the screen. The voice of the controller on Earth, who had been giving the daily instructions, simply stopped in the middle of a sentence and was replaced by a soft, endless hiss.

Commander Noor Hale put down her cup of tea and floated to the communications console. Pip, the young engineer, was already there with his fingers on the keyboard. "I have tried the backup frequency," he said. "The same noise. I have restarted the receiver twice. Nothing."

"Is the antenna damaged?" asked Noor. Pip typed quickly. "The self-test says that the antenna is working correctly," he said, frowning. "The receiver says that everything is normal. The cables are fine. The power is on. It looks like a perfect system, which listens to nothing."

"A perfect system cannot be silent without a reason," said Noor. She looked at the clock. The next scheduled call was in twelve minutes. If it failed, the controllers on Earth would start to worry. "Let us make a list of what could be wrong. Inside, our equipment. Outside, the signal on the way to us."
Pip took a pen and drew two columns on the whiteboard: Inside and Outside. He put a question mark in the middle.
ch.clue: The self-test says that the antenna is working correctly
ch.q: What has Pip discovered so far?
o: The backup frequency works but the main one does not
The antenna is broken and needs to be replaced
The power supply of the base has failed completely
The equipment reports no fault, yet no signal arrives
The controller on Earth has switched off the radio
ch.hint: Pip anten, alıcı, kablo ve güç testlerini yaptı. Hepsi sağlam görünüyor ama sinyal gelmiyor. Bu durumda sorun nerede olabilir?
ch.why: Tüm testler sistemin sağlam çalıştığını gösteriyordu, ama hiç sinyal gelmiyordu; yani sorun ekipmanda görünmüyordu.

text: They began with the inside, because it was the part they could control. Pip connected a test generator to the receiver and sent a small signal into it, exactly as if it were coming from the antenna. On the screen, the signal appeared at once, bright and clear, a sharp peak above the noise. "The receiver hears it," he said. "So the receiver is not deaf."

Then he did the same with the cable that connected the antenna to the base. Again, the test signal passed without any loss. The last part was the antenna itself, a tall white dish on the surface, pointed at the Earth. A camera on the roof showed the dish clearly, still aimed at the blue planet in the black sky. There was no dust on it and no visible damage.

"The inside is fine," said Noor. "We have tested the receiver, the cable and the antenna, one by one, and each of them works. The problem must be outside the base." She turned to the second column on the whiteboard. "What could stop a radio signal on its way from Earth to the Moon?"

Pip laughed nervously. "In theory, three things," he said. "The transmitter on Earth, an obstacle in the path, or something in space that disturbs the signal. We know the Earth has not moved, and nothing flies between us."
"Then let us look at the third," said Noor. "I will call the solar observatory."
ch.clue: The inside is fine
ch.q: What do the tests of the receiver, cable and antenna show?
o: The base equipment works, so the problem must be elsewhere
The antenna is not pointing at the Earth any more
The whole system must be replaced before the next call
The receiver cannot hear weak signals from far away
The cable is too old and loses part of the signal
ch.hint: Pip alıcıya, kabloya ve antene ayrı ayrı test sinyali gönderdi ve hepsi çalıştı. Bu, sorunun üsteki cihazlarda olma ihtimali hakkında ne söyler?
ch.why: Alıcı, kablo ve anten tek tek test edildi ve hepsi çalışıyordu; bu yüzden sorun üssün dışında olmalıydı.

text: Noor phoned the solar observatory in a few seconds, using the base's slow laser link, which still worked and which Earth did not use for ordinary calls. The duty officer, a quiet man named Dr. Idris, answered at once and seemed relieved to hear from her.

"I was about to call you," he said. "Forty minutes ago, a large flare broke out on the surface of the Sun, followed by a mass of charged particles. It is a strong storm. It is passing the Earth and the Moon right now. Satellites around the Earth are reporting disturbance in their radio links. The particles fill the space between us with electrical noise, a kind of invisible fog. It does not break anything, but it drowns the weak signals."

Pip, listening beside her, made a long whistle. "So the receiver is fine," he said, "but the signal from Earth is covered by the noise." Dr. Idris agreed. "The storm will last about an hour. After that, communications will slowly come back. For now, I suggest that you use the laser link, which is not affected, for important messages."

Noor thanked him and ended the call. She looked at the whiteboard, where the Inside column was full of crosses and the Outside column was still empty. She took the pen and wrote a single word in it: Sun.
ch.clue: drowns the weak signals
ch.q: Why can the base not hear the radio from Earth?
o: The Earth has moved out of the antenna's view
The laser link has stopped all other communications
A solar storm is filling space with noise that covers the signal
The Sun has damaged the antenna with strong heat
The observatory has switched off the transmitter
ch.hint: Dr. Idris güneş patlaması ve yüklü parçacıklar anlatıyor. Bu parçacıklar uzayda ne yapıyor ve zayıf radyo sinyaline ne oluyor?
ch.why: Güneş fırtınası uzayı elektriksel gürültüyle dolduruyor, zayıf radyo sinyalini bastırıyordu; üssün cihazları sağlamdı.

text: For the next hour, the crew of Moonbase Selene worked on the things they could do without a radio. Pip wrote a short report on the failure, with the times and the tests, so that he would not forget a single detail. Noor sent the necessary message by the laser link: all well, radio quiet because of the storm, we will report when it clears. A small green light confirmed that the message had arrived.

At 15:25, a soft click came from the speaker, and the hiss changed. Then, from the middle of the noise, a distant voice rose, thin and broken at first, then stronger. "...Selene, this is Control. Do you hear us? Selene, please answer." Pip jumped and almost hit the ceiling. Noor pressed the button. "Control, this is Selene," she said. "We hear you, loud and clear. We were quiet because of the solar storm."
"We know," said the controller, laughing. "We lost you for sixty-five minutes. Everybody was worried."

When the call was over, Noor turned to Pip. "What did we learn?" she asked. Pip thought. "That the first thing to check is not always the machine," he said. "If every test inside says 'normal', then it is time to look outside."
"Write that in the report," said Noor, smiling.
ch.clue: look outside
ch.q: What lesson does Pip draw from the experience?
o: A radio always fails when the antenna is old
The laser link must replace the main radio
The commander must always call the observatory first
Reports should not be written during an emergency
If every internal test is normal, the cause may be outside
ch.hint: Pip en sonda ne öğrendiğini söylüyor: bütün iç testler "normal" çıkıyorsa ne yapmak gerekir?
ch.why: Pip, içerideki bütün testler normal çıkıyorsa nedenin dışarıda olabileceğini fark etti.

outro: Bağlantı bir saat sonra geri geldi; neden, Güneş'ten gelen bir parçacık fırtınasıydı. Noor şunu söyledi: bir sistem susarsa önce kendi ayıbımızı değil, çevreyi kontrol etmeliyiz.

title: The Two Dates
hero: Tarihçi Dr. Amira Kent ve asistanı Leo
intro: Bir kasaba müzesine bağışlanan günlük, 1816 yılında yazıldığını iddia ediyor. Dr. Amira Kent ile Leo, kâğıdı, mürekkebi ve içindeki tarihleri inceleyerek günlüğün gerçekten o yıla ait olup olmadığını araştırıyor.

text: The small museum of Marlow had received many gifts over the years: old buttons, pieces of crockery, medals, and rusty keys. But the package that arrived on Tuesday was different. It came from the family of a late schoolteacher, in a wooden box tied with a ribbon, and inside it, wrapped in a yellow cloth, lay a thin leather book. On the first page, in brown ink, someone had written a title: The Journal of Thomas Ashby, Fisherman, 1816.

Dr. Amira Kent, the museum's historian, turned the pages very slowly with a pair of white gloves. Her assistant Leo stood beside her. "1816," he said. "That is the year without a summer, isn't it? When a volcano in Indonesia made the weather cold, and crops failed all over Europe. A diary from that year would be very valuable for our local history."

"It would be, if it is real," said Amira. "The family believes it is. The schoolteacher told them that it was written by an ancestor. But I have been fooled before." She held the first page against the light. "The paper looks old, and the writing looks old. It has been well cared for. But anyone can write in brown ink on a yellow page."
She put the journal on the table. "Before we decide anything, let us examine it, as if it were a piece of evidence."
ch.clue: I have been fooled before
ch.q: What is Amira's attitude to the journal?
o: She will refuse to open it because it is too old
She thinks the family wants to make money from it
She wants to return it to the family at once
She is sure that it is a valuable genuine diary
She wants to examine it carefully before believing it
ch.hint: Amira günlüğün eski göründüğünü ama bunun yeterli olmadığını söylüyor ve "delil gibi inceleyelim" diyor. Bu tutum ne anlama geliyor?
ch.why: Amira günlüğün eski görünmesine rağmen hemen inanmak istemedi; önce bir delil gibi dikkatle incelemek istedi.

text: Leo carried the journal to the laboratory on the second floor, where there was a good lamp and a microscope. He placed a page under the lens, and Amira looked at the fibres. "Old paper from before 1850 was made from cotton and linen rags," she said, "which makes it soft, with long, uneven fibres. Later paper contains wood pulp, which is cheaper, and the fibres are short and regular. Look."

Leo looked. The fibres in the picture were short and neat, like a field of tiny straws. "Wood pulp," he said slowly. "Is it possible in 1816?" Amira shook her head. "Not for books of this kind. Wood pulp paper came into common use in the 1860s and 1870s. The paper of this journal could not have been made before about 1870."

She turned the pages carefully to the last one and held a small lamp against the ink. "The ink is a dark brown iron gall, which was used for centuries. It could belong to any period. But the paper is clear evidence, and it says that the book was made at least fifty years after the date written on its first page."
Leo took off his glasses. "So it is a fake?" he asked. "It is certainly not what the title claims," said Amira. "But I would like to know what it is."
ch.clue: could not have been made before about 1870
ch.q: What does the paper tell Amira about the journal?
o: It was written on the paper of an older book
It was made at least fifty years after 1816
It was made from linen rags in the year 1816
It was made in a different country from the text
It was damaged by water over the years
ch.hint: Odun hamurundan yapılan kâğıt 1860-70'lerde yaygınlaşıyor. Bu günlüğün kâğıdı odun hamuruysa, günlük en erken ne zaman yapılmış olabilir?
ch.why: Kâğıt odun hamurundan yapılmıştı ve ancak 1870 dolaylarından sonra üretilebilirdi; yani 1816'dan en az elli yıl sonra yapılmıştı.

text: Amira turned back to the text, this time reading with great attention. The writing was a careful, rounded hand, with short sentences about fish, weather, and the price of salt. On page 12, he complained of a poor catch, and on page 23, he described a storm in which a neighbour lost his boat. It all looked authentic. "If someone wanted to make a forgery," Leo said, "they would put in some famous events, wouldn't they? Like the volcano, or the cold summer."

"They would," said Amira. "And this book does not. Look at page 40, where the writer tells us about the harvest. He says that it was an average year. In 1816, the crops failed over all Europe. A fisherman in the south of England, writing in that summer, would have complained about the rain." She read on. "And here, on page 55, there is a comment in pencil, in the margin. Look at it."
In the margin, in small grey letters, someone had written: Copied from Grandfather's old book, March 1891. A.A.
Leo was silent for a moment. "Copied," he said. "So the journal in the box is not the original. It is a copy, written in 1891, by a descendant, from an older book which has been lost."
"That would explain the paper, and the average harvest, and the careful hand," said Amira. "Everything that bothered us."
ch.clue: Copied from Grandfather's old book, March 1891
ch.q: What does the pencil note on page 55 reveal?
o: The journal was stolen from the grandfather's house
The writer was named A.A. and lived in 1816
The book was written by a famous author in 1891
The journal is a later copy of an older book
The harvest of 1891 was better than the harvest of 1816
ch.hint: Sayfa 55'in kenarındaki kurşun kalem notunda "Büyükbabamın eski kitabından kopyalandı, Mart 1891" yazıyor. Bu not günlüğün ne olduğunu gösteriyor?
ch.why: Not, günlüğün 1816'daki özgün kitap değil, 1891'de bir torun tarafından eski bir kitaptan yapılmış bir kopya olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: In the museum's small meeting room, Amira explained her findings to the director and to the schoolteacher's daughter, who had come from the city. "The journal is not what the first page says," she said gently. "The paper dates from about 1890. The note in pencil shows that A.A., probably a granddaughter or a grandson of Thomas Ashby, copied the text from an older book in March 1891. The original has not survived."
The daughter's face fell. "So it is a fake," she said quietly. "Then it is worth nothing."

"No," said Amira. "It is not a fake. A forgery wants to deceive. This one has a note that says exactly what it is. It is a family copy, made with love by a person who wanted to preserve the words of an ancestor. And that is valuable in another way. Without that copy, we would not know about Thomas Ashby at all. The text it contains is probably a faithful record of a fisherman's life in the year 1816, even if the book itself is a later one."

She asked the museum's director whether it could be displayed with an honest label. He agreed. On the card in the glass case, they wrote: Copy made in 1891 of the lost journal of Thomas Ashby, 1816. Donated by the family.
ch.clue: It is not a fake. A forgery wants to deceive
ch.q: Why does Amira say that the journal is not a fake?
o: It does not try to deceive: it openly says it is a copy
It was written by Thomas Ashby himself in 1816
The paper is exactly as old as the first page says
The family has proved that it is a valuable original
The museum has decided to buy it at a good price
ch.hint: Amira'ya göre sahtecilik, kandırmak ister. Bu günlükte ise kopya olduğunu söyleyen bir not var. Bu fark neden önemli?
ch.why: Günlük kimseyi kandırmaya çalışmıyordu; bir kopya olduğunu açıkça söyleyen bir not taşıyordu ve bu yüzden sahte değil, aile kopyasıydı.

outro: Günlük 1816'nın değil, yaklaşık 1890'ın ürünüydü; sahte değil, bir torunun kopyasıydı. Amira şunu söyledi: eski görünen her şey eski değildir, ama kopya olması da onu değersiz yapmaz.

title: The Failed Cake
hero: Dr. Ilan Voss ve asistanı Dana
intro: Bir okul kantininde pişirilen kekler iki hafta üst üste sönük ve yoğun çıkıyor. Dr. Ilan Voss ile asistanı Dana, tarifi, kabartma tozunu ve fırın sıcaklığını bilimsel bir deney gibi sınayarak nedenini arıyor.

text: The school canteen at Hartley Primary had a famous lemon cake, and the cook, Mrs. Rudd, had baked it every Friday for fifteen years. The children loved it. But for two weeks in a row, the cakes had come out of the oven small, flat, and heavy, like a sweet brick. The children politely left them on their plates, and Mrs. Rudd, who was upset, phoned the university, where her nephew Dana worked as a research assistant.

Dana brought Dr. Ilan Voss to the kitchen on a Thursday afternoon. Ilan, a calm man with round glasses, put on an apron and looked at the ingredients on the table. "Mrs. Rudd," he said, "has anything changed in the recipe?"
"Nothing," she answered at once. "Same flour, same sugar, same eggs, same lemons. I make the same cake in the same oven, at the same temperature."

"Then we should do this as an experiment," said Ilan. "It is a simple one, if we are careful. There are five main things which could affect a cake: the flour, the eggs, the butter, the raising agent, and the oven. We will bake small cakes, but we will change only one thing at a time, and keep all the others exactly the same."
Dana opened his notebook. "That way," he said, "when a cake is good, we know exactly why."
ch.clue: we will change only one thing at a time
ch.q: Why will Ilan change only one ingredient at a time?
o: To be sure which change causes the difference
To follow the old recipe from fifteen years ago
To keep the children from seeing the failed cakes
To make the experiment faster than a normal bake
To use fewer ingredients in each small cake
ch.hint: Ilan beş olası nedeni sayıyor ve her seferinde yalnızca birini değiştirmek istiyor. Bu yöntem hangi soruya cevap verir?
ch.why: Her seferinde yalnızca bir şey değiştirirsek, sonucun hangi değişiklikten kaynaklandığını kesin olarak anlarız.

text: They started with the two easiest checks. Dana put a small thermometer inside the oven, set the dial at 180 degrees, and waited ten minutes. The thermometer showed 178. "A very small difference," said Ilan. "Cakes do not mind two degrees. The oven is not the problem."

Next, they tested the flour. Mrs. Rudd took out the big bag she had used for the last month, and Dana opened a new packet from the supermarket. They baked two small cakes in two identical tins, one with each flour, with the same amounts of everything else and the same time in the oven. Mrs. Rudd watched through the glass door, her hands twisted in her apron.

After thirty minutes, Ilan took out the cakes and put them side by side on the table. Both had risen only a little, and both were dense and pale in the middle. Dana measured them with a ruler. "The cake with the old flour is 3.1 centimetres high," he said. "The one with the new flour is 3.2. Practically identical."

"So it is not the flour," said Ilan. "And it is not the oven. We have crossed two things from the list." He looked at Mrs. Rudd. "Tell me about your raising agent, the baking powder. Where do you keep it?"
"On the shelf above the sink," she said. "Near the steam of the kettle."
ch.clue: Practically identical
ch.q: What have the first two tests shown?
o: Mrs. Rudd has been using the wrong recipe
The oven is much too hot for the small cakes
Neither the oven nor the flour is responsible for the flat cakes
The thermometer in the oven was broken
The new flour makes a taller cake than the old flour
ch.hint: Fırın 180 yerine 178 derece gösterdi, iki farklı un da neredeyse aynı yükseklikte kek verdi. Bu iki sonuç neyi dışarıda bırakıyor?
ch.why: Fırının sıcaklığı doğruydu ve eski ile yeni un neredeyse aynı sonucu verdi; bunlar sorunun nedeni değildi.

text: Ilan took the tin of baking powder from the shelf. It was an old tin, with a rusty rim, and the label was half washed away by steam. "How long have you had this?" he asked. Mrs. Rudd thought. "More than a year," she said. "I only use a small spoon in each cake, so it lasts a long time."

"Baking powder works because it contains a chemical that reacts with water and with heat to make bubbles of gas," said Ilan. "These bubbles make the cake rise. But if the powder absorbs moisture from the air before it goes into the cake, the reaction happens slowly in the tin, and the gas escapes. By the time you use it, there is little left."

He gave Dana a clean glass and a spoon. "A simple test," he said. "A teaspoon of baking powder in a half cup of hot water. If it is fresh, it will fizz strongly at once." Dana poured the hot water, added a spoonful from Mrs. Rudd's tin, and they watched. A few weak bubbles appeared on the surface and died.
Then Dana tried the same with a new tin from the shop. The water foamed and rose almost to the rim of the glass.
"There is our answer," said Ilan quietly. "The old powder is nearly dead."
ch.clue: A few weak bubbles appeared on the surface and died
ch.q: What does the glass test show about Mrs. Rudd's baking powder?
o: It is perfectly fine and the cause is somewhere else
It is stronger than the new baking powder
It reacts too quickly and burns the cake
It contains a different chemical from the shop's powder
It has lost most of its power to make bubbles
ch.hint: Eski kabartma tozu sıcak suda sadece birkaç zayıf kabarcık verdi, yenisi ise köpürdü. Bu fark eski tozun durumu hakkında ne söylüyor?
ch.why: Eski kabartma tozu sıcak suda yalnızca birkaç zayıf kabarcık verdi; gaz üretme gücünü büyük ölçüde kaybetmişti.

text: But Ilan was a careful scientist, and he did not want to stop with a single test. "A glass of water is evidence," he said, "but the proof is the cake." Dana mixed two batches of batter, identical in every way: the same flour, the same eggs, the same lemons, the same amounts. The only difference was the raising agent: in one bowl, two teaspoons of the old powder, in the other, two teaspoons of the new. They baked both in the same oven, on the same shelf, for the same time.

When the timer rang, Dana opened the oven door and made a small noise of surprise. The cake with the new powder had risen high and golden, with a dome in the middle, a full two centimetres taller than the other. The cake with the old powder was flat and dense, exactly like the ones from the canteen.
Mrs. Rudd threw the old tin into the bin with great energy. "Fifteen years," she said, "and I never thought of it. I will write the date on every tin from now on."
"A good idea," said Ilan. "And a bonus: you can use the same test at home. Hot water, a spoon of powder. If it foams, you are safe."
On Friday, the children of Hartley Primary ate every crumb of the lemon cake.
ch.clue: The only difference was the raising agent
ch.q: Why is the second baking experiment stronger evidence than the glass test?
o: It was done by the school cook and not the scientist
Two identical cakes differing only in the powder gave different results
It showed that the old oven works better than a new one
It used a larger quantity of lemons and flour
It was repeated for fifteen years with the same powder
ch.hint: İki hamurun her şeyi aynı, yalnızca kabartma tozu farklıydı ve sonuçlar da farklı çıktı. Bu düzen neden bir bardaktaki testten daha güçlü kanıt?
ch.why: İki kek yalnızca kabartma tozu bakımından farklıydı ve sonuçları da farklı çıktı; bu, nedenin toz olduğunu doğrudan gösteriyordu.

outro: Sorun, bir yıl önce açılmış ve nemle ıslanmış kabartma tozundaydı. Yeni kutuyla keklerin hepsi kabardı. Ilan şunu yazdı: bir deneyde aynı anda yalnızca bir şeyi değiştirirsen, neyin işe yaradığını bilirsin.

title: The Anonymous Letter
hero: Muhabir Jonas Reid ve fotoğrafçı Ellie
intro: Kingsbridge Daily'ye imzasız bir mektup geliyor: belediye başkanının, bir inşaat şirketinden hediye aldığını iddia ediyor. Jonas Reid ile Ellie, mektubu yayımlamadan önce her iddiayı doğrulamaya çalışıyor.

text: The envelope was on Jonas's desk on Tuesday morning, among the usual advertisements and invitations. It was white, with a first-class stamp and a London postmark, and it had no sender's address. Inside was a single typed sheet, signed with the words A concerned citizen.

Jonas read it twice, then called Ellie, who was drinking her coffee at the next desk. "Listen to this," he said. "The mayor of Kingsbridge, Mr. Frost, has received an expensive present from Brightside Construction, the company that has just won the contract to build the new sports centre. The present is a holiday for two in Spain, paid by the company. The contract was awarded one week after the holiday. This is corruption, and the town has a right to know."

Ellie whistled. "That is a very serious accusation," she said. "Who is the writer?" "I have no idea," said Jonas. "No name, no phone, nothing. The letter gives no proof at all. It does not name the hotel, it does not give the date of the holiday, and it does not say how the writer knows."

Mrs. Cole, the editor, came to the door, having heard the end of the conversation. "Do not print a word," she said, "until you can prove it. If it is true, it is the biggest story of the year. If it is false, we could be sued, and we would destroy a man's reputation."
"Where do I begin?" asked Jonas. "With the facts that can be checked," said Mrs. Cole.
ch.clue: The letter gives no proof at all
ch.q: What is the main problem with the anonymous letter?
o: It does not mention the name of the mayor
It makes a serious accusation without giving any proof
It was posted from London instead of Kingsbridge
It is too long for the paper to print in full
It was typed on a computer and not written by hand
ch.hint: Mektup ciddi bir suçlama yapıyor ama otel, tarih, kaynak gibi hiçbir kanıt vermiyor. Editör bu durumda ne yapmamasını söylüyor?
ch.why: Mektup çok ciddi bir suçlama yapıyordu ama hiçbir kanıt vermiyordu; bu yüzden doğrulanmadan yayımlanamazdı.

text: Jonas wrote a list on a sheet of paper, splitting the letter into separate claims, each of which could be tested. First: Brightside Construction won the contract for the sports centre. Second: the contract was awarded on a certain date. Third: the mayor took a holiday in Spain. Fourth: the company paid for it.

The first two were easy, because public contracts are public documents. At the town hall's website, Jonas found the minutes of the council meeting. Brightside Construction had indeed won the sports centre contract, and the decision was taken on the 14th of June. The second claim was true. The third could be checked on the mayor's own social media pages, which showed a smiling Mr. Frost on a beach, with a date: 21st of May.

"So he did go on holiday," said Ellie, "and the contract was awarded three weeks later, not one week." Jonas wrote the dates beside the claims. "The letter said a week. It is wrong in that detail. That does not mean that it is false in the rest. But it shows that the writer is not very exact."

"The fourth claim is the real question," said Ellie. "Who paid for the hotel?" Jonas underlined it twice. "That is the one we have no way to check. And without it, the other three are just a man's holiday and a company's contract."
ch.clue: the contract was awarded three weeks later, not one week
ch.q: What have Jonas and Ellie found out so far?
o: The dates in the letter are all exactly right
The company did not win the sports centre contract
Everything in the letter has been fully proved
Three claims are partly true, but nothing yet shows who paid for the holiday
The mayor never went on holiday to Spain
ch.hint: Jonas dört iddiayı sıraladı. Hangileri doğrulanabildi ve doğrulanması en önemli olan, yani otelin parasını kimin ödediği sorusu çözüldü mü?
ch.why: Sözleşmenin kazanılması ve tatilin yapılması doğrulandı, ama tatilin parasını kimin ödediği hâlâ bilinmiyordu.

text: For the fourth claim, Jonas needed somebody who knew. He phoned the town hall's press office and asked, formally, whether the mayor had paid for the holiday himself. The answer came by email two hours later, polite and very short: The Mayor's private holiday is a private matter and not a subject for the press.

"That is not a denial," said Ellie. "It is not an answer either," said Jonas. He phoned Brightside Construction, and a spokeswoman told him, in a cool voice, that the company never commented on its hospitality. It was not a denial, either.

On Thursday, Jonas tried another approach. He searched the register of members' interests, a public document where every councillor must list gifts above a certain value. The mayor's page for the year was open to anyone who asked. Under the heading Gifts and Hospitality, there was one entry, dated 3 May: Accommodation, Costa del Sol, 6 nights, from Brightside Construction Ltd. Estimated value: £1,400.

Jonas photocopied the page and put it on Ellie's desk. "He declared it," he said. "It is in the public record, signed by him." Ellie read the line twice. "So the letter was right about the gift," she said, "but is the gift a crime, if he declared it?"
ch.clue: Estimated value: £1,400
ch.q: What does the register of interests show?
o: The mayor himself declared the gift from Brightside Construction
The mayor hid the gift and never wrote it down
The gift was worth more than ten thousand pounds
The company denied that it had paid for anything
The press office confirmed that the holiday was free
ch.hint: Çıkar kayıt defterinde belediye başkanı kendi imzasıyla neyi bildirmiş? Bu bilgi gizli bir şey mi, yoksa herkesin görebileceği bir kayıt mı?
ch.why: Başkan, tatili Brightside Construction'ın ödediğini kamuya açık kayıt defterine kendisi yazmış ve imzalamıştı.

text: Jonas wrote the article on Friday morning, and Mrs. Cole read it standing at his desk. "The facts are clear," he said. "A company that was awarded a public contract paid for the mayor's holiday three weeks before it was awarded. He declared it, which is correct. But the timing is a legitimate public question, and the council should explain why the mayor took part in the decision to give the contract to a company that had given him a present."

"And the letter?" asked Mrs. Cole. "I do not quote it," said Jonas. "The letter said a week, and it was three. It said corruption, and I have no proof of any agreement. I only report what is on the record."

The headline was cautious: Mayor declared holiday paid by firm that later won £6m contract. Beneath it, Jonas had put the mayor's reply, which arrived at five o'clock: he had taken no part in the vote, and had left the room, as the minutes confirmed.

"It is smaller than the letter promised," said Ellie, looking at the front page. "It is true," said Mrs. Cole. "That is why people will trust it." On Saturday, the councillors announced that they would hold a public review of the awarding procedure.
ch.clue: I only report what is on the record
ch.q: Why does Jonas not quote the anonymous letter in his article?
o: The letter was written in a very bad style
The editor does not like anonymous writers
Its claims were not exact and he could not prove them
It had been sent to a rival newspaper first
The mayor asked him not to use the letter
ch.hint: Mektup bir haftadan söz ediyordu ama gerçek üç haftaydı ve yolsuzluğu kanıtlayacak bir anlaşma yoktu. Jonas haberi neye dayandırdı?
ch.why: Mektupta kesin olmayan ve kanıtlanamayan iddialar vardı; Jonas yalnızca resmî kayıtlarda bulunan, doğrulanmış gerçekleri yazdı.

outro: İddianın yarısı doğruydu, yarısı yanlıştı. Gazete yalnızca doğrulanan kısmı yazdı. Jonas şunu söyledi: bir haber, kaynağın ne kadar emin olduğuna değil, ne kadar kanıt sunduğuna göre değerlendirilir.

title: The Missing Trout
hero: Park korucusu Wren Calder ve köpeği Bracken
intro: Vadideki derede her yıl yumurtlayan alabalıklar bu sonbahar ortadan kayboldu. Wren Calder ile Bracken, su sıcaklığını, akıntıyı ve nehrin yukarısındaki değişiklikleri izleyerek balıkların nerede olduğunu arıyor.

text: Every October, when the days grew short and the water cold, the trout of Alder Brook swam up from the lower river to lay their eggs in the clean gravel beds near the old stone bridge. Ranger Wren Calder had counted the nests for nine years. She knew the exact places, a series of pale oval patches on the riverbed, where the fish had cleared the stones with their tails.

This year, on the twelfth of October, she and Bracken walked along the bank in their rubber boots and found nothing. The gravel was clean and grey, with no pale patches at all. She walked the whole length of the stretch, four hundred metres, bending down and looking in the clear water, while Bracken drank noisily from the stream.

On the next Monday, she walked it again. Still nothing. By the end of the second week, she was sure. "In nine years, I have never had fewer than fourteen nests," she told Bracken, sitting on the wall of the bridge. "This year, zero."

"What could make a whole population of fish disappear in a summer?" she asked, half to herself. She counted the possibilities on her fingers. They could have died, from pollution or disease. They could have been caught by anglers. They could have moved elsewhere. Or something could be stopping them from arriving.
She took out her phone and began to write a list of checks.
ch.clue: This year, zero
ch.q: What problem does Wren discover in October?
o: The trout have built their nests in the wrong place
The gravel beds have been covered with mud
There are no trout nests at all in the usual gravel
Fewer than fourteen nests were counted this year
The river has become too warm for the fish
ch.hint: Wren dokuz yıl boyunca en az on dört yuva saymış. Bu yıl iki hafta yürüdükten sonra kaç yuva buluyor?
ch.why: Wren, her yıl en az on dört yuva bulunan çakıllı yatakta bu yıl hiç yuva bulamıyordu.

text: Wren started with the most obvious possibility, pollution. She took samples of the river water at three places, and the laboratory in town tested them for chemicals and oxygen. The results arrived by email on Thursday. The water was clean, rich in oxygen, with no trace of chemicals. The temperature was nine degrees, perfect for the fish.

The second possibility was fishing. She phoned the local anglers' club, and the secretary, an old man called Mr. Pike, who had fished in the valley for forty years, told her that the club had a rule: no fishing in Alder Brook in October, to protect the breeding fish. "Nobody breaks it," he said. "Not in my club." She checked the register of licences, and there were no reports of any large catch in the past months.

"So the fish did not die and were not caught," she said to Bracken that evening, in her kitchen. "Then either they went away, or they never arrived." She drew a map of the river on the back of an envelope. The brook flowed from the hills in the north, through the old bridge, and joined the big river a few kilometres south. The trout lived in the big river for most of the year, and swam up the brook to breed. "They must travel upstream from the south," she said. "If something stops them, we would find a lot of fish waiting somewhere downstream."
On Friday morning, she put on her boots and began to walk the brook from the bottom.
ch.clue: either they went away, or they never arrived
ch.q: What has Wren found out about the pollution and the fishing?
o: The laboratory has lost the samples she sent
The temperature is much too cold for breeding fish
The water is polluted and the fish have died
The anglers took all of the trout from the brook
The water is clean and no one has been fishing the breeding fish
ch.hint: Laboratuvar sonuçları su hakkında ne dedi ve olta kulübü balık avı hakkında ne söyledi? İkisi de balıkların ölümünü açıklıyor mu?
ch.why: Su temiz ve oksijence zengindi, kulüp de Ekim'de avlanmanın yasak olduğunu söylüyordu; yani ne kirlilik ne avcılık balıkların yokluğunu açıklıyordu.

text: Wren walked upstream from the confluence with the big river, one slow step after another, with Bracken splashing ahead. After about two kilometres, the brook passed under a concrete road bridge, and just above it she heard a sound she did not know: the roar of water falling over a wall.

It was a new structure, a low wall of grey concrete across the whole width of the brook, with a small gate in the middle. The water poured over the top in a thin sheet, and on the other side, it fell to a deep pool. The wall was about eighty centimetres high. A metal sign on a post read: Flow measurement station. Installed July. Gate to be opened for fish passage in autumn.

Wren leaned over the edge of the pool, and her heart began to beat faster. In the dark water, hundreds of fish were swimming slowly in circles, with their silver bellies catching the light. Trout, hundreds of them, all packed together below the wall, trying again and again to jump up and failing, their bodies hitting the concrete.
"There you are," she said softly. "All of you. Waiting." The gate was closed with a padlock. Someone had installed a wall in July and forgotten the autumn opening.
ch.clue: Gate to be opened for fish passage in autumn
ch.q: Where are the trout, and why are they there?
o: In a deep pool made by the laboratory
Below a new wall, which blocks their way upstream
In the big river, because the brook is too shallow
At the old stone bridge, near their old nests
Above the wall, where they are safe from the anglers
ch.hint: Wren yeni bir beton duvar ve kapının önünde yüzlerce balık görüyor. Balıklar neden orada toplanmış olabilir? Duvarın üzerindeki tabelaya da bak.
ch.why: Balıklar, Temmuz'da yapılan yeni duvarın altında toplanmıştı; duvar, sonbaharda açılması gereken kapağı kilitli olduğu için yukarı çıkmalarını engelliyordu.

text: Wren photographed the wall, the sign, the padlock and the crowd of fish, and sent them to the river authority with a short message: Urgent. Trout cannot pass. Please open the gate. She did not wait for an answer. By eleven o'clock, she was in the authority's office in town, where a technician named Mr. Lowe, red with embarrassment, found the key in a drawer.

"The measurement team installed the station in July," he said. "They were supposed to open the gate on the first of October and they forgot. I am very sorry." He drove with her to the brook, and together they climbed down to the wall. The padlock was rusty, and he needed some oil. When the gate swung open, with a loud metallic noise, a strong current of water rushed through the gap.

For a minute nothing happened. Then, one by one, the trout began to turn their heads towards the opening. A large silver one, perhaps two kilos, shot through the gap like an arrow, followed by a second, then a third, then a whole line of them, climbing the current towards the gravel beds.
Wren counted them quietly with her clicker. "Thirty-two," she said, when the stream finally slowed. Then she smiled at Mr. Lowe. "And tomorrow," she said, "I will count the nests."
ch.clue: like an arrow
ch.q: What happens when the gate is opened?
o: The trout wait in the pool until the next morning
The wall breaks and the pool empties completely
The water level falls and the fish are left in the pool
The trout swim through the gap towards the upstream gravel beds
The fish swim back to the big river and leave
ch.hint: Kapı açılıp güçlü bir su akıntısı geçmeye başlayınca balıklar hangi yöne dönüyor ve nereye gidiyor?
ch.why: Kapı açılınca balıklar boşluktan geçip üst taraftaki çakıl yataklarına doğru yüzmeye başladı.

outro: Balıklar, yukarıdaki bir baraj kapağının açılmamasından dolayı geçemedikleri yerde bekliyordu. Kapak açıldı ve balıklar yumurtlamaya geldi. Wren şunu yazdı: doğada kaybolan bir şey bazen sadece yolu kapalı olandır.

title: The Label Mix-Up
hero: Küratör Hugo Laurent ve güvenlik görevlisi Mina
intro: Müzedeki iki vazo, açılıştan sonra yanlış etiketlerle sergileniyor. Biri Çin'e, diğeri Yunanistan'a ait olmalı. Hugo Laurent ile Mina, kayıt defterine ve vazoların kendisine bakarak hangi etiketin hangisine ait olduğunu çözüyor.

text: On the afternoon after the opening of the new exhibition, a retired teacher stopped Mina, the night guard, in the corridor of the City Museum. She had come early to see the ancient vases, and she was puzzled. "Excuse me," she said. "I am not an expert, but I think that two of your labels are the wrong way round.
