The black vase with the running figures says it is Chinese, from the Tang dynasty. And the blue one with dragons says it is Greek. They look the opposite to me."

Mina looked at the two vases in their glass cases. The teacher was right. The black one, with pale orange figures of men running, a pattern which Mina had seen in a book about Greece, was labelled Chinese porcelain jar, Tang dynasty, c. 700 AD. The blue and white one, with a coiled dragon on the side, was labelled Greek amphora, c. 500 BC.

She thanked the teacher and went to find Hugo Laurent, the curator, who was in his office with the catalogue. He listened with a growing frown. "Two labels in the wrong places," he said. "On the opening day. That is a very bad mistake." He took off his jacket. "But before we change them, we must find out which is the error: the labels, or our ideas about the vases. I do not want to make a second mistake while correcting the first."
"How do we know?" asked Mina. Hugo took the thick register from the shelf. "Every object has a number," he said.
ch.clue: we must find out which is the error
ch.q: Why does Hugo not simply swap the labels immediately?
o: He does not trust the teacher's opinion about the vases
He has no time because the museum is about to close
He thinks that the labels are right and the vases are wrong
He wants to be sure that the swap is correct first
He prefers to ask the director what he should do
ch.hint: Hugo etiketlerin değişmesi gerektiğini düşünüyor ama hemen değiştirmek istemiyor. Neden? İkinci bir hata yapmaktan kaçınmak için ne yapması gerekir?
ch.why: Hugo, düzeltme sırasında ikinci bir hata yapmamak için önce hangi bilginin doğru olduğundan emin olmak istedi.

text: The register was a big book with a cloth cover, where every object in the museum was recorded when it arrived: a number, a description, the date, and the donor. Hugo turned the pages until he found the vases. There were two entries on the same page. Entry 1187: Greek amphora, black-figure style, 6th century BC, height 38 cm, donated by Sir Alfred Penn. Entry 1188: Chinese jar, blue-and-white, Tang period, height 24 cm, donated by Miss Clara Wu.

"Look at the heights," said Mina. She measured the black vase through the glass with a small ruler. "It is about thirty-eight centimetres," she said. "And the blue one is about twenty-four." Hugo nodded slowly. "So the register says that the tall black one is the Greek amphora, and the small blue one is the Chinese jar. It agrees with what the teacher thought, and with the vases themselves."

"Then the labels have been swapped," said Mina. "But how? They were printed correctly, weren't they?" Hugo turned to the end of the entry and read a note in a small hand: Labels printed 2 May. Delivered to the gallery staff.
"We shall have to ask the gallery staff how they put them up," said Hugo. "But first, let us check one thing more. A register can have mistakes, too."
ch.clue: Entry 1187
ch.q: What does the register show about the two vases?
o: The tall black vase is Greek and the small blue one is Chinese
Both vases were donated by the same person
The register has no information about the vases
Both vases are Greek but from different centuries
The tall black vase is Chinese and the small blue one is Greek
ch.hint: Kayıt defterine göre 1187 numaralı Yunan amforası 38 cm ve siyah figürlü, 1188 numaralı Çin vazosu ise 24 cm ve mavi-beyaz. Hangi vazo hangi ülkeye ait?
ch.why: Kayıt defterine göre uzun siyah vazo Yunan amforasıydı, küçük mavi vazo ise Çin vazosuydu; etiketler yer değiştirmişti.

text: Hugo did not quite trust the register, and he had a good reason. In the previous decade, a new assistant had once copied several numbers wrongly. He wanted a second source. On the shelf was an older book, the donors' letters, in a grey file. He found the letter of Sir Alfred Penn, dated 1952. In his careful handwriting, Sir Alfred had written about his gift: I am delighted to give to the museum my beloved black-figure amphora, which my father brought from Athens in 1911.
Then he found Miss Wu's letter, from 1968. It described her donation as a small blue jar of the Tang period, bought by her grandfather in Shanghai.

"Two independent sources," said Mina. "The register and the donors' own letters. They agree." Hugo closed the file with a sigh of relief. "Now we are sure. The labels have been swapped, not the vases. The tall black vase from Athens must have the Greek label, and the small blue jar from Shanghai the Chinese one."

They went together to the gallery and opened the first case with a key. Hugo carefully removed the label and put the other in its place. The teacher, who had come back with a friend, saw them and smiled. "Thank you," she said. "I knew they were wrong."
"You were right," Hugo said. "You see, it is useful to have visitors who look carefully."
ch.clue: Two independent sources
ch.q: Why does Hugo look for a second source?
o: The first source did not give the height of the vases
The donors' letters are more beautiful than the register
A register alone can contain a mistake, so he wants confirmation
The teacher told him to read the letters
The register was written by a person he does not like
ch.hint: Hugo kayıt defterinin de hata içerebileceğini söylüyor ve donör mektuplarına bakıyor. Neden ikinci bir kaynağa ihtiyaç duyuyor?
ch.why: Hugo, kayıt defterinin de yanlış olabileceğini düşünüyordu ve bilgiyi bağımsız bir ikinci kaynakla doğrulamak istedi.

text: Next morning, Hugo asked the two gallery assistants to come to his office. They were young, and they were frightened. "I am not here to punish anyone," he said. "I want to understand how it happened, so that it will not happen again."

The first assistant, a tall boy called Nick, explained slowly. "The labels were delivered in a box on Friday evening, in a pile, with no order. We had a list that gave the order of the cases in the gallery, but it was a long list. We put them up late at night." The second, a girl named Priya, added: "The labels do not have object numbers. They only have the name and the description. When we put them up, we looked at the vases, and thought that the dark vase was too old to be the Greek one, so we assumed that..."

"You made an assumption," said Hugo. "It was reasonable. But it was wrong." He took a pen and wrote on his pad. "The mistake is not yours alone. A label with no number on it cannot be checked. From now on, every label will have the register number printed in a corner, and you will check it against the case before you put it up."
He looked up and smiled. "And next time, ask the register, not the vase."
ch.clue: A label with no number on it cannot be checked
ch.q: What change does Hugo decide to make?
o: The labels will be printed in a different colour
The museum will use only the vases' real names
The register will be replaced with a computer list
The assistants will no longer put up the labels
Every label will have the register number, so it can be checked
ch.hint: Etiketlerde nesne numarası yoktu ve bu yüzden kontrol edilemiyordu. Hugo bu hatanın tekrarlanmaması için ne yapıyor?
ch.why: Hugo, her etiketin köşesine kayıt numarasının basılmasına karar verdi, böylece etiket ilgili nesneyle karşılaştırılabilecekti.

outro: Etiketler yer değiştirdi ve düzeltildi. Hugo, kayıtlarda her eserin bir numarası olması gerektiğini ve etiketlere de aynı numaranın yazılması gerektiğini söyledi.

title: The Clockmaker's Workshop
hero: Oyun testçileri Zoe ve Max
intro: Zoe ve Max, bir saatçinin eski atölyesine kilitli. Duvarda durmuş saatler, bir mantık bulmacası ve dişli çarklar var. Her ipucu bir sonraki kilidin anahtarı. Kalan süre elli beş dakika.

text: The door of the clockmaker's workshop closed behind Zoe and Max with a soft, wooden click. A single lamp lit a long room full of tools, springs and little brass wheels, and on the wall hung five clocks, all of them stopped. Above the door, a small screen showed the time: 55:00, and the numbers began to fall.

"Five clocks," said Max, reading the little cards under each. "Each one shows a different time: 3:10, 5:40, 7:25, 9:05, and 11:50. And there is a note: The clockmaker stopped these clocks one by one during a single day, from the first to the last. Put them in the order in which he stopped them. The time of the last one opens the door."

Zoe stood in front of the wall. "But the clocks are hanging in the wrong places," she said. "And a clock face does not say whether it is morning or evening. We need the story." She found a folded paper in a drawer, with five short lines. "He could not sleep, and stopped the first clock in the dark, before dawn. He stopped the second when the milkman came at first light. He stopped the third when he sat down to supper. He stopped the fourth when the tower bell rang nine times. And the last one he stopped at the end of the day, just before midnight."
Max took a pencil. "Five events," he said, "and five times. We have to match each time with the right event."
ch.clue: stopped the first clock in the dark, before dawn
ch.q: What is the main task in the first puzzle?
o: Repairing the five clocks so that they all work again
Counting how many times the tower bell rang in a day
Finding the one clock which shows the correct time now
Adding up all the times shown on the five stopped clocks
Matching each clock to an event, to find the order in which they stopped
ch.hint: Not, saatleri durdukları sıraya dizmeni istiyor. Saat yüzü sabah mı akşam mı olduğunu söylemiyor; bunu anlamak için neye bakmalısın?
ch.why: Bulmaca, her saati hikâyedeki bir olayla eşleştirip durdukları sıraya koymayı istiyordu.

text: They went through the lines one at a time. Before dawn, in the dark: that had to be an early hour such as ten past three. The milkman at first light: the sun rises early in summer, so the time was twenty to six. Supper: an ordinary evening meal, at twenty-five past seven. The bell rang nine times at about nine o'clock, so the clock which showed five past nine belonged there. And the end of the day, just before midnight, was ten to twelve.

"They fit perfectly," said Max, writing the times in a column. "3:10, then 5:40, then 7:25, then 9:05, then 11:50. Each is later than the one before it. If we had put 7:25 in the morning, the supper line would not make sense, and the milkman would come after supper."

Zoe took the clocks down from the wall, one at a time, and hung them in the frames from left to right. As the last frame filled, the five clock faces lit up with a faint green glow, and a small drawer slid out below the final clock with a ratchet noise.
"The last clock shows ten to twelve," said Zoe. "That is the time that opens the door, but we need something more. Look inside the drawer."
ch.clue: just before midnight, was ten to twelve
ch.q: Which clock stopped first, and which stopped last?
o: First: 9:05. Last: 7:25
First: 3:10. Last: 11:50
First: 5:40. Last: 9:05
First: 7:25. Last: 5:40
First: 11:50. Last: 3:10
ch.hint: Hikâye şafaktan önce başlıyor ve gece yarısından önce bitiyor. Bu iki olaya uyan saatler hangileri?
ch.why: İlk saat şafaktan önceki 3:10, son saat ise gece yarısından önceki 11:50'ydi.

text: Inside the drawer lay three gear wheels of different sizes, with numbers of teeth printed on a tag: 12, 18, and 30. A card was tied to them: The shaft of the clock needs a wheel that turns exactly once while the small 12-tooth wheel turns five times. Place the correct wheel.
"A gear problem," said Max, who loved them. "When two gears mesh, the same number of teeth must pass on both wheels. A small wheel turns fast, and a large one turns slowly."

Zoe took the pencil. "The small wheel has 12 teeth and turns five times. That is 5 times 12, so sixty teeth pass. The big wheel must also let sixty teeth pass while it turns once. So it must have sixty teeth." She counted the numbers on the tag with the point of the pencil: 12, 18, 30. "None of them is sixty."

"Maybe the tag is wrong," said Max. He took each wheel and counted the teeth around the rim, patiently, with his finger. The tag was right. Twelve, eighteen, thirty. Zoe looked at the screen above the door, where the numbers read 31:15. "Then the wheel we need is not in the drawer," she said. "The drawer only gives us the rule."
ch.clue: so sixty teeth pass
ch.q: How many teeth must the correct wheel have?
o: Seventeen
Twelve
Thirty
Sixty
Eighteen
ch.hint: Küçük 12 dişli çark beş tur atıyor. Büyük çark bir turda aynı sayıda diş geçirmeli. Beş kere on iki kaç eder?
ch.why: Küçük çark beş turda 5 × 12 = 60 diş geçirdiği için doğru çarkın 60 dişi olmalıydı.

text: Max looked around the long room again, this time not at the walls but at the shelves. On the highest one, behind a row of dusty tools and a jar of screws, stood a large brass wheel the size of a plate. He climbed on a stool and took it down. It was heavy and cold, and the teeth around the rim were tiny.

Zoe counted them with her finger, row by row, while Max held the lamp, and she put a pencil mark on the first tooth so that she would not count it twice. "Sixty," she said, when she reached the mark where she had started. "Exactly sixty."

They fitted the wheel on the shaft of the great clock in the corner. It slipped into place with a deep, satisfying clunk, and the pendulum began to swing, slowly, with a sound like a heartbeat. A panel opened in the wall, and behind it, a keypad. Zoe typed 1150, the last time on the wall.
The door opened. The numbers over it showed 12:40. "We solved it with twelve minutes left," said Max, "and the key to everything was to read the card, not to trust the tag."
ch.clue: Exactly sixty
ch.q: Where was the correct wheel, and what opened the door?
o: On a high shelf, and the time of the last clock typed on the keypad
Behind the clocks, and the sum of all five times
Inside the pendulum, and the time of the first clock
Under the stool, and the number of the lamp
In the drawer, and the number of teeth on the tag
ch.hint: Zoe ve Max doğru çarkı nerede buldu ve kapıyı açmak için tuş takımına ne yazdılar? Bulmacanın ilk bölümünü hatırla.
ch.why: 60 dişli çark yüksek bir rafta duruyordu ve kapı, son saatin zamanı olan 11:50'nin (1150) girilmesiyle açıldı.

outro: Kapıdaki son çark yerine oturdu ve atölyenin kapısı açıldı. Oyun yöneticisi, iyi bir bulmacanın her zaman tek bir doğru cevabı olduğunu ve bunu bulmanın sabır istediğini söyledi.

title: The Double Booking
hero: Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ve stajyer Sam
intro: Check-in tezgâhında aynı koltuk iki yolcuya birden verilmiş. İkisi de rezervasyon onayını gösteriyor. Dara Mills ile Sam, kayıtlara bakarak hangisinin gerçekten o koltuğu satın aldığını ve diğerine ne yapılacağını çözüyor.

text: It was the busiest Saturday of the summer, and the check-in hall at Heathfield Airport was full of families with big suitcases. At the transfer desk, a man and a woman stood side by side, each holding a phone, and the argument between them had been going on for ten minutes. Dara Mills was called over by a nervous young agent.

"I have a booking confirmation for seat 14A," said the man, a tall, grey-haired traveller called Mr. Evans. "I paid for it three weeks ago." "So did I," said the woman, Ms. Torres, shaking her phone. "I booked it last month. And look, I have a confirmation with my name on it, and the same seat number."

Dara looked at both screens. They did look identical: the same airline logo, the same flight number, the same date. Only the names were different. "Both of you have a confirmation for seat 14A on flight HA412," she said. "That should not be possible. A seat can be sold to one person only." She turned to Sam, her trainee, who was standing behind her with a notebook. "Sam, go to the system and look up the seat. And ask them to be patient."
"There is only one seat 14A," said Ms. Torres, "and I will not give it up." Mr. Evans crossed his arms. "Neither will I," he said.
ch.clue: That should not be possible
ch.q: Why is Dara surprised when she sees the two confirmations?
o: A seat can be sold to only one person
Both of them booked at the same time
The names on both are exactly the same
The two passengers are on different flights
The confirmations are not printed on paper
ch.hint: İki yolcu da aynı uçuş ve aynı koltuk için onay gösteriyor. Dara'ya göre bir koltuk kaç kişiye satılabilir?
ch.why: Bir koltuk yalnızca bir kişiye satılabilir; iki onayın aynı koltuğu göstermesi mümkün olmamalıydı.

text: Sam typed the flight number into the airline's reservation system and opened the seat map. Seat 14A was marked with a small grey square: occupied. He clicked on it. A box opened with a single name: Torres, M. Booking date: 14 June. Ticket status: issued.
"That is Ms. Torres's seat," said Sam. "Her booking is in the system and her ticket has been issued." He looked at the other name. "But Mr. Evans does not appear on this flight at all."

"Let me see," said Dara. She pushed the chair closer and typed the name Evans. A short list came up. "Here is an Evans, booking date 3 July, flight HA412, seat 14A, status: cancelled." She frowned. "It was cancelled? When?" Sam clicked on the line and read the details aloud. "The cancellation was made on 4 July, one day after the booking, with a note: Refunded to the original card. Refund reference RF-83921."

"So Mr. Evans did book 14A," said Dara. "But he cancelled it, and was refunded, the next day. The seat was released and, a month before the flight, it was available again." She looked at the screen with a puzzled expression. "But Ms. Torres had booked it on 14 June, before him. The system gave the same seat to the second person while the first was still there."
"That is a system error," said Sam. "But his booking was cancelled, so his confirmation is no longer valid."
ch.clue: Refunded to the original card
ch.q: What does the reservation system show?
o: Both bookings were cancelled and refunded by the airline
The seat was never sold to either of the passengers
Ms. Torres holds the seat, and Mr. Evans's booking was cancelled and refunded
Mr. Evans holds the seat, and Ms. Torres's ticket was cancelled
Both passengers hold valid tickets for the same seat
ch.hint: Sistemde 14A'nın sahibi kim görünüyor ve Mr. Evans'ın rezervasyonunun durumu ne? İptal ve geri ödeme kaydına dikkat et.
ch.why: Sistemde 14A, düzenlenmiş bir biletle Ms. Torres'e aitti; Mr. Evans'ın rezervasyonu ise ertesi gün iptal edilmiş ve parası iade edilmişti.

text: Dara went back to the desk and explained the findings to the two passengers, as simply and as kindly as she could. Ms. Torres listened with a small smile of relief. Mr. Evans, however, did not move. "That is impossible," he said. "I never cancelled anything. I am going to Madrid for my daughter's wedding."

"Mr. Evans," said Dara, "could you open your emails, please, and look for any message from the airline in July?" He sighed and began scrolling, with his thick fingers. After a minute, he stopped, and his face changed. "There is one, on the fourth of July. Subject: Your booking has been cancelled. I thought it was an advertisement. I did not open it."

"And did you make another booking, Mr. Evans?" asked Dara gently. He thought for a moment, then took out his wallet and found a second printout, with a different reference. "Yes," he said slowly. "On the fifth. My wife told me that the first booking had the wrong date, so I cancelled it on the website and booked another... on this very flight, I think. Another seat." He held the paper towards her. It said: Seat 22C.

"Then you were never on 14A at all," said Dara. "The old confirmation is still on your phone, but the ticket that you actually hold is for 22C. A window seat, I believe?" Mr. Evans stared at the paper, then began to laugh.
ch.clue: Another seat
ch.q: What explains the confusion about seat 14A?
o: Ms. Torres had booked the seat for the wrong flight
The reservation system was broken on the whole flight
The airline gave the seat to a third passenger
Mr. Evans's phone was showing a confirmation from another airline
Mr. Evans cancelled his first booking and then bought seat 22C
ch.hint: Mr. Evans'ın e-postasında 4 Temmuz tarihli bir iptal mesajı ve cüzdanında farklı bir rezervasyon belgesi var. Bu ikinci belgede hangi koltuk yazıyor?
ch.why: Mr. Evans ilk rezervasyonunu iptal edip yeni bir rezervasyon yapmıştı; gerçek bileti 22C içindi ve eski onay telefonunda kalmıştı.

text: Sam printed the boarding passes for both passengers. Ms. Torres received hers with a brilliant smile: Seat 14A. Mr. Evans's showed 22C, and Dara asked the agent at the gate to check that the seat was next to a window, as he had apparently requested. She told him that it was, and it was an exit row, with more space for his long legs.

"I am very sorry that I made such a fuss," said Mr. Evans, rubbing his forehead. "I was so sure." Dara smiled. "It is a common mistake," she said. "An old confirmation can remain on a phone for months, and the email about the cancellation is often taken for an advertisement. There is a lesson in it: before an argument, check the date on the document, not only its look."

When the passengers had gone, Sam closed his notebook. "How did you know to look at the cancellation first?" he asked. "I did not know," said Dara. "I only knew that two confirmations cannot both be right, and that the system keeps a history. When two people disagree, look for the records which are older than their quarrel."
On the way to the gate, Mr. Evans stopped for a moment at the information desk and left a small box of chocolates. The label said: For the lady with the patient face.
ch.clue: check the date on the document
ch.q: What advice does Dara give?
o: Never trust a confirmation printed on paper
Check the dates on the documents before arguing
Always book a window seat for long flights
Ask the airline to give each person a new seat
Delete old emails from the airline immediately
ch.hint: Dara, Mr. Evans'a bir ders olarak ne söylüyor? Belgenin görünüşü mü, yoksa tarihi mi önemli?
ch.why: Dara, tartışmadan önce belgenin yalnızca görünüşüne değil, tarihine bakmak gerektiğini söyledi.

outro: Yolculardan biri aynı biletin iki kez satın alınmış kopyasına sahipti ve para iadesi aldı. Dara şunu söyledi: bir çatışmayı çözmek için önce kimin haklı olduğunu değil, kayıtların ne gösterdiğini bulmalıyız.

title: The Auctioneer's Silence
hero: Dedektif Edmund Crane ve asistanı Tess
intro: Prestijli bir müzayedede, açık artırmaya çıkan nadir bir saatin değeri son anda sebepsizce düştü ve saat çok düşük bir fiyata satıldı. Edmund Crane ile Tess, salondaki sessizliğin ve satıcının davranışlarının ardındaki gerçeği çözmeye çalışıyor.

text: The auction house of Whitcombe & Sons was not a place where strangers were noisy. On the evening of the sale, about eighty people sat on rows of velvet chairs in a hall panelled with dark wood, and a lean auctioneer named Mr. Vane stood at a high desk, with an ivory gavel in his right hand. The fourteenth lot of the evening was a pocket watch, made in Geneva in 1887 by a maker whose name collectors pronounced with a reverent drop of the voice. The catalogue estimated its value at between forty and sixty thousand pounds.

Edmund Crane, who had been invited by the house's owner, Mrs. Whitcombe, to sit in the last row, watched the bidding begin. Vane opened at twenty thousand. A man in the front raised a numbered paddle: twenty-two. A woman on the left replied at once with twenty-five. Then, quite suddenly, the room went quiet. Vane looked around with the patience of a man who had seen many auctions die, repeated the figure, raised his gavel, and, after what Tess, sitting beside Edmund, counted as four slow seconds, brought it down. Sold, for twenty-five thousand pounds, to the lady on the left.

Mrs. Whitcombe came to Edmund's side at the interval, pale, her hands folded tightly. "It was worth twice that," she said. "Perhaps three times. The two people who were bidding for it have each been buying from us for years, and neither stopped by anything but a decision. I have been in this business for thirty years, Mr. Crane, and a room does not fall silent like that without a reason."
Edmund said nothing. He had noticed something about the silence, and he wished to be sure of it first.
ch.clue: a room does not fall silent like that without a reason
ch.q: What is the main reason for Mrs. Whitcombe's concern?
o: The auctioneer was rude to the bidders who sat in the front rows
The watch sold for far less than its likely value, after unusually sudden silence
The catalogue had given a wrong date for the watch's manufacture
Too few people had come to the sale to bid for the watch
The winner of the auction refused to pay the price which she offered
ch.hint: Mrs. Whitcombe saatin tahmin edilen değerin yarısına satıldığını ve oda birdenbire sustuğunu söylüyor. Onu rahatsız eden şey neydi: fiyat mı, salonun aniden susması mı, yoksa ikisi birden mi?
ch.why: Mrs. Whitcombe, saatin tahmin edilen değerinin çok altında, rekabet birdenbire kesilerek satılmasından rahatsızdı.

text: When the sale was over, Edmund asked Mr. Vane for the bidding record of lot fourteen. Auction houses keep a precise log of each paddle number, the time of each bid, and the amount, and Vane, who was uneasy but correct, gave him a printed sheet. There were only two bidders on the sheet: paddle 61, the man in the front, and paddle 17, the woman on the left. Edmund read the sequence slowly: 61 at twenty-two thousand, 17 at twenty-five, and then nothing.

Tess had been reading the registration list. "Paddle 61 is a Mr. Dunmore," she said, "a dealer from Leeds who has attended eleven of your sales in the last three years. Paddle 17 is a Ms. Calloway, also a dealer, who has attended nine. They are, as Mrs. Whitcombe said, regular clients. But look at the list of lots on which each of them has bid."

She laid a second sheet beside the first. Edmund ran his finger down the columns. In the past three years, there had been fifty-three lots in the same category as the watch, fine antique timepieces. Dunmore had bid on twenty-six of them and won twelve. Calloway had bid on twenty-four and won eleven. "Neither has ever bid on the same lot as the other," said Tess slowly. "Not once. They share the same field, the same sales, the same room, and yet in three years they have never competed."

Edmund took off his spectacles and cleaned them with his handkerchief, a gesture that Tess had learned to recognise. "Two rivals who never compete," he said. "It is an interesting arithmetic. Tonight is the first time they have bid against each other, and the contest lasted exactly two bids."
ch.clue: in three years they have never competed
ch.q: What pattern do the records reveal about the two bidders?
o: They have never attended the same sale in the history of the auction house
They bid on every lot, and one of them always raises the price at the last moment
They have each lost money at every sale they have attended in the last three years
They attend the same sales and specialise in the same field but never bid against each other until this lot
They have both been banned from other auction houses for dishonest bidding
ch.hint: Kayıtlara göre Dunmore ile Calloway aynı alanda ve aynı satışlarda yer alıyor ama üç yılda bir kez bile aynı eşya için teklif vermemişler. Bu, rakip iki satıcı için nasıl bir örüntü?
ch.why: İki satıcı aynı alanda ve aynı satışlardaydı ama üç yıl boyunca hiç aynı eşya için rekabet etmemişti; bu, olağan rekabete uymayan bir örüntüydü.

text: Edmund did not accuse anyone that evening. Instead, he asked Mrs. Whitcombe for the security recordings of the hall during the sale, which the house kept for insurance purposes. The next morning, he and Tess sat in her office and watched the recording of lot fourteen on a small screen, frame by frame, with the sound turned off.

At first, there was nothing unusual: a hundred little movements of the audience, a cough, a hand lifted to loosen a collar. But when Edmund slowed the picture to a quarter speed, he began to see a pattern in the movements of Mr. Dunmore. Each time that Vane named a price, Dunmore's left hand moved, very slightly, to his right wrist, where he wore a plain steel watch. Twice his fingers touched the winder. After the second bid, he did it again, three times, each time with a small turn of the crown.

"He is not winding it," said Tess. "A modern watch does not need to be wound so often, if it is automatic." Edmund nodded. "A gesture is a language, Tess, if two people have agreed what it means." He moved the picture to the left of the hall. Ms. Calloway, who sat eight rows behind Dunmore, had been looking at him without moving her face. At the moment of Dunmore's third gesture, she lowered her paddle to her lap, and she kept it there.
"It is a signal," said Tess. "And she obeyed it."
"She lowered her paddle exactly when he touched the winder for the third time," said Edmund. "Consider what that means for our two rivals."
ch.clue: A gesture is a language, Tess, if two people have agreed what it means
ch.q: What do the recordings suggest about Dunmore and Calloway?
o: They had agreed on a secret signal that told Calloway when to stop bidding
They were both trying to attract the attention of the auctioneer
They were arguing quietly with each other across the width of the hall
They had never met before the evening of the auction
They were checking the time to be sure that the sale would finish soon
ch.hint: Dunmore her fiyat açıklandığında kol saatinin kurmasına dokunuyor ve üçüncü dokunuştan hemen sonra Calloway paletini indiriyor. Bu iki hareket arasındaki ilişki neyi düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Dunmore'un kol saatine dokunuşu ile Calloway'in paletini indirmesi tam olarak çakışıyordu; bu, önceden kararlaştırılmış gizli bir işaret olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: The proof that Edmund needed arrived by the afternoon post. Mrs. Whitcombe, who had been advised to look in her own files, found a record that no one had thought to compare: the invoices for the watch's consignment. The watch had been consigned by the estate of an elderly collector, with a reserve price, the minimum at which it could be sold, of fifteen thousand pounds. Both dealers had been given the catalogue three weeks before the sale. Neither had ever seen the reserve.

Edmund sat across from the two dealers in Mrs. Whitcombe's office on Thursday morning, with Tess taking notes at a small table. He did not raise his voice. "You are both experienced and respectable people," he said. "I do not intend to call the police. But I want to describe an arrangement that I think exists, and you will tell me if I am wrong. Two dealers who rarely compete agree that, on a lot that interests them both, one will bid and the other will stay silent. They have a signal. The cheaper the winning price, the greater the margin. Afterwards, they hold a second, private auction, in which the two of them bid for the item among themselves, and the difference between the public price and the private price is divided equally."
Dunmore looked at his hands. Calloway looked at the window. It was she who spoke at last, in a low voice: "We have done it on eleven lots in three years."

"Then every honest bidder who sat in your hall on those eleven evenings," said Edmund, "paid, in effect, for your arrangement." Tess closed her notebook. The house wrote to all the estates affected the following week.
ch.clue: a second, private auction
ch.q: What was the dealers' arrangement?
o: They bought the watch together and gave it to the museum as a gift
They bribed the auctioneer to set a lower reserve price for the watch
They agreed not to compete in public and then shared the profit of a later private resale between themselves
They bid up the price of the watch so that the estate would receive more money
They reported each other to the owner of the auction house for cheating
ch.hint: Edmund iki satıcının halka açık müzayedede rekabet etmeyip sonra kendi aralarında ikinci bir özel müzayede yaptığını söylüyor. Bu düzenin kazancı nereden geliyor?
ch.why: İki satıcı halka açık müzayedede rekabet etmeyip fiyatı düşük tutuyor, sonra özel bir ikinci müzayedede farkı kendi aralarında paylaşıyordu.

outro: Saatin fiyatı, salondaki iki alıcının önceden anlaşması sonucu düşürülmüştü. Edmund şunu söyledi: bir pazar, katılımcıların rekabet ettiğini varsaydığında çalışır; sessizlik çoğu zaman en yüksek sesle konuşan kanıttır.

title: The Reassuring Scan
hero: Dr. Mara Quinn ve hemşire Joe
intro: Kırk yaşındaki bir öğretmen, aylardır süren sırt ağrısı nedeniyle defalarca hastaneye geliyor. Her seferinde görüntüleme normal çıkıyor ve ona stres olduğu söyleniyor. Dr. Mara Quinn ile hemşire Joe, tüm kayıtları yeniden okuyarak normal sonuçların neyi gözden kaçırmış olabileceğini araştırıyor.

text: When Mr. Hollis came in for the fourth time in five months, the receptionist at the Westbridge outpatient clinic gave him a smile that was kind and slightly tired. He was a primary-school teacher, forty years old, tall and lean, and he walked with the careful, tilted posture of a man who has learned to carry pain. His file lay open on Dr. Mara Quinn's desk, and Nurse Joe, who had been assigned to help her review long-term cases, placed beside it a stack of printed reports.

"Four visits, three different doctors," said Joe. "Every one of them has written the same sentence in the conclusion: no structural cause identified, symptoms probably related to stress and posture." Mara turned the pages. In February, an X-ray of the lower spine, normal. In April, an MRI of the lumbar spine, normal, with a note that there was a very mild, age-appropriate wear in two discs. In June, blood tests: normal. Physiotherapy had been prescribed, with an exercise sheet.

"He tells us the pain is on the right side," said Joe, "low in the back, sometimes spreading round towards the front, and it comes in waves, not constantly. It is worse in the evening. He cannot sit for long in his classroom." Mara looked up. "Waves," she said. "Do we have any record of what he says about the urine?"

Joe checked the notes. "Not a word," he said. "Nobody has asked him." Mara put her pen on the desk and looked at the closed door of the consulting room, where, through the glass, a tall figure in a grey cardigan was waiting with his hand pressed to his side.
ch.clue: it comes in waves, not constantly
ch.q: Which detail in Mr. Hollis's description makes Dr. Quinn suspect that the earlier diagnosis may be wrong?
o: His MRI showed a mild, age-appropriate wear in two discs
He is a teacher who spends many hours standing in front of a classroom
The pain comes in waves and spreads round the side, which is unusual for a spinal problem
The physiotherapy he was given did not include enough exercises
He has had normal results from every one of his blood tests
ch.hint: Ağrı dalgalar hâlinde geliyor ve yandan öne doğru yayılıyor. Bu tür bir ağrı omurga sorunundan çok neyi düşündürebilir? Mara'nın idrar hakkında soru sorması da bir ipucu.
ch.why: Ağrının dalgalar hâlinde gelmesi ve yandan öne yayılması, omurga sorunları için alışılmış bir tablo değildi; Mara bu yüzden başka bir kaynak olduğunu düşündü.

text: Mr. Hollis sat down slowly, with one hand still pressed to his right side. Mara introduced herself and Joe, and explained that she was going to read the whole history again, from the beginning, because she thought that something might have been missed. It was a sentence that patients did not hear often, and he relaxed a little. "I am tired of being told it is stress," he said. "I am a calm man. I teach six-year-olds."

"Tell me about the last waves of pain," said Mara. "When did the latest one begin?" He thought. "On Sunday night. It started low in the back, and then it moved forward. It was so strong that I could not lie down. I walked around the kitchen for two hours. It lasted about forty minutes and went away." Mara wrote quickly. "Did you notice anything else, then or on the days afterwards? Anything about passing water?"

Mr. Hollis frowned. "As a matter of fact, yes. The next morning it was darker than usual, almost pink. I thought I had eaten something strange, beetroot perhaps. It happened twice in the spring, too, I think, but I did not mention it. It did not hurt. It seemed unconnected."

Joe, who had been standing quietly by the window, turned his head. Mara kept her face calm. "One more question. Do you drink much water during the day?" "Hardly any in school," said Mr. Hollis. "There is no time. A cup of tea in the morning, a cup at lunch. I make up for it at home, a little."
Mara closed the file, took a fresh sheet from the drawer, and wrote one word at the top, with a question mark after it.
ch.clue: almost pink
ch.q: What new information does Mr. Hollis give that was missing from the earlier reports?
o: A habit of sitting in a bad position for several hours every day
A history of spinal injuries in his family during the past generations
A wish to leave his job as a teacher because of the noise in the classroom
Regular visits to a physiotherapist, which have made his back worse
Occasional pink-coloured urine after the attacks of pain, and little fluid intake at work
ch.hint: Hasta ağrı atağından sonra idrarın pembe olduğunu ve gün içinde çok az sıvı aldığını söylüyor. Bu iki bilgi neden daha önceki raporlarda yoktu ve ne tür bir sorunu düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Hasta ağrıdan sonra pembe idrar fark ettiğini ve işte çok az su içtiğini söylüyordu; bu bilgiler önceki raporlarda yoktu, çünkü kimse sormamıştı.

text: Mara asked Joe to bring the radiology reports of the MRI and the X-ray, and to read the exact words of the description, not the conclusion. He read slowly. The X-ray covered the lumbar spine, from the twelfth thoracic vertebra to the sacrum. The MRI was a sequence of the lumbar region only. "The field of view," Joe read, "includes the vertebral column, the discs, the spinal canal and the adjacent paraspinal muscles. The kidneys are not included in the sequences."

"They are not included," said Mara. "It is a matter of design. A scan answers a question, and the question that was asked was about the spine: is there a damaged disc, is there pressure on a nerve? The answer, in each case, was no. A radiologist does not describe organs that are not in the picture, and nobody asked them to."

She turned to a second page. "Look at the blood tests. Creatinine normal. A kidney with a small obstruction can function normally for months, because the other one compensates. And the urine tests." She frowned at the sheet. "There are none. In five months, four visits, nobody ordered a urine test."

Joe put the reports back in order. "So we have a patient whose pain comes in waves, spreads towards the front, is accompanied by dark urine, and who drinks very little water, and who has been examined with tests which were designed to look at everything except the one place where those symptoms would begin."
"I should like an ultrasound of the kidneys this afternoon," said Mara, "and a urine sample now, before he goes home."
ch.clue: The kidneys are not included in the sequences
ch.q: Why did the earlier scans fail to find the cause of the pain?
o: The machines were old and produced pictures that were not clear
They were designed to examine the spine and did not include the kidneys
The radiologists were not experienced enough to read the pictures
The patient moved too much while the pictures were being taken
The scans were taken at the wrong time of the day
ch.hint: MRI raporunda görüntüleme alanının omurgayı, diskleri ve kasları kapsadığı, böbreklerin ise dışarıda kaldığı yazıyor. Normal sonuçlar neden ağrının sebebini ortaya çıkarmadı?
ch.why: Taramalar yalnızca omurgayı incelemek için tasarlanmıştı ve böbrekleri kapsamıyordu; normal sonuç yalnızca bakılan bölgenin normal olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: The urine sample showed what Mara had expected: a small number of red blood cells, invisible to the eye, but clearly present under the microscope. The ultrasound, which a radiographer named Mrs. Oyelaran carried out that afternoon, took less than fifteen minutes. Mr. Hollis lay on the couch with his shirt pulled up, and the radiographer moved the probe slowly over his right side, looking at a grey screen where shapes appeared and vanished.

She stopped at one position and tapped a key to freeze the picture. "There," she said quietly, to Mara, who stood behind her. In the kidney, a small white spot cast a thin black shadow behind it. "A stone. About six millimetres. And the ureter above it is a little wider than it should be, which means that it is slowing the passage of urine."

Mara explained to Mr. Hollis, in plain words, what it was. A stone had formed in his kidney, probably over the past year, helped by the little water that he drank. From time to time, it moved and blocked the tube that carries urine, and the kidney, full of pressure, sent out waves of pain. "It also explains why the scans of your back were normal, because your back is healthy. The pain was only passing through it."
"Five months," said Mr. Hollis, and then he began to laugh, helplessly, with his face in his hands. "Five months of exercises for my posture."
"Six millimetres will probably pass with plenty of water and a medicine to relax the tube," said Mara. "But we shall also take a small second look in three months."
ch.clue: The pain was only passing through it
ch.q: What is the final diagnosis, and how does it explain Mr. Hollis's symptoms?
o: Stress which causes physical pain and a change in the colour of the urine
An infection of the bladder that has spread to the spine
A muscle strain caused by sitting in a poor position at work
A kidney stone that intermittently blocks the urinary tract, causing waves of pain and traces of blood
A damaged spinal disc that presses on a nerve in the lower back
ch.hint: Ultrasonda böbrekte yaklaşık 6 mm'lik bir taş ve genişlemiş bir üreter görülüyor. Bu bulgu dalgalar hâlinde ağrıyı, pembe idrarı ve normal omurga görüntülerini nasıl birlikte açıklıyor?
ch.why: Böbrek taşı ara sıra idrar yolunu tıkıyor, bu da dalgalar hâlinde ağrıya ve idrarda az miktarda kana yol açıyordu; omurga ise sağlıklıydı.

outro: Ağrının kaynağı omurga değil, böbrekteki küçük bir taştı ve sırt görüntülemesi o bölgeyi kapsamıyordu. Mara şunu yazdı: normal bir tetkik, yalnızca bakılan yerin normal olduğunu söyler; hastanın ağrısının nerede olduğunu söylemez.

title: The Drifting Station
hero: Komutan Noor Hale ve mühendis Pip
intro: Yörüngedeki bir istasyonun konumu, hiçbir motor çalıştırılmadığı hâlde, her gün birkaç metre değişiyor. Komutan Noor Hale ile mühendis Pip, sensör verilerini, yakıt kayıtlarını ve mürettebatın günlük işlerini inceleyerek bu gizemli sürüklenmenin nedenini araştırıyor.

text: The orbital station Meridian circled the Earth every ninety-three minutes, at an altitude of about four hundred kilometres, and it was one of the best-monitored objects in human history. Its position was tracked by ground radar, by satellite navigation, and by a set of star trackers on its own hull, and the three systems usually agreed to within a few centimetres. On the morning of the sixty-first day of the mission, Pip, the station's flight engineer, brought a printout to Commander Noor Hale in the central module, and she saw at once from his face that it was not good news.

"The ground has sent us a note," he said. "They report that our orbit is not where the prediction says it should be. The difference is small, about eleven metres, but they say it was six metres last week, and two the week before." Noor looked at the graph. The line was straight, almost ruled, and climbing gently to the right. "No engine firing since day forty," she said. "That is in the log, and I signed it."

"Correct," said Pip. "In addition, the attitude control thrusters have fired only twice, for the docking manoeuvre, and both burns are accounted for. The drift is not explained by anything we have done."

Noor tapped the graph. "A straight line," she said. "Not a jump, not a curve. Something is acting on the station gently and constantly, as a hand would, pushing a boat. A single event leaves a mark at a single time. This is a process." She turned to the window, where the blue curve of the Earth slid slowly by.
"Make a list of everything on the station that produces a force," she said. "Even a tiny one."
ch.clue: A single event leaves a mark at a single time
ch.q: What does the shape of the graph tell Noor about the cause of the drift?
o: The cause is a single large impact from a piece of space debris
The cause is the docking manoeuvre that was carried out on day forty
The cause is an error in the ground radar's measurements
The cause is a continuous, steady process rather than a single event
The cause is a failure of the star trackers on the hull
ch.hint: Grafik düz ve düzenli bir çizgi, ani bir sıçrama ya da eğri değil. Noor bunu "bir süreç" olarak yorumluyor. Düz bir çizgi ne tür bir nedenle uyumlu?
ch.why: Grafik düz bir çizgiydi; bu, tek bir olayın değil, istasyona sürekli ve hafifçe etki eden bir sürecin sonucu olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: Pip made the list on the wall of the module with a grease pencil, a long and untidy one: engines, thrusters, solar panels, antennas, the robotic arm, the waste system, the water recycler, the exercise machines. Then, together with Noor, he began to cross things out, giving a reason for every line.

The engines and thrusters had been checked: the valves were closed and the fuel gauges unchanged, since day forty. The solar panels did generate a very small force, because sunlight itself pushes on a surface, but its direction changed twice every orbit, as the panels turned to follow the sun, and its effect averaged to zero over a day. The antennas and the robotic arm were stationary. The exercise machines produced vibrations, but they were internal forces, and an object cannot push itself by pushing against its own parts. "Newton's third law," said Pip. "Whatever the crew do inside, the centre of mass does not move."

"That is the key," said Noor. "Only something that leaves the station can change its motion, something that carries momentum away. A gas, a fluid, a particle. If we are losing mass in one particular direction, even at a trickle, we are being pushed in the opposite one."

Pip looked at the remaining words on the wall: the waste system, the water recycler. He walked slowly to the recycler's panel, a grey box that purified the crew's water and the humidity of their breath. A little green light blinked on the front. A second line of data showed a number: Daily vented vapour, 0.4 kg.
"We vent forty decagrams of water vapour into space every day," he said. "Always from the same outlet. Always in the same direction."
ch.clue: an object cannot push itself by pushing against its own parts
ch.q: Why does Noor focus on something that leaves the station?
o: Only a flow of matter leaving the station can change its overall motion
The crew's exercise machines are too heavy to be moved
Internal forces are the only ones that can alter an orbit
The solar panels always push the station in the same direction
Objects in space cannot be affected by any outside force
ch.hint: Pip "Newton'un üçüncü yasası"ndan söz ediyor: iç kuvvetler kütle merkezini değiştiremez. İstasyonun hareketini değiştirebilecek tek şey ne olabilir?
ch.why: İç kuvvetler kütle merkezini değiştiremeyeceği için yalnızca istasyonu terk eden bir madde akışı genel hareketi değiştirebilirdi.

text: "Forty decagrams a day is not a lot," said Noor, taking a pencil. "Let us see whether it is enough." She wrote the figures in the margin of the printout. The vapour left through a nozzle at a speed that Pip estimated, from the manufacturer's data, at about four hundred metres per second. Momentum is mass times velocity: 0.4 kilograms times 400 metres per second gave a push of 160 kilogram-metres per second every day. The station's mass was 420 tonnes. Dividing, she found that each day the venting changed the station's velocity by less than half a millimetre per second.

"That is nothing," said Pip. "You could walk faster than that on your hands." "Wait," said Noor. "A change in speed of a station in orbit does not move it by a few millimetres. It moves it into a slightly different orbit, with a slightly different period. A tiny difference in speed, repeated for two months, accumulates. Every orbit, the station arrives at the same point a fraction of a second early or late. And after hundreds of orbits, the early arrivals add up to metres."

She drew a second, slower line below the first. "In sixty days, that makes about thirty seconds of arrival time at a fraction of a metre per second. The ground says eleven metres. Doing the calculation again with the real period, I get a number between nine and thirteen."
"It fits," said Pip, almost in a whisper. He had not realised that he was holding his breath. "But why did nobody notice it on the first mission, or the second?"
"Because on those missions," said Noor, "the outlet pointed somewhere else."
ch.clue: the outlet pointed somewhere else
ch.q: Why does a very small daily push produce a measurable drift?
o: The station is very light, so that it is easily moved by any force
The ground radar measures distances only in whole kilometres
The tiny change in speed is repeated every day and accumulates over hundreds of orbits
The push gets larger each day because the nozzle widens with use
The vapour leaves the nozzle at a speed greater than the speed of light
ch.hint: Noor, günde yarım milimetreden az hız değişiminin yüzlerce yörünge boyunca birikmesini anlatıyor. Küçük ama sürekli tekrarlanan bir etki zamanla ne yapar?
ch.why: Çok küçük hız değişimi her gün tekrarlanıyor ve yüzlerce yörünge boyunca birikerek ölçülebilir bir sapmaya dönüşüyordu.

text: The solution, once they understood it, was almost embarrassingly simple. Noor wrote to the ground team the same evening, with Pip's calculations attached, and proposed two options. The first was to correct the orbit with a short engine burn, which would cancel the drift, but would use fuel, and the drift would return. The second was to remove its cause. The vent could be rotated by a bracket, a job that the crew had already done in training, and pointed in a direction that changed with every orbit, so that the small pushes would cancel each other over a day instead of adding up.

Mission Control approved the second, with a recommendation to do both. Three days later, Pip and a colleague, wearing the heavy suits, floated out of the airlock and, in a two-hour spacewalk, removed four bolts, turned the nozzle through ninety degrees, and fastened it again. A new plate was fitted to deflect the plume of vapour. They returned with a sigh of relief and a cold supper.

The graph in the central module, which Noor kept on the wall, was a different shape the following month. The straight line, climbing gently to the right, flattened out, hesitated, and then began to wobble gently around zero, like a heartbeat. The ground reported that the position error was under half a metre.
"What is your conclusion?" asked Noor, standing in front of it with her arms folded. "That a small constant force is more dangerous than a large rare one," said Pip. "Because nobody looks for it."
ch.clue: so that the small pushes would cancel each other over a day
ch.q: How was the problem finally solved?
o: By moving the station to a much higher and quieter orbit
By firing the main engine once every day to correct the orbit
By replacing the solar panels with a lighter and smaller design
By stopping the crew from using the water recycler for the rest of the mission
By rotating the vent so that its pushes no longer add up in one direction
ch.hint: Mürettebat tahliye ağzını döndürdü. Böylece küçük itmeler tek yönde birikmek yerine ne yapıyor? Bu, sorunun kaynağını mı ortadan kaldırıyor, yoksa sadece düzeltiyor mu?
ch.why: Mürettebat tahliye ağzını döndürerek küçük itmelerin tek yönde toplanmasını önledi; böylece sapmanın nedeni ortadan kalktı.

outro: Sürüklenmeye, istasyondan her gün düzenli olarak dışarı atılan kullanılmış su buharı neden oluyordu; sızıntı çok küçük, ama aylarca sürdüğünde etkisi ölçülebilirdi. Noor şunu yazdı: küçük ve düzenli bir kuvvet, büyük ve nadir bir kuvvetten daha uzun etki bırakır.

title: The Missing Decade
hero: Tarihçi Dr. Amira Kent ve asistanı Leo
intro: Bir liman kasabasının tarihi kayıtlarında 1840'lı yıllardan bir on yıl, tamamen eksik. Dr. Amira Kent ile Leo, belediye arşivlerini, kilise defterlerini ve eski mektupları karşılaştırarak bu sessizliğin yangın mı, ihmal mi, yoksa bilinçli bir silme mi olduğunu araştırıyor.

text: The town archive of Port Sheldon occupied three rooms on the first floor of a Victorian building near the harbour, and Dr. Amira Kent had been working in it, with her assistant Leo, for six weeks. The commission was a straightforward one: to prepare a catalogue of the council's papers for a museum exhibition on the town's nineteenth-century history. Everything had gone smoothly until the day when Leo, arranging the great bound volumes of council minutes on a long shelf, stopped and began to count.

"There is something wrong with the dates," he said. "Look. Volume eleven ends in December 1841, and volume twelve starts in January 1852. Nothing in between. And the numbers are consecutive: eleven, twelve. There is no volume missing from the sequence. The books simply continue, as if nothing had happened."

Amira took both from the shelf and compared the bindings, which were identical. She opened the end of volume eleven. The last page held the minutes of a meeting in December, concluding with the usual formula, and then there was a blank page, and a blank back cover. In volume twelve, the first entry was dated the second of January 1852, and began in the middle of a discussion of the harbour tax, without any introduction.

"The sequence of volumes was numbered afterwards," said Amira thoughtfully. "Someone arranged these books to give the impression of continuity, which means that someone knew there was a gap and wanted it to be invisible. A natural loss, a flood or a fire, would leave a damaged volume, or a missing number. This is neater than that."
Leo put the books on the table side by side. "Ten years," he said. "Ten years of a town's life."
ch.clue: someone knew there was a gap and wanted it to be invisible
ch.q: Why does Amira doubt that the gap is the result of a natural accident?
o: The binding of the twelfth volume is different from that of the eleventh
The books are in a very bad condition, with a lot of damage from water
The council wrote very short minutes during the years of the gap
The earlier volumes are all missing and only the later ones have survived
The volumes are numbered consecutively, as if someone had arranged them to hide the gap
ch.hint: Ciltler 11 ve 12 olarak ardışık numaralanmış ve eksik bir cilt numarası yok. Doğal bir kayıp (yangın, sel) genellikle nasıl bir iz bırakırdı ve burada ne farklı?
ch.why: Ciltler ardışık numaralanmıştı ve hasar ya da eksik numara yoktu; bu düzen, birinin boşluğu görünmez kılmak istediğini düşündürüyordu.

text: If the council had kept silent, perhaps the church had not. Amira and Leo walked to St Brannock's, the old parish church on the hill, where the vicar, a stooped and generous man, allowed them to consult the registers of baptisms, marriages and burials. The books were heavy, in cracked leather, and the handwriting of the curates changed every few years like the weather.

They looked first at the years 1842 to 1851. The baptisms and marriages continued at an ordinary rate, perhaps fifty or sixty baptisms a year. The burials, however, told another story. In the winter of 1846, the number of entries on a single page was more than the number for the whole of the previous year. Amira counted them with her pencil: eighty-three burials in November and December alone. In the margin, in a different ink, a curate had written a single word at the top of the page and underlined it: Cholera.

"A major epidemic," said Leo, "and it is not mentioned in any council record, because the council record is missing." Amira turned the pages. "The burials begin in the second week of October, which means that the first deaths must have occurred in the first. It rises quickly, then peaks in late November, and falls away after Christmas. Total deaths: three hundred and nine. In a town of about four thousand people, that is almost eight per cent."
Leo took off his glasses. "The disappearance of the minutes is beginning to look less like an accident, and more like an act."
Amira closed the register gently. "Let us not jump to conclusions. First we must find out what the council did, and what it was afraid people might read."
ch.clue: eighty-three burials in November and December alone
ch.q: What does the parish register reveal that the council records do not?
o: A period of very few deaths in the town between 1842 and 1851
A serious cholera epidemic in the winter of 1846, causing hundreds of deaths
A change of vicar in the winter months of the year 1846
A decision by the council to build a new church on the hill
A sudden increase in the number of weddings in the autumn of 1846
ch.hint: Mezar kayıtlarında 1846 kışında olağanüstü artış var ve bir rahip kenara "Cholera" yazmış. Bu kayıt kasabanın o yılları hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Mezar kayıtları 1846 kışında yüzlerce ölümle birlikte bir kolera salgınını gösteriyordu; bu, belediye kayıtlarında hiç yer almıyordu.

text: Where could the council's decisions during the epidemic still be traced? Amira reasoned that a town does not govern itself in isolation: it writes to its neighbours, its superiors, its creditors, and a letter has two homes, one with the sender and one with the receiver. In the county record office, forty kilometres inland, she found the correspondence of the Board of Health for the years in question, and read it with Leo, hour after hour, in a bright reading room.

The relevant folder contained fourteen letters from Port Sheldon, signed by the mayor, Mr. Aldous Penrose. The earliest, dated 9 October 1846, reported with confidence that there were "a few cases of an ordinary fever, which are well in hand". The second, a week later, repeated it. The third, on 30 October, begged for medical supplies. But it was the fourth letter that stopped Leo in the middle of a sentence. It was a reply from the county physician, dated 6 November, and the language was severe: You inform me that your Council has decided not to close the port to shipping, in spite of the advice of your own doctor, on the ground that trade must not be interrupted before Christmas. I must record my strongest objection. I understand that the sickness arrived on a ship from the Baltic in the last week of September, and that the cargo was unloaded without inspection.

"They knew it was cholera on the ninth of November," said Leo. "They knew where it came from. And they kept the harbour open for trade." Amira read the physician's last sentence again, then slowly lowered the page.
"Now," she said, "we begin to understand why the council would prefer that nobody read its minutes."
ch.clue: the cargo was unloaded without inspection
ch.q: What do the letters in the county record office show about the council's conduct?
o: The council closed the port immediately and asked the county for medical help
The county physician approved of the way in which the council had acted
The cargo from the Baltic was inspected and found to be free of disease
The council kept the port open for trade despite medical advice, and played down the danger
The mayor refused to write any letters to the county during the epidemic
ch.hint: Vali hekim, konseyin doktorunun tavsiyesine rağmen limanı Noel'e kadar ticarete açık tuttuğunu ve geminin yükünün denetlenmeden indirildiğini yazıyor. Konseyin davranışı hakkında ne anlaşılır?
ch.why: Mektuplar, konseyin tıbbi öneriye rağmen limanı ticaret için açık bıraktığını ve tehlikeyi küçümsediğini gösteriyordu.

text: Back in Port Sheldon, Amira and Leo returned to the council volumes and, this time, looked not at the contents but at the physical structure. Leo examined the spine of volume twelve under a lamp with a magnifying glass. "Look," he said. "At the front of the book, a thin strip of paper, a stub, remains in the gutter, where a page has been cut out. The cut is straight and careful. And there is another stub, and another." He counted them. "Thirty-one pages cut out, all at the start of the book."

"The volume that now starts in January 1852," said Amira, "originally began earlier. Someone removed the first thirty-one pages, which covered the last months of 1846, and the volumes for the years in between, 1842 to 1845 and 1847 to 1851, were removed, too, and the numbers adjusted. It was not enough to hide the winter of the epidemic, because that would have attracted attention. They removed an entire decade, so that the absence would look like an accident of the past."

They found the proof in the mayor's own hand, in a bundle of private papers donated to the library in 1923 by his granddaughter. In a letter to his brother, written in 1852, Penrose confessed that he and two councillors had ordered the destruction of the minutes, after the families of the victims began to talk of a trial. I have taken away the record of our choice, he wrote. They cannot punish what they cannot read.
"He was wrong," said Leo. "It was only a question of looking in the right drawer."
The exhibition opened in the spring with a new room, called The Missing Decade. It displayed the stubs, the burial registers and the physician's letter, side by side.
ch.clue: They cannot punish what they cannot read
ch.q: How did Amira and Leo discover why the pages were missing?
o: By finding cut stubs in the volume and a confession in the mayor's private letter
By reading a newspaper article from the year of the epidemic
By finding the missing volumes in a box in the basement of the church
By comparing the handwriting of the curates with that of the councillors
By asking the vicar, who knew the whole story from his predecessors
ch.hint: Cildin başında kesilmiş sayfaların kalıntıları ve belediye başkanının kardeşine yazdığı özel bir mektup var. Bu iki kanıt birlikte kaybolan kayıtlar hakkında ne gösteriyor?
ch.why: Ciltte kesilmiş sayfa kalıntıları ve belediye başkanının özel mektubundaki itiraf, kayıtların bilerek yok edildiğini gösteriyordu.

outro: Kayıtlar, kasabanın bir salgın sırasında yaptığı hatalı bir karantina kararını gizlemek için yok edilmişti; ama karar, başka bir yerde yazılan mektuplarda hayatta kalmıştı. Amira şunu söyledi: bir kayıt silinebilir, ama bir olayın tüm izlerini silmek çok daha zordur.

title: The Reproducible Result
hero: Dr. Ilan Voss ve asistanı Dana
intro: Dr. Voss'un laboratuvarındaki bir yeni ilaç adayı, bir ekipte güçlü sonuç veriyor ama başka bir şehirdeki ekipte aynı deneyi tekrarlayınca hiçbir etki göstermiyor. Ilan Voss ile Dana, iki laboratuvarın yöntemlerini karşılaştırarak farkın nerede olduğunu arıyor.

text: The paper that came out of Dr. Ilan Voss's laboratory in March was received with the warm interest that scientists reserve for results which might one day help a patient. The compound, which the team called V-212, was a small molecule that, in cultures of human liver cells, reduced the damage caused by a toxin by almost seventy per cent. Dana, who had performed most of the experiments, had checked each figure three times before submission. The effect was large, clean and consistent: eight experiments, eight positive results.

Six months later, an email arrived from Professor Okafor's laboratory in another city, a respected group that had tried to repeat the work. Ilan read it twice, and then called Dana into his office. "They followed our protocol," he said, "as closely as the methods section allowed. They made the cells, added the toxin, and treated them with V-212 at the same concentrations. They did three independent experiments with six samples each, and found no protective effect, whatever. The difference between treated and untreated cells is smaller than the margin of error."
Dana felt her stomach tighten. "Either our result is a mistake," she said, "or theirs is. I have checked our numbers. We recorded everything, and the controls behaved perfectly."

"I believe you," said Ilan. "And I have no reason to doubt Professor Okafor. In science, there are two failures that are painful: a result that is false, and a result that is true only in one place. The second is harder to see." He stood up and took a clean notebook. "Let us write down everything that differs between the two laboratories, however small. Not what we think matters, but everything."
ch.clue: a result that is true only in one place
ch.q: What is the main problem facing Ilan and Dana?
o: The same experiment gives a strong effect in one laboratory and none in another
The experiment was carried out with too few samples in Dana's laboratory
Professor Okafor's laboratory has not published its results in a journal
Dana made a mistake in the figures which she submitted to the journal
The compound V-212 is toxic to the liver cells in both laboratories
ch.hint: Ilan'ın laboratuvarında sekiz deneyin hepsi olumlu çıkmış, Okafor'un laboratuvarında ise etki hiç yok. Ilan iki acı başarısızlıktan söz ediyor. Burada karşılaşılan sorun hangisi?
ch.why: Aynı deney bir laboratuvarda güçlü etki gösterirken diğerinde hiç etki göstermiyordu; Ilan bunu "yalnızca bir yerde doğru olan sonuç" olarak adlandırıyordu.

text: It took them most of a week to compile the list, with the help of long telephone calls to Professor Okafor's postdoctoral researcher, a patient and precise young man named Dr. Lindqvist. The calls were friendly, but, as Ilan noticed, they revealed how many details a published protocol leaves out, because nobody thinks they matter.

The two laboratories used the same cell line, obtained from the same supplier, at the same passage number. They used the same toxin, from the same batch. They used the same plastic plates, the same incubators, set at the same temperature and the same proportion of carbon dioxide. The same V-212 had been sent by Dana to Lindqvist, in a sealed vial, and he had confirmed its purity with his own instrument. Dana read out the points one by one and Ilan crossed them off. "Same supplier, same batch, same temperature. Both groups do the counting with the same automated reader."

"Now the differences," said Ilan. Dana read from the second page. "Our incubator is in the basement and theirs is on the third floor. We change the culture medium every two days, and they change it every three. They count the cells at forty-eight hours, we count at seventy-two. We are in a city at sea level, they are at about eight hundred metres." She hesitated. "And there is one more thing. They buy their culture medium from a company, a ready-made product. We make ours ourselves, from a recipe that the laboratory has used for fifteen years. We add the serum, the glucose, the amino acids, and a small amount of a supplement which Dr. Lindqvist's protocol does not mention at all."
Ilan put down his pen. "Which supplement?" he asked quietly.
ch.clue: does not mention at all
ch.q: What is the most important difference that Dana discovers between the two protocols?
o: Dana's laboratory uses a different cell line from the one used by Dr. Lindqvist
The incubators in the two laboratories were set at very different temperatures
Dana's laboratory prepares its own culture medium with an extra supplement, while the other uses a commercial product
The two laboratories used toxins from completely different manufacturers
Dr. Lindqvist counted the cells before adding the toxin and not after it
ch.hint: Dana, kendi laboratuvarının kültür sıvısını (medium) kendisinin hazırladığını, diğer laboratuvarın ise hazır bir ürün kullandığını ve protokolde anılmayan bir katkı olduğunu söylüyor. Bu fark neden önemli?
ch.why: Dana'nın laboratuvarı kültür sıvısını kendi hazırlıyor ve protokolde anılmayan ek bir katkı kullanıyordu; diğer laboratuvar ise hazır ürünü kullanıyordu.

text: "It is called N-acetyl-something," said Dana, looking through the old recipe card pinned to the wall of the cell room. "A small amount of an antioxidant, added by the laboratory since before I joined. It is in the recipe as a line called 'additive B', and I have never thought about it. It protects the cells from damage by oxygen in the incubator."

Ilan said nothing for a moment. Then he gave a short, dry laugh, and sat on a stool. "An antioxidant. And the toxin that we use to injure the cells does its damage partly by creating oxidative stress." He drew a quick diagram on the whiteboard: toxin, arrow, oxidative stress, arrow, cell death. And beside it, a second arrow from V-212. "What if V-212 works by a mechanism that depends on the presence of that antioxidant? For instance, if V-212 does not protect the cells directly, but strengthens the effect of a molecule that is already there?"

"In Okafor's laboratory," said Dana slowly, "the commercial medium has no such supplement. So V-212 has nothing to strengthen." "It is a hypothesis," said Ilan, "not a conclusion. But it is testable, and it makes a clear prediction. If we remove the supplement from our own medium, our result should disappear. And if we add it to Lindqvist's, his result should appear."

Dana was already pulling a notebook towards her. "Four conditions," she said. "With and without V-212, with and without the supplement. I can start tomorrow. I will ask Dr. Lindqvist to run the same four in parallel."
ch.clue: it makes a clear prediction
ch.q: What hypothesis do Ilan and Dana develop?
o: The cells in Dr. Lindqvist's laboratory are resistant to every kind of toxin
The supplement is toxic and reduces the effect of the toxin in the cells
The commercial medium contains a chemical that blocks the action of V-212
V-212 destroys the antioxidant and, in this way, kills the liver cells
V-212 may only work when an antioxidant supplement is present in the culture medium
ch.hint: Ilan'ın hipotezine göre V-212, ortamda antioksidan katkı varsa etki ediyor. Bu hipotez, iki laboratuvarın farklı sonuçlarını nasıl açıklar?
ch.why: Hipoteze göre V-212 yalnızca ortamda antioksidan katkı bulunduğunda koruyucu etki gösteriyordu; ticari ortamda bu katkı olmadığı için etki görülmüyordu.

text: Three weeks later, the answer arrived in a table, and when Dana had finished typing it, she turned the screen towards Ilan without saying anything. The experiment had been repeated in both laboratories, with the same plates, on the same days, with identical protocols and the four combinations. In Dana's own laboratory, with the supplement, V-212 reduced cell damage by sixty-eight per cent, as in the original paper. Without the supplement, the reduction was four per cent, within the range of error. In Dr. Lindqvist's laboratory, the results were mirror images: without the supplement, four per cent. With the supplement added by hand, sixty-four.

"It is the same result in two places," said Dana. "It simply needs a condition we did not know about." Ilan read the numbers a second time, then smiled, with a deep satisfaction. "It means that our first paper was correct, and incomplete. We described an effect and gave it as a property of the compound. It is a property of the compound in a particular environment."

He drafted a short note for the journal that afternoon, to be published as a correction: the original conclusions stood, but with the added statement that the effect depended on an antioxidant co-factor. He also put the full recipe of the medium in the methods section, with every ingredient, and, at Dana's suggestion, wrote to Professor Okafor with a joint authorship proposal for a second paper about the mechanism.

"What have we learned?" Dana asked, as she closed the laptop. "That a reproducible result," said Ilan, "is not one that works for the person who found it. It is one that works for the person who has the instructions."
ch.clue: It is a property of the compound in a particular environment
ch.q: What conclusion do Ilan and Dana reach after the four-condition experiment?
o: The compound V-212 has no effect on cells in any environment
The original result was correct but depended on a condition which the paper had not described
The commercial medium is better than the medium made in the laboratory
Professor Okafor's laboratory had not followed the protocol correctly
The original result was a mistake which must be withdrawn from the journal
ch.hint: Destek maddesi olmadan etki %4'e düşüyor, destekle %68'e çıkıyor ve iki laboratuvarda da aynı. Ilan'a göre bu, ilk makale hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: İlk sonuç doğruydu ama yayımlanan yöntemde anılmayan bir koşula (antioksidan katkıya) bağlıydı; yani eksikti, yanlış değildi.

outro: Fark, hücrelerin kültürlendiği sıvının içindeki bir katkı maddesindeydi: bir laboratuvar kendi karışımını hazırlıyordu, diğeri ticari bir ürün kullanıyordu. Ilan şunu yazdı: bir sonuç, başka kimse yapamıyorsa, bir keşiften çok bir koşul haline gelir.

title: The Quoted Expert
hero: Muhabir Jonas Reid ve fotoğrafçı Ellie
intro: Ülke çapında yayımlanan bir haber, 'önde gelen bir uzmanın' yeni bir diyetin kalp hastalığını yüzde otuz azalttığını söylediğini yazıyor. Jonas Reid ile Ellie, uzmanın kim olduğunu, ne söylediğini ve çalışmanın gerçekte neyi gösterdiğini araştırıyor.

text: By the time Jonas Reid arrived at the Kingsbridge Daily on Monday morning, the headline had been shared across the town's social media pages more than four thousand times. It had appeared in a national newspaper on Sunday, in bold letters across a picture of a bowl of olives and fish: New diet cuts heart disease by 30%, says leading expert. Beneath it, a short article of about four hundred words explained that Professor Alan Mercer, of a university in the north, had studied the eating habits of twenty thousand adults for twelve years, and had found that those who followed the so-called Atlantic diet, rich in fish, vegetables and olive oil, suffered almost a third fewer heart attacks.

Mrs. Cole called Jonas into her office. "Three readers have emailed us this morning," she said, "asking whether the town's doctors are going to prescribe it. The local health food shop has already put up a poster. I should like a piece that tells our readers what this means, and whether it is true. Do not be dramatic. Simply find out."

"A single study, a single expert," said Jonas, looking at the article. "The newspaper does not give the title of the research, nor the journal in which it appeared. It mentions the professor's name and his university, and it says that the diet 'cuts' heart disease. That is a verb about cause. I want to see the original."

Ellie, who was waiting by the door with her camera bag over her shoulder, grinned. "You are going to read a scientific paper," she said. "On a Monday." "I am going to find the paper," said Jonas, "and see what it says before anyone tells me what it means."
ch.clue: That is a verb about cause
ch.q: What does Jonas notice about the way the newspaper describes the research?
o: It claims that the research was carried out in the town of Kingsbridge
It says that the diet cuts heart disease, a phrase which suggests cause, without naming the study
It says that the diet is dangerous and should not be used by anyone
It reports that the study followed only twenty adults for a few weeks
It names the study and the journal but gives the wrong name for the professor
ch.hint: Jonas "cuts" fiilinin bir neden-sonuç ifadesi olduğunu söylüyor ve gazetenin çalışmanın adını ya da dergisini vermediğini fark ediyor. Haberin dilinde onu şüphelendiren iki şey nedir?
ch.why: Haber "diyet kalp hastalığını azaltıyor" diyerek bir neden-sonuç ilişkisi ima ediyordu ve çalışmanın adını ya da yayımlandığı dergiyi vermiyordu.

text: It took Jonas about forty minutes to find the paper. The professor's university had a press office, and a young woman there, after some polite hesitation, sent him a link to the study in a medical journal and a short summary prepared for the media. He read the summary first, and then, with a cup of tea going cold at his elbow, the paper itself.

The study was real, and it had been carefully done. Mercer's team had followed twenty thousand adults, aged between forty-five and seventy, for twelve years. At the start, each participant filled in a long questionnaire about what they ate, and the researchers rated each diet on a scale from zero to ten, according to how closely it resembled the Atlantic pattern. During the following years, they recorded heart attacks. At the end, they compared the top quarter of the scale with the bottom quarter. The heart attack rate in the top group was thirty per cent lower.

Ellie, reading over his shoulder, said, "So it is true." "It is true that the people in the top group had fewer heart attacks," said Jonas. "That is a statement about what happened. What the newspaper said is a statement about why it happened. And there is a sentence in the paper's own discussion which the newspaper did not quote." He pointed at the screen: This is an observational study, and it cannot prove that the diet itself caused the difference. People who follow such a diet may also differ from the others in other ways.
"They did not tell the participants what to eat," said Ellie slowly. "They simply watched what people chose."
"Exactly," said Jonas. "And that is a very different thing."
ch.clue: it cannot prove that the diet itself caused the difference
ch.q: What kind of study did Professor Mercer's team carry out?
o: An experiment in which participants were told exactly what to eat for twelve years
A review of previous studies which had all given the same conclusion
A laboratory study of the effects of fish oil on the hearts of animals
An observational study that recorded what people chose to eat and later compared their health
A survey of doctors about their opinions on the best diet for patients
ch.hint: Araştırmacılar katılımcılara ne yiyeceklerini söylemedi, sadece ne seçtiklerini izledi. Bu tür çalışmaya ne ad verilir ve ne kadar kanıt sağlar?
ch.why: Çalışma, insanların kendi seçtikleri yiyecekleri kaydedip sağlıklarını sonradan karşılaştıran gözlemsel bir çalışmaydı; neden-sonuç ilişkisini kanıtlayamazdı.

text: Jonas wanted to understand why the authors themselves were cautious. He telephoned Professor Mercer, who proved to be a courteous man with a slight Scottish accent and, as Jonas later wrote, none of the certainty that the headline attributed to him. "I am afraid that the newspaper did not quite capture my view," said the professor. "I told the reporter that we had found a strong association. She wrote that we had shown a cause. They are not the same sentence."

"What else, in your opinion, could explain the difference?" asked Jonas. Mercer took a moment. "Think about who, in our population, follows a pattern of fish, vegetables and olive oil, which is more expensive than a diet of processed food. In our data, those people were on average wealthier, better educated, more likely to exercise regularly, less likely to smoke, and more likely to see a doctor early. We tried to adjust for such factors statistically, and the association remained, though it became smaller, about twenty per cent rather than thirty. But no adjustment can remove every difference between groups of people who choose differently."
