"So the lower heart attack rate might partly be the effect of the way of life that goes with the diet?" Jonas wrote the words carefully. "Quite possibly," said Mercer. "The only way to be certain is a trial, in which people are assigned at random to a diet, and followed. There have been a few such trials, with a Mediterranean diet, and they show a real benefit, though a smaller one than the observational studies. It is a promising idea. It is not proved."
"And the figure of thirty per cent," said Jonas, "which everyone shared?" The professor sighed. "That was the first number that we calculated, before the adjustments."
ch.clue: no adjustment can remove every difference between groups of people who choose differently
ch.q: Why might the real benefit of the diet be smaller than thirty per cent?
o: People who follow the diet also differ in wealth, exercise and smoking, which affect heart health
The study lasted only a few weeks, which is too short to show a real change
The researchers made a mistake in counting the heart attacks in the second group
The participants who ate fish had less access to doctors than the others
The twenty thousand adults were all too old for the diet to have any effect
ch.hint: Profesör, diyeti izleyen insanların daha zengin, daha eğitimli, daha çok egzersiz yapan ve daha az sigara içen kişiler olduğunu söylüyor. Bu farklar kalp sağlığını nasıl etkileyebilir ve yüzde 30'u nasıl etkiler?
ch.why: Diyeti izleyenler zenginlik, egzersiz ve sigara gibi kalp sağlığını etkileyen başka bakımlardan da farklıydı; bu faktörler düzeltildiğinde fark yaklaşık yüzde 20'ye düşüyordu.

text: Jonas wrote the piece on Tuesday afternoon, and it was not the kind of article that anyone would share four thousand times. Its headline was careful: Atlantic diet linked to fewer heart attacks, but the study cannot prove that it is the cause. Beneath it, he explained in plain language what an observational study is, why the adjustments reduced the figure from thirty to twenty per cent, and what a randomised trial would add. He quoted Professor Mercer's remark about the difference between an association and a cause, and the local doctor, Dr. Nasser, who said that she would recommend more fish and vegetables to anybody, on the grounds that they were good for health in general, but that nobody should expect a diet alone to protect them from a heart attack.

Mrs. Cole read it standing, as she always did. "It is a good piece," she said. "But I would like you to anticipate the question that the readers will ask. They will say: so should we eat the diet or not?"

Jonas had already thought of it. At the end, he had written: The study gives no reason to avoid the Atlantic diet and some reason to try it. What it does not give is a guarantee. A shared headline promises a result. A good study offers a direction.

"Leave that last sentence," said Mrs. Cole. Ellie's photograph, a plain table with bread, fish and a bowl of green salad, ran across two columns. The shop's poster stayed in the window, but, in the corner, somebody had added a small card with the title of the study.
ch.clue: A shared headline promises a result. A good study offers a direction.
ch.q: What is the main message of Jonas's article?
o: The diet is a proven cure which every reader should follow at once
Doctors in Kingsbridge will soon refuse to treat patients who eat badly
The diet is linked to fewer heart attacks, but the study cannot prove that it is the cause
The newspaper that published the first story deliberately lied to its readers
The study is false and the professor invented the results to become famous
ch.hint: Jonas'ın makalesinin başlığı çalışmanın "bağlantı" gösterdiğini ama "nedensellik" kanıtlayamadığını söylüyor. Makalenin ana mesajı bu ayrımı mı vurguluyor yoksa diyeti reddediyor mu?
ch.why: Makale, diyetin daha az kalp krizi ile ilişkili olduğunu ama çalışmanın bunun nedeni olduğunu kanıtlayamadığını söylüyordu.

outro: Uzman gerçekti, çalışma da gerçekti; ama haber, bir gözlem çalışmasını bir neden-sonuç kanıtı gibi sunuyordu. Jonas şunu yazdı: iki şeyin birlikte görülmesi, birinin diğerine yol açtığı anlamına gelmez.

title: The Silent Orchard
hero: Park korucusu Wren Calder ve köpeği Bracken
intro: Vadideki eski bir meyve bahçesinde, bahar çiçeklenmesi sırasında hiçbir arı görünmüyor ve ağaçlar neredeyse hiç meyve vermiyor. Wren Calder ile Bracken, bahçeyi ve çevresini inceleyerek arıların neden kaybolduğunu ve bunun bahçenin geleceği için ne anlama geldiğini araştırıyor.

text: At the top of the valley, where the road dwindled to a track and the track to a grassy path, there was an orchard that the people of the village called the Old Garden. It had about sixty apple and pear trees, planted by a family that had vanished from local memory, and which now belonged to the National Trust. Ranger Wren Calder had visited it every May for eleven years, because it was one of the loveliest sights in the valley: a white and pink cloud of blossom, and in it, a deep, continuous hum of bees.

This May, she walked through the gate on a warm, windless morning and stopped. The trees were in full blossom, as beautiful as ever, with petals already beginning to fall. But the hum was missing. She stood at the centre of the orchard with her head tilted, and Bracken, who sensed her mood, stood beside her with his ears forward. There was the sound of a chaffinch, and the rustle of the grass. There were no bees.

She counted for ten minutes by the clock, as she had done in previous years, watching a single tree. In the first year of her records, she had counted an average of forty visits by bees to a branch in ten minutes. This morning she counted three: two small flies, and one bumblebee that stayed for a few seconds and flew away towards the hill.

"The trees are fine," she said to Bracken. "They are flowering well. The weather is perfect. It is the visitors who have stopped coming." She wrote a short note in her book, and underlined one sentence: The orchard is not empty. It has been avoided.
ch.clue: It has been avoided
ch.q: What distinguishes this May from the previous years in the Old Garden?
o: The trees have no blossom at all because of a late frost in April
The weather is cold and wet so the bees stay in their hives
The trees flower normally, but almost no bees visit the blossom
The orchard has been sold to a family that cuts the trees down
The bees are present but they are too tired to visit the flowers
ch.hint: Ağaçlar çiçek açmış, hava güzel, ama arılar yok. Wren "bahçe boş değil, kaçınılıyor" diye yazıyor. Bu durumda sorunun ağaçlarda mı, yoksa arılarda mı olduğunu ayıran ipucu ne?
ch.why: Ağaçlar normal çiçek açıyordu, hava da uygundu, ama arılar neredeyse hiç gelmiyordu; yani sorun çiçeklerde değil, ziyaretçilerdeydi.

text: Wren spent the next week looking for the missing bees, and it was not easy to find a trace of them. The simplest explanation was that a disease had wiped out the local hives. She visited the apiary of Mr. Dunstan, the beekeeper who kept eight hives at the edge of the valley, a kilometre and a half from the orchard. He was a small, sunburnt man with a slow smile, and he walked her between the white boxes without gloves.

"They are in good health," he said. "Strong, busy, plenty of brood. I have had no losses this spring, which is not common. I have checked them for mites, as I do every month, and for disease. Nothing." He lifted a frame from the nearest hive, thick with bees and with a smell of wax and honey. "What puzzles me is that they are not going to the orchard. Every year, in May, they go down in a stream. This year, they leave the hive and fly in the other direction, to the lime trees by the road, and to the meadow on the south slope, and they bring back plenty of pollen. But not from the Old Garden."

"You are sure they avoid it?" asked Wren. "I marked fifty bees with a little spot of paint last week," said Mr. Dunstan, "and watched where they went. Forty-one flew south. Seven went east. Two went north. None went west."

Wren looked at the hills, where the lime trees were fresh and green. "West is the direction of the orchard," she said. "They have the whole valley open to them, and they choose to fly around one place. Something there is saying no."
ch.clue: None went west
ch.q: What does Mr. Dunstan's experiment with the marked bees show?
o: The hives are too far from the orchard for any bees to reach it
The painted bees die because of the paint and cannot be followed
The bees are sick and cannot fly as far as the orchard
The bees prefer to visit the orchard but are prevented by wind
The bees are healthy, but they avoid flying in the direction of the orchard
ch.hint: Dunstan elli arıyı boyayıp izledi: kırk biri güneye, yedisi doğuya, ikisi kuzeye gitti, batıya ise hiçbiri gitmedi. Bu sonuç arıların sağlığı ve davranışı hakkında ne söylüyor?
ch.why: Arılar sağlıklıydı ama kasıtlı olarak bahçenin bulunduğu batı yönüne gitmiyorlardı; bahçeye giden yolda bir şey onları uzak tutuyordu.

text: Wren drew a line on the map, from Mr. Dunstan's apiary, straight west, towards the orchard, and followed it with her finger beyond the gate. Between the hives and the Old Garden, about four hundred metres from the trees, there was a large rectangular field marked simply Longcroft. It was the only open land that the bees would have crossed on their way. The previous summer, it had been a field of barley. She walked there the next morning with Bracken, and stopped at the gate.

The field was a sheet of brilliant yellow, a carpet of flowering oilseed rape, shining in the sun. It was in full bloom, a perfect meal for a bee, and in the whole of the field, which she examined from the gate for a quarter of an hour, she did not see a single insect. At the edge of the track, a small signboard was fixed to a post, with a printed label in blue letters. It was the farmer's notice of work: Seed treated with ThiaGuard. Do not graze. Keep animals and pets out for 14 days after spraying.

Wren read it twice, and took a photograph. "ThiaGuard," she said. "I have not met it before." Her phone had enough signal to find a data sheet, and she read it standing in the gateway with a hand over the screen against the sun. The active substance was a systemic insecticide, absorbed by the plant and carried into the pollen and nectar. Bees that visit the flowers of a treated crop can be affected for days.
"The orchard is not the problem," she said slowly to Bracken. "It is the road to it."
ch.clue: carried into the pollen and nectar
ch.q: Why is the oilseed rape field dangerous for bees?
o: The rape plants release a smell that makes bees forget the way home
The plants are treated with a systemic insecticide which passes into their pollen and nectar
The flowers have been cut so that no pollen can be collected from them
The field is covered with a net which traps the bees as they fly across
The farmer keeps animals in the field which frighten the bees
ch.hint: ThiaGuard sistemik bir böcek ilacı: bitki tarafından emilip polen ve nektara taşınıyor. Bu, kanola çiçeğini ziyaret eden arılar için ne anlama gelir?
ch.why: İlaç sistemikti ve bitkinin poleni ile nektarına geçiyordu; çiçekleri ziyaret eden arılar günlerce etkilenebilirdi.

text: The farmer of Longcroft turned out to be a young woman named Ms. Perrin, who had taken over the land from her father two years earlier. Wren found her in the farmyard, cleaning a sprayer, and began, as gently as she could, with the question of how the crop was doing. Ms. Perrin was proud of the yellow field. She had chosen the oilseed rape because of the prices, and the seed treatment, she explained, had been recommended by the supplier. "It protects the young plants from beetles. I did not think about the bees. The salesman said it was safe if one did not spray during the flowering."

"The treatment is in the seed," said Wren, "not on the leaves. It goes into the plant and into the flower." She showed her the data sheet, with the paragraph about pollinators underlined. Ms. Perrin read it with a growing frown, and sat on the edge of an old trough. "I had no idea," she said. "Mr. Dunstan is my neighbour. I have known him all my life. I would never have wished to harm his bees."

"It is nobody's fault," said Wren. "The information was hard to find. But there are alternatives. Another seed treatment, or a different crop on this field next year, such as beans, which bees love and which add nitrogen to the soil. The Trust could help with the cost."

The next spring, Longcroft was a field of pale-flowered field beans. On the third of May, Wren walked through the gate of the Old Garden, with Bracken at her heels, and heard it before she saw it: a deep, steady hum, rising from sixty trees. She counted for ten minutes. Thirty-seven visits.
ch.clue: The information was hard to find
ch.q: How was the problem solved in the following year?
o: The insecticide was washed away by heavy rain over the winter
The beekeeper moved his hives to a different valley far away
The orchard was cut down and replaced by a field of oilseed rape
The farmer changed the crop to beans and the bees returned to the orchard
The Trust bought all the farms around the orchard and closed them
ch.hint: Wren çiftçiye tohum ilacının arılara etkisini gösterdi ve alternatif sundu. Ertesi bahar Longcroft'ta ne ekiliydi ve arılara ne oldu?
ch.why: Çiftçi ekinini bakla ile değiştirdi ve ertesi bahar arılar bahçeye geri döndü.

outro: Arılar, bahçenin yakınındaki bir tarlaya sıkılan yeni bir ilacın bulaştığı çiçeklerden kaçınıyordu. Çiftçi ilacı bırakınca, bir sonraki yıl arılar geri döndü. Wren şunu yazdı: bir ekosistemde sessizlik genellikle boşluk değil, bir uyarıdır.

title: The Borrowed Masterpiece
hero: Küratör Hugo Laurent ve güvenlik görevlisi Mina
intro: Büyük bir sergi için ödünç alınan değerli bir portre müzeye geliyor, ama sigorta uzmanı tablonun boyutunun kayıtlardakinden birkaç santim farklı olduğunu fark ediyor. Hugo Laurent ile Mina, çerçeveyi, arka yüzü ve nakliye belgelerini inceleyerek tablonun gerçekten orijinal olup olmadığını araştırıyor.

text: The portrait of Lady Ashworth arrived at the City Museum on a Tuesday afternoon, in a crate lined with grey foam and carried by four men in white gloves. It was the centrepiece of the new exhibition on portraits of the eighteenth century, and it had been borrowed, after eight months of negotiation, from a private collection in Scotland. The insurers had valued it at four million pounds.

According to the museum's procedure, every incoming object is measured and compared with the loan agreement before it is unpacked completely. Hugo Laurent was present with the insurance assessor, a precise woman named Ms. Brandt, who carried a steel tape and a clipboard. When the front of the crate was removed, the painting was lifted onto a padded table in the conservation room, and Ms. Brandt measured it twice, murmuring the numbers. Then she measured it a third time and said, in a neutral tone, "Mr. Laurent, there is a discrepancy."

"The loan agreement," she read from the clipboard, "states that the framed painting measures 112 by 87 centimetres. This one is 112 by 90. The height is the same. The width is three centimetres more." Mina, who had come in to accompany the transport and was standing by the door, said quietly, "It is a very small difference."

"For a four-million-pound painting," said Ms. Brandt, "it is a large one. A discrepancy between the document and the object may mean an error in the document, or a different object. I am obliged to record it, and the insurance cannot be activated until it is explained."
Hugo looked at the painting, a young woman with a pale face and an amused mouth, and then at the clipboard. "Then we shall explain it," he said.
ch.clue: A discrepancy between the document and the object may mean an error in the document, or a different object
ch.q: Why is the three-centimetre difference important to the insurer?
o: It proves that the museum measured the painting with a faulty tape
It means that the exhibition has no room for such a wide painting
It shows that the crate was too small to carry the painting safely
It may mean that the document is wrong or that the object is not the one described
It means that the painting was damaged during the journey from Scotland
ch.hint: Ms. Brandt, belge ile nesne arasındaki farkın iki şeyden birini gösterebileceğini söylüyor. Sigortacı bu farkı neden açıklanmadan kabul edemez?
ch.why: Ölçü farkı, belgenin yanlış olabileceğini ya da nesnenin belgelenen nesne olmayabileceğini gösteriyordu; açıklanmadan sigorta etkin olamazdı.

text: Hugo's first thought was that the difference might lie in the frame rather than the painting. Together with a conservator named Dr. Osei, he moved the painting to a bench under a bright lamp and examined the back. A painting of this kind consists of a canvas stretched on a wooden frame, called a stretcher, and then placed in an ornamental outer frame. The loan agreement gave only the outer measurements, with the frame included.

Dr. Osei measured the canvas alone, with the help of a thin ruler, by lifting the edge of the outer frame gently and looking at the picture beneath it. The visible part was 98 by 73 centimetres, and the part hidden by the frame, folded around the edges of the stretcher, added a few more. "The canvas appears to be exactly what the catalogue says," he said. "Ninety-eight and a half by seventy-three and a half. The painting itself is right. The difference is in the frame, which is three centimetres wider than recorded."

Hugo turned the outer frame slowly in the light. It was a handsome piece, carved and gilded, with a pattern of leaves at the corners. "A frame can have been changed," he said. "It may have been replaced at some point in its history, and the loan form may have been made from an old record." He bent to look at the wood on the back. "And if it was replaced, there will be signs. Look at the colour of the wood on this side, and on this one."
Ms. Brandt came closer. On the left side of the frame, the back was a deep brown, polished by age. On the right side, the wood was pale and fresh in colour, with the sharp marks of a different tool.
ch.clue: the part hidden by the frame
ch.q: What do Hugo and Dr. Osei discover when they examine the painting?
o: The canvas matches the catalogue, but the frame is wider and appears partly to be a replacement
The measurements on the loan form are correct and the tape was wrong
The painting is a copy that was made on a different canvas
The canvas is three centimetres wider than recorded and has been cut
The frame is exactly right but the canvas has been replaced by a larger one
ch.hint: Boyanın kendisi katalogdaki ölçüye uyuyor, ama çerçeve üç santim daha geniş ve bir tarafı farklı renkte. Fark tuvalde mi, yoksa çerçevede mi?
ch.why: Tuval katalogdaki ölçüye uyuyordu; fark çerçevedeydi ve çerçevenin bir kısmı sonradan değiştirilmiş gibi görünüyordu.

text: A replaced frame was a plausible explanation, but it did not yet explain why the loan agreement recorded a smaller measurement. Hugo wanted to know when the change had been made, and by whom, because if the frame had been altered recently, the owner might have forgotten to update the form, or the picture's history might include an incident that the museum should know about. He asked the registrar to find every document about Lady Ashworth that the museum had received, and by evening he had a folder of seven items on his desk.

The first was the loan agreement, signed in March, with the measurement 112 by 87. The second was a condition report written in the Scottish house in the previous year by a restorer, with a photograph and the same measurement. But the third, a catalogue from a 1962 exhibition in Edinburgh in which the portrait had been shown, gave a measurement of 112 by 90, and so did the fourth, a record from a Glasgow auction in 1938. Only the two most recent documents gave 87.

Mina had been reading over his shoulder. "So the older documents agree with the painting as it is today," she said, "and the newer ones disagree. The frame is not new. It is old, and it has been the same for a hundred years. The recent forms are the ones that are wrong."

"The question is where the error began," said Hugo, "and I think I see the pattern. The restorer's report is dated last year. Did anyone remeasure the frame then, or did they copy the figure from an earlier form?" He picked up the last sheet and found, at the bottom, a signature and a short note: dimensions taken from the insurance schedule of 1994.
ch.clue: dimensions taken from the insurance schedule of 1994
ch.q: What do the older documents show?
o: Older records show that the frame was changed in the previous year
Older records are missing so the history of the frame is unknown
Older records give the same measurement as the actual frame, so the recent forms contain the error
Older records state that the portrait was a different size at an earlier time
Older records confirm the figure in the loan agreement of March
ch.hint: 1962 kataloğu ve 1938 müzayede kaydı, tablonun bugünkü çerçevesiyle uyumlu olan 90 cm genişliği veriyor, yalnızca yeni belgeler 87 cm diyor. Bu fark hangi belgelerde hatalı olabilir?
ch.why: Eski kayıtlar çerçevenin bugünkü ölçüsüyle (90 cm) uyuşuyordu, yani hata yakın tarihli formlarda başlamıştı.

text: Hugo telephoned the owner's agent in Scotland that evening, and found him an uncomplicated, helpful man named Mr. Rennie. "I am sorry that you have had to go to such trouble," he said, after listening to the story. "Let me look at the insurance schedule of 1994." There was a rustle of papers. "Here it is. The painting is described as 112 by 87. But I notice that the description says 'canvas dimensions', not 'framed dimensions'. I think that someone in the 1990s measured the canvas with the stretcher, and then, over the years, each document copied the number and added the word 'framed'. The restorer, the lawyer and the museum all took the figure from the previous form, and no one ever took a ruler to the frame."

"The error has been copied for thirty years," said Hugo. "And nobody noticed, because the painting never travelled before." Mr. Rennie laughed softly. "In that case, I am grateful to your Ms. Brandt, who measured it three times."

When the call was over, Hugo wrote a short note for the museum's file: the framed dimensions of the portrait of Lady Ashworth are 112 by 90 centimetres. The loan agreement was amended and signed by both parties the next morning, and the insurance was activated at noon. In the conservation room, Ms. Brandt placed a small, neat label on the back of the frame, with the correct measurements and the date on which they had been checked.
"What have we learned?" asked Mina. "That a document is a memory," said Hugo, "and memories are copied. The only way to be sure of an object is to look at the object."
ch.clue: no one ever took a ruler to the frame
ch.q: How did the incorrect measurement come to be in the loan agreement?
o: The frame was cut by three centimetres during the journey to the museum
The museum measured the painting incorrectly when the crate arrived
The painting had been replaced by a different one in the previous year
The owner deliberately gave a smaller measurement to reduce the insurance
An early document recorded the canvas size, and later forms copied it as the framed size
ch.hint: Mr. Rennie 1994 sigorta çizelgesinin "tuval ölçüsü" yazdığını, sonraki belgelerin ise bunu "çerçeveli ölçü" diye kopyaladığını söylüyor. Hata nasıl yayılmış?
ch.why: Eski bir belge yalnızca tuvalin ölçüsünü yazmıştı ve sonraki formlar bu rakamı çerçeveli ölçü olarak kopyalamıştı; kimse çerçeveyi ölçmemişti.

outro: Tablo gerçekti, ama çerçevesi iki yüz yıl önce değiştirilmişti ve kayıtlardaki ölçü eski çerçeveye aitti. Hugo şunu yazdı: bir belgedeki rakam nesneyi değil, nesnenin belgelendiği anı ölçer.

title: The Cartographer's Study
hero: Oyun testçileri Zoe ve Max
intro: Zoe ve Max bu kez bir haritacının çalışma odasında. Duvarlarda haritalar, masada bir pusula, cetvel ve şifreli bir defter var. Her harita bir sonraki bulmacanın anahtarı. Kalan süre altmış dakika.

text: The door of the cartographer's study closed with the soft, well-oiled click of a very expensive lock. In the lamplight, Zoe and Max saw a long room with a sloping ceiling, a great oak desk, and maps on every wall, all of them framed and carefully labelled with brass plates. On the desk lay a brass compass, a long steel ruler and a leather notebook with a clasp. Above the door, a small display showed the time: 60:00.

A card on the desk was propped against the lamp. Max picked it up and read it aloud. "The cartographer left his keys in the place that is exactly twelve kilometres from the lighthouse, in a straight line, towards the north-east. The first map shows the lighthouse. Use the scale, find the place, and read the number written there."

Zoe walked to the first map, a large chart of a coast with a spiral of small islands. The lighthouse was marked with a red star at the lower edge. At the bottom of the map, there was a scale bar: a line divided into segments, with the words 1 cm = 3 km. "That is simple," she said. "Twelve kilometres is four centimetres. We measure four centimetres from the star with the ruler, in the direction north-east."

"Careful," said Max, looking at the compass rose in the corner. "On a map, north is usually at the top, but not always. Look at the arrow." Zoe leaned closer. The arrow pointing to N was not straight up the page. It pointed to the upper left, at an angle of about forty-five degrees.
"So the top of the map is not north," said Zoe slowly. "The cartographer turned this map, and made us read it carefully."
ch.clue: The arrow pointing to N was not straight up the page
ch.q: Why can Zoe not simply measure towards the upper right of the map to find north-east?
o: The ruler is too short to measure four centimetres on the page
The lighthouse is not marked on the map in the right place
The map has no scale, and the distances cannot be calculated
The compass on the desk shows that north is in the opposite direction
The north arrow on this map points to the upper left, so the directions on the page are rotated
ch.hint: Haritada kuzey oku sayfanın üstünü değil, sol üst köşeyi gösteriyor. Bu durumda "kuzeydoğu" sayfada hangi yöne denk gelir?
ch.why: Kuzey oku sayfanın sol üstüne baktığı için haritadaki yönler döndürülmüştü; sayfanın üstü kuzey değildi.

text: Zoe held the ruler against the page, and Max helped by pressing the corner of the map with two fingers. "Let us do it step by step," she said. "On this map, north points to the upper left. That means that if I turn my head forty-five degrees to the left, the top of the page would be north. East is ninety degrees clockwise from north, and north-east is halfway between the two. So I must find the direction that lies exactly between the two, and lay the ruler along it." She put the ruler on the star of the lighthouse and drew a very faint pencil line along that direction. "Four centimetres," she said, and made a small mark. The mark fell in the middle of a tiny island, almost invisible, with a number printed on it in a very small font: 7.

Max checked the arithmetic twice, because a single slip with a ruler could cost them ten minutes. "Four centimetres at three kilometres each makes twelve. And the island is exactly at the end of the line." He read the number again. "Seven. The first digit, probably." A little drawer in the frame of the map opened with a click, and a small brass key fell into his palm. A label was tied to it: Second map. Use the compass.
"That was only the first," said Zoe, glancing at the clock, which showed 54:20. "But we have understood the trick. The cartographer does not like the obvious."
ch.clue: north-east is halfway between the two
ch.q: In which direction on the page does Zoe draw her line, and why?
o: Towards the upper left, because that is the direction of the north arrow
Straight up the page, because north-east lies halfway between north (up-left) and east (up-right)
Towards the upper right, because north-east is always at the top right
Towards the left, because east is on the right side of the page
Straight down the page, because the lighthouse is at the bottom of the map
ch.hint: Kuzey sol üstte ve doğu sağ üstte olduğuna göre, kuzeydoğu bu ikisinin tam ortasındadır. Bu yön sayfada nereye bakar?
ch.why: Kuzey sol üstte, doğu sağ üsttedir; ikisinin tam ortası olan kuzeydoğu ise sayfada düz yukarıyı gösterir.

text: The second map was smaller, an old-fashioned chart of a harbour with five buildings drawn in perspective, and a brass plate that read: A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north. Zoe took the compass from the desk, and read the instructions on the card beneath the glass: Stand at the Customs House. The warehouse is on a bearing of 135 degrees. The church is on a bearing of 225 degrees. What is the angle between the warehouse and the church, as seen from the Customs House?

"That is simpler than I feared," said Max. He took a pencil and drew a quick diagram on the margin of the notebook. "A bearing of zero is north. Ninety is east, a hundred and eighty is south, two hundred and seventy is west. A hundred and thirty-five is half way between east and south, so the warehouse is to the south-east. Two hundred and twenty-five is half way between south and west, so the church is to the south-west."

"And the angle between them is the difference," said Zoe. "Two hundred and twenty-five minus a hundred and thirty-five." She did the subtraction slowly, because the clock on the wall was reading 47:10 and she was aware of Max's attention. "It is ninety degrees," she said. "They are at right angles. And the card says that the answer is the second digit of the code."

Max wrote 9 and 0 side by side in the notebook, and then frowned. "The code has a digit, not a pair. It must be only the first figure of the answer, that is, nine, divided by..." He looked back at the card, where in the corner a line in tiny type said: Use the number of tens.
ch.clue: Two hundred and twenty-five minus a hundred and thirty-five
ch.q: What is the angle between the warehouse and the church, seen from the Customs House?
o: 45 degrees
135 degrees
360 degrees
90 degrees
180 degrees
ch.hint: Depo 135 derecede, kilise 225 derecede. İki yön arasındaki açı iki sayının farkıdır. 225 eksi 135 kaç eder?
ch.why: Açı, iki kerterizin farkıdır: 225 − 135 = 90 derece.

text: "The number of tens in ninety is nine," said Zoe. "So the second digit is 9, and the code begins 7, 9." The second brass key unlocked a glass case on the wall, in which, under a black cloth, there was a third map: a modern street plan of a city, ruled in squares, with letters along the top and numbers down the side. On a card pinned to its frame were four short lines.

Grid reference: first the letter, then the number. The museum is at D4. The station is two squares to the east of the museum and three to the south. The post office is at the station's reference with the letter moved three steps backwards in the alphabet. The code's last two digits are the number in the post office's reference, written twice.

Max traced the lines with his finger. "The museum is at D4. East means to the right, so the letters go forward: D, E, F. Two squares east is F. South means down, and the numbers grow downwards, so three squares south is 4 plus 3, which is 7. The station is at F7." He frowned. "Now, the post office is the station's reference with the letter moved three steps backwards: F, E, D, C. It is C7."
"The number in the reference is 7," said Zoe. "Written twice: 77." She read aloud the digits that they had collected: seven, nine, seven, seven. The clock showed 22:05.
"It is a long code," said Max, "but it has the shape of a story. And it is the only one that the notebook has accepted so far." He carried the notebook to the desk, and opened the clasp.
ch.clue: the letter moved three steps backwards in the alphabet
ch.q: What is the grid reference of the post office, and what two digits does it give?
o: C7, so the last two digits are 77
F7, so the last two digits are 77
C4, so the last two digits are 44
I7, so the last two digits are 77
D4, so the last two digits are 44
ch.hint: İstasyon F7. Postane, istasyonun harfi alfabede üç adım geriye götürülerek bulunuyor. F'den üç adım geri hangi harf? Numara aynı kalıyor.
ch.why: İstasyon F7'ydi; harf üç adım geriye gidince postane C7 oluyor ve numara iki kez yazılınca 77 çıkıyor.

outro: Son harita yerine oturduğunda gizli bölme açıldı ve Zoe ile Max dışarı çıktı. Oyunun yaratıcısı, en iyi bulmacaların oyuncuya bir şey öğrettiğini ve bu odanın da ölçek, yön ve koordinat gibi kavramlara dayandığını söyledi.

title: The Expired Visa
hero: Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ve stajyer Sam
intro: Bir iş seyahati yapan genç bir mühendis, geçerli bir vizesi olduğuna emin. Havalimanı sistemi ise vizesinin üç gün önce sona erdiğini gösteriyor. Dara Mills ile Sam, pasaportu, vize belgesini ve giriş-çıkış kayıtlarını karşılaştırarak gerçek durumu bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: At nine o'clock on a Friday evening, the immigration hall at Heathfield was almost empty. Dara Mills was finishing her last report of the day when Sam, her trainee, came to the door of her office with a look that she recognised: the face of a young person who had run into something that was not in the manual. "There is a passenger at the desk," he said. "A Mr. Reyes, an engineer from Manila. He is leaving for Singapore on the ten-forty flight. The system says that his visa is expired, and the airline will not let him board."

Dara followed him down the corridor. At the desk, a slim man in a dark suit was standing with a travel bag over his shoulder, and with the calm that comes from complete certainty. "There must be an error," he said. "I have a business visa for the United Kingdom, issued for a stay of six months. I arrived on the fifth of March and I leave tonight, the twenty-fifth of April. I have been very careful about the dates. I have checked them on the visa itself."

Dara took the passport and opened it at the visa page, a printed sticker with a photograph, a number, and a table of dates. It stated: Valid from 03/02/2025. Valid until 03/08/2025. Duration of stay: 6 months. On the airline's screen, the same record said: Expiry: 3 February. Status: expired, 81 days.

"Mr. Reyes," said Dara, putting the passport down very gently, "the system says that your visa ended in February. You say that it lasts until the summer. One of you is mistaken, and I would like to find out who."
ch.clue: Valid until 03/08/2025
ch.q: What is the conflict between Mr. Reyes and the airline's system?
o: He believes the visa is valid until the summer, but the system shows that it expired in February
He has no visa at all and the airline refuses to check his documents
He wishes to stay longer than six months but the system does not allow it
He is travelling on a passport which belongs to another person
He arrived on the wrong date and the system has recorded another arrival
ch.hint: Vize sayfasında 03/02/2025 ve 03/08/2025 tarihleri yazıyor ama Mr. Reyes yazın bittiğini, sistem ise Şubat'ta bittiğini söylüyor. İki tarafın okuması neden farklı?
ch.why: Mr. Reyes vizenin yaza kadar geçerli olduğunu düşünüyordu, sistem ise vizenin Şubat'ta sona erdiğini gösteriyordu.

text: Dara looked at the sticker and then at the man's face, and she thought she understood, but she was careful. A hurried officer does not say what she sees; she asks a question that makes the passenger say it. "Mr. Reyes, when you read this line, 'Valid from 03/02/2025,' what date does it mean to you?"

"The second of March," he answered at once. "March, the third month, the second day. I arrived on the fifth of March, which is three days later. And 'valid until 03/08' is the eighth of March... " He stopped. "No. That cannot be right. It must be the third of August. Six months. I am confusing myself."

"Take your time," said Dara. "In the Philippines, as in the United States, the month usually comes first. And what does 'six months from 2 March' give you?" "The second of September," he said. "But the visa says 03/08, which in my reading is the eighth of March, which is only six days. It must be the third of August, then, I suppose, which gives five months..."

"Mr. Reyes," said Sam quietly, "may I show you something?" He pointed to the small line of printed type below the table, in a font so small that it was almost unreadable: Date format: DD/MM/YYYY. The passenger put on his glasses and read it, with a slow expression of dismay.
"Day, month, year," he said. "In your country, and in this one, the day comes first."
"So the date '03/02' means the third of February," said Dara. "And your visa began three weeks before you landed."
ch.clue: Date format: DD/MM/YYYY
ch.q: What explains the confusion over the dates on the visa?
o: Mr. Reyes had changed the dates on the sticker with a pen
The visa was printed with the wrong dates by an error of the embassy
The visa uses day-month-year, while Mr. Reyes read the dates as month-day-year
The passport has two visa stickers with different dates on each
The airline's system counts the months in a different calendar
ch.hint: Vize etiketinin altındaki küçük yazı tarih biçiminin GG/AA/YYYY olduğunu söylüyor. Mr. Reyes tarihleri nasıl okumuş ve bu neden sorun yaratmış?
ch.why: Vizedeki tarihler gün-ay-yıl biçimindeydi, Mr. Reyes ise onları ay-gün-yıl olarak okumuştu; bu yüzden vizenin başlangıç ve bitişini yanlış anlamıştı.

text: "Let us read the visa again," said Dara, "this time as it was written." She took a notepad. "Valid from 03/02/2025: day three, month two, so the third of February. Valid until 03/08/2025: day three, month eight, so the third of August. The visa is valid from the third of February until the third of August, a period of six months. That agrees with the line 'Duration of stay: 6 months'. The sticker is perfectly consistent."

Mr. Reyes sat down on the plastic chair beside the desk. "Then the visa is valid until August," he said, with relief. "I did not read the dates wrongly after all..." But Dara shook her head gently. "You read the visa correctly in one respect and incorrectly in another. It is valid until August. But the system says that it expired in February. Both cannot be right."

"Wait," said Sam. He had been tapping on the keyboard. "I have the system's record. The visa number is the same, the name is the same, but the expiry is entered as 3 February. And the validity start date is blank." He turned the screen. "I think I know what happened. The officer who entered the data at the first port of entry, in March, typed the first date in the box for the expiry, and left the second one out. The two dates are in the same format as the visa, but they are in the wrong fields."
"A data entry error," said Dara. "The visa itself is perfectly valid." She looked at the clock. It was ten past ten. "Mr. Reyes, your flight leaves in thirty minutes. Please do not move."
ch.clue: The two dates are in the same format as the visa, but they are in the wrong fields
ch.q: What is the real source of the 'expired' status in the airline's system?
o: Mr. Reyes had stayed in the country for longer than six months
The visa was cancelled by the embassy after he entered the country
The passport expired three days before the date of the flight
The system uses a different calendar from that of the visa sticker
An officer entered the start date in the expiry field when the record was made
ch.hint: Sam sistem kaydında geçerlilik başlangıcının boş, bitişin ise 3 Şubat olduğunu görüyor. Bu iki bilgi kayıt sırasında yapılmış nasıl bir hatayı gösteriyor?
ch.why: Kaydı giren görevli başlangıç tarihini yanlışlıkla bitiş alanına yazmıştı; vizenin kendisi geçerliydi.

text: Dara knew that she had very little time, and that what she needed was authority, not just a correct diagnosis. A visa that is valid on paper and invalid in the system will stop a passenger at the gate, and the airline's staff could not be expected to override the computer on the word of an immigration officer alone. She telephoned the duty supervisor, a quiet man named Mr. Okoro, who had the right to correct the records, and explained the problem in three sentences, reading him the numbers on the sticker and on the screen.

"Photograph the visa page and send it to me," said Mr. Okoro. "I will change the entry and make a note of the reason." In less than two minutes, a message appeared on Sam's screen: Record corrected. Valid from 03/02/2025. Valid until 03/08/2025. Status: valid. Reason: data entry error, port of entry, 5 March. Dara printed it, stamped it, and gave a copy to Mr. Reyes with the passport.

He took it as if it were made of glass. "I thought that I was going to miss the meeting in Singapore," he said. "I will always check the format of the dates now." Dara smiled. "It is an ordinary mistake, and a very expensive one. Governments agree on a great many things, and the order of the numbers in a date is not among them." She walked him to the gate herself.
When he had gone, Sam looked at the screen with the corrected record for a while, then took a marker and wrote on the whiteboard in the office: 03/02 = 3 February or 2 March? Always ask which.
ch.clue: Governments agree on a great many things, and the order of the numbers in a date is not among them
ch.q: What is the final lesson of the case?
o: Passengers should arrive at the airport at least four hours before the flight
The same numbers can mean different dates in different formats, so the format must always be checked
Immigration officers should refuse to answer questions from passengers
Computer records are always more reliable than printed documents
Visas should always be written in words and never in numbers
ch.hint: Dara, tarihlerdeki rakam sırasının ülkelere göre değiştiğini söylüyor ve Sam tahtaya "Always ask which" yazıyor. Bu olaydan çıkan ders nedir?
ch.why: Aynı rakamlar farklı biçimlerde farklı tarihler anlamına gelebilir; bu yüzden tarih biçimi her zaman kontrol edilmelidir.

outro: Vizenin süresi, yolcunun anladığından farklı bir tarihe göre hesaplanıyordu: belgedeki tarihler gün-ay-yıl biçimindeydi ve yolcu bunları ay-gün-yıl diye okumuştu. Dara şunu söyledi: aynı rakamlar iki ülkede iki farklı tarih olabilir; bu yüzden önce biçimi öğrenmeliyiz.

title: The Perfect Alibi
hero: Dedektif Edmund Crane ve asistanı Tess
intro: Bir iş adamı, ortağının öldürüldüğü gece, kilometrelerce uzakta bir konferansta olduğunu söylüyor ve bunu belgeliyor. Edmund Crane ile Tess, kusursuz görünen bu mazeretin içindeki küçük ayrıntıları yeniden değerlendiriyor.

text: Richard Maddox had a splendid alibi, and he knew it. On the night that his business partner, Gerald Finch, was found dead in the offices of their company in Leeds, he was, by every account, a hundred and eighty miles away in a conference hotel in Edinburgh, speaking at a dinner in front of three hundred people. The police had checked the booking, the entrance record, and the programme. There was even a recording of the evening, which the organisers had made for the members who could not attend.

Edmund Crane was asked to review the case by Mrs. Finch, who did not believe that her husband had died by accident, as the coroner's first report had suggested. He and Tess sat in the drawing room of her house, listening to her describe the two men's partnership: eighteen years, a small manufacturing firm that had grown into a large one, and, in the last year, a bitter quarrel over the sale of the business. Gerald, she said, had refused to sell. Richard had wanted to.

"And the police are satisfied that Mr. Maddox was in Edinburgh?" Edmund asked. "Entirely," said Mrs. Finch. "He gave his talk at nine o'clock, and the doctor says that Gerald died between nine and ten. It is impossible, Mr. Crane. The man was on a stage in Scotland when my husband was dying in Leeds."

Tess, who had been taking notes, looked up. "A perfect alibi," she said. Edmund took a moment before answering. "In my experience," he said, "the word 'perfect' is not often found in nature. Things that happen by chance are usually a little untidy. Let us look for the untidy part."
ch.clue: Things that happen by chance are usually a little untidy
ch.q: Why does Edmund distrust the alibi, even before he has seen the evidence?
o: The recording of the dinner was made by the police and not by the organisers
It appears too perfect, and real events usually contain small irregularities
Mrs. Finch is not telling the truth about her husband's partner
Maddox has a bad reputation among the people of Leeds
The hotel in Edinburgh is far too expensive for a small company
ch.hint: Edmund "mükemmel" kelimesinin doğada nadir bulunduğunu ve olayların genellikle biraz dağınık olduğunu söylüyor. Bir mazeretin fazla kusursuz olması neden şüphe uyandırabilir?
ch.why: Edmund'a göre rastlantıyla gerçekleşen olaylar genellikle biraz düzensizdir; fazla kusursuz bir mazeret hazırlanmış olabilirdi.

text: The organisers of the Edinburgh conference were a professional association of engineers, and the secretary, a helpful and slightly nervous man named Mr. Calder, was only too glad to give Edmund and Tess a copy of the recording. They watched it that afternoon in Edmund's office, on a laptop, with the curtains drawn.

It was a fine piece of work. A camera at the back of the hall showed the whole room, the long tables with white cloths, the glitter of the glasses, and the stage, where a man in a dark suit stood at a lectern with a glass of water. It was Maddox, certainly, talking with ease and a few jokes, about the future of manufacturing. A clock on the wall behind him was visible, and it showed nine o'clock. The speech lasted twenty-two minutes and ended with applause.

"It is genuine," said Tess, almost with regret. "Three hundred people applauding." Edmund played it again, more slowly. He did not watch the speaker but the audience, and then the walls, and then the windows, three tall ones on the left of the hall, whose curtains were open.
"Tess," he said, "do you see the windows?" She leaned closer. "Daylight," she said. "Quite bright. It is nine in the evening in Scotland, in the middle of November. It should be completely dark."

"On the night in question," said Edmund quietly, "sunset in Edinburgh was at ten past four. I looked it up this morning. The light in this hall is not the light of the evening. It is the light of the afternoon."
ch.clue: The light in this hall is not the light of the evening
ch.q: What irregularity does Edmund discover in the recording?
o: The speaker's voice does not match the movement of his lips
The clock behind the speaker is moving backwards
The audience is much smaller than the three hundred reported
The windows show bright daylight although the clock says nine in the evening
The recording has been edited so that some of the speech is missing
ch.hint: Videodaki pencerelerden gün ışığı giriyor, ama saat akşam dokuzu gösteriyor ve Kasım ayında Edinburgh'ta güneş çok erken batıyor. Bu fark kaydın ne zaman çekildiği hakkında ne söyler?
ch.why: Pencerelerden gün ışığı giriyordu ama saat akşam dokuzdu; Kasım'da akşam dokuzda dışarısı karanlık olmalıydı, yani kayıt gece çekilmemişti.

text: Edmund asked Mr. Calder a question that surprised him. "Was there a rehearsal, by any chance, the day before the dinner?" The secretary hesitated. "Of course," he said. "We always have a technical rehearsal in the hall on the afternoon before the event, to test the cameras and the microphones. All the speakers are invited to give a few minutes of their talk. It is not usual that a speaker gives his full speech, but Mr. Maddox insisted. He said that he wished to time it."

"And was it recorded?" "The cameras were switched on. We keep the rehearsal files, on a separate drive, in case of a technical fault." Mr. Calder found it and played it for them. The camera angle was the same, and the hall was the same, with the long tables and the white cloths. In the rehearsal, however, there were no guests: only a few men in shirtsleeves, setting up the microphones, and a row of empty chairs. A man in a dark suit stood at the lectern, and began to speak.

Tess put her hand to her mouth. "It is the same speech," she said, "word for word. The same jokes. And the clock behind him, at the same angle, says four o'clock." Edmund took the two files and placed them side by side on the screen. In one, the hall was full, loud with the applause. In the other, it was almost empty. But the speaker's voice, from the first word to the last, was the same.
"The recording of the dinner, which the police have seen, was not a recording of the dinner," said Edmund, "but a rehearsal, to which someone has added a crowd."
ch.clue: a rehearsal, to which someone has added a crowd
ch.q: What is the true nature of the 'recording of the dinner'?
o: It is the rehearsal of the previous afternoon with applause and an audience added afterwards
It is a recording of a different speaker who looks like Maddox
It is a film made by the police to reconstruct the events of the evening
It is a recording of the real dinner which has been made darker by a computer
It is an earlier talk by Maddox, given to an audience of engineers in Leeds
ch.hint: Prova kaydındaki konuşma, akşam yemeği kaydındakiyle kelimesi kelimesine aynı; sadece prova kaydında seyirci yok. Yemeğin kaydı gerçekte ne olabilir?
ch.why: Yemek kaydı, bir önceki öğleden sonraki provanın kaydıydı; seyirci ve alkış sonradan eklenmişti.

text: If the recording was false, then the alibi had to be false, and Edmund went back to the police with Mr. Calder's two files. Inspector Hale, who had been sure of the case, watched both and said nothing for a long time. Then he picked up the telephone. Within the hour, the police were asking Mr. Maddox about his movements for the whole of the evening.

The answer came in pieces, as such answers do. The hotel in Edinburgh confirmed that Maddox had registered on the afternoon of the rehearsal. But the night porter remembered that the guest in room 214 had left by the side door at about five o'clock on the evening of the dinner, in a hurry, carrying a small bag. A traffic camera on the A1, picked out by the police from a thousand hours of footage, showed Maddox's grey car heading south at ten to six. A petrol station in Northumberland recorded the card payment at eight minutes past seven. And at twenty to nine, a camera in the car park of a service area outside Leeds had caught him walking towards his car, alone, with a hand in his pocket.

"Four hours, from five to nine," said Tess. "A hundred and eighty miles. Quite possible." "He arranged for the recording of the rehearsal to be played at nine o'clock in the hall," said Edmund. "A technician, who thought it was a replay for the late guests, switched it on. The audience was told that the speaker would be 'in a different room'. Nobody saw him between eight and ten."

When Maddox was shown the traffic footage, he said nothing for a long time. Then he asked for a lawyer. Mrs. Finch came to Edmund's office on the following Monday, and he told her that the alibi had been very good, and that it was its goodness that had given it away.
ch.clue: Nobody saw him between eight and ten
ch.q: How did Maddox create the impression that he was in Edinburgh at nine o'clock?
o: He travelled to Leeds by train while the audience was listening to him
He asked a friend with a similar voice to give the speech in his place
He left the hotel early and arranged for the rehearsal recording to be played to the guests at the dinner
He bribed the hotel manager to say that he had stayed in the hotel all night
He gave the speech earlier in the evening and then took a flight to Leeds
ch.hint: Kamera kayıtları Maddox'un öğleden sonra otelden çıkıp güneye sürdüğünü gösteriyor; yemekte ise prova kaydı oynatılmış. Alibiyi nasıl kurmuş?
ch.why: Maddox oteli erken terk etti ve yemekte seyirciye prova kaydının oynatılmasını sağladı; böylece dokuzda Edinburgh'ta olduğu izlenimi yarattı.

outro: Mazeret, konferansın bir gün önce kaydedilmiş bir bölümüne dayanıyordu; adam cinayet gecesi kayıttaki oturumda değil, odasında oturduğunu göstermişti. Edmund şunu söyledi: kusursuz bir mazeret, çoğu zaman hazırlanmış bir mazerettir.

title: The Sleepy Driver
hero: Dr. Mara Quinn ve hemşire Joe
intro: Elli yaşında bir kamyon şoförü, son aylarda gündüz uykusu yüzünden iki kez trafik kazasından kıl payı kurtulmuş. Dr. Mara Quinn ile hemşire Joe, uyku düzenini, yaşam tarzını ve fiziksel bulguları değerlendirerek nedenini araştırıyor.

text: Mr. Garrick, a long-distance lorry driver of fifty, sat in Dr. Quinn's consulting room with the careful stillness of a man who has been frightened. His employer had sent him to the clinic, he explained, after two incidents within two months. In the first, he had drifted onto the hard shoulder of a motorway at night and been woken by the rumble of the rumble strip. In the second, a week ago, he had nodded off for a second or two at a red light in the afternoon, and had woken to the horn of the car behind. "No one was hurt," he said. "But I do not know how many more of those I have in me."

Nurse Joe, who had taken his weight and blood pressure, laid the figures on the desk. Mr. Garrick weighed 118 kilograms, and his blood pressure was 158 over 96, which was high. His neck, as Joe noted, measured 46 centimetres. Dr. Quinn read the numbers without comment and turned to the man.

"Tell me about your sleep," she said. "I sleep eight, sometimes nine hours," he answered. "In my bed, in a quiet room when I am at home, and in the cab when I am on the road. I go to bed at ten, and I get up at six. I do not drink coffee after four. I have done everything that they tell you." He rubbed his eyes. "And still I fall asleep in the middle of the day, like a baby. When I was thirty, I could drive for twelve hours."

"A man who sleeps nine hours does not usually fall asleep at traffic lights," said Dr. Quinn thoughtfully. "Either he is not sleeping the nine hours that he thinks, or something is wrong with the quality of them."
ch.clue: A man who sleeps nine hours does not usually fall asleep at traffic lights
ch.q: What puzzle does Dr. Quinn identify in Mr. Garrick's account?
o: He works for twelve hours without any rest at night
He has not been to a doctor for more than twenty years
He reports long hours of sleep, yet he falls asleep in the daytime
He drinks too much coffee in the afternoon and the evening
He sleeps only three or four hours because of the lorry's noise
ch.hint: Şoför gece sekiz dokuz saat uyuduğunu söylüyor ama gündüz trafik ışığında uyuyakalıyor. Dr. Quinn'e göre bu iki bilgi birlikte ne düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Şoför uzun süre uyuduğunu söylüyordu ama gündüz uyuyakalıyordu; bu, uykunun süresinde değil kalitesinde bir sorun olabileceğini düşündürüyordu.

text: Dr. Quinn asked whether Mr. Garrick slept alone, and a small, almost shy smile crossed his face. "My wife, Helen, sleeps in the spare room now," he said. "We had a bit of a falling-out about it. She says that I snore like a lorry. Loudly, and not continuously. She says that sometimes it stops completely, and then I make a sort of choking noise and begin again." He shrugged. "I have never heard it myself, of course."

Joe, who was writing, glanced up. Dr. Quinn kept her voice level. "Does she say how long it stops, when it stops?" "She says that she once timed it, with the clock on her phone. About twenty seconds, perhaps more. She counted, and she told me that it frightened her. I thought she was exaggerating."

"I should like to ask Mrs. Garrick a few more questions," said Dr. Quinn. "She is a very important witness. Will you ask her to telephone me?" He agreed. Then she asked him about the mornings. Did he wake with a headache? He did, three or four mornings a week. Did he wake with a dry mouth? Always. Did he need to pass water in the night? Twice, at least. Did he feel rested, even after nine hours in bed?
"Never," said Mr. Garrick, and his voice cracked. "That is the strange thing. I wake up exhausted. I feel as though I have worked all night."

Joe put down his pen. On the examination couch, Dr. Quinn found Mr. Garrick's throat narrow, and the soft tissue at the back of it large, so that it was difficult to see the tonsils. She looked at Joe, and he nodded very slightly, because the same thought had occurred to both.
ch.clue: it stops completely, and then I make a sort of choking noise and begin again
ch.q: What do the wife's observations and the morning symptoms suggest?
o: He suffers from a lack of vitamins which makes him weak in the morning
He is dreaming vividly all night and has no real rest
He has a very bad cold which causes his snoring and headaches
He is drinking alcohol during the night to help him to sleep
His breathing stops repeatedly during sleep, so that he never sleeps deeply
ch.hint: Karısı horlamanın bazen yirmi saniye kadar tamamen durduğunu, sonra boğulur gibi bir sesle yeniden başladığını söylüyor. Sabah baş ağrısı, ağız kuruluğu ve dinlenmemiş hissetme ne düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Gece boyunca solunumu tekrar tekrar duruyordu; bu yüzden derin uyuyamıyor, sabahları yorgun ve baş ağrılı uyanıyordu.

text: Mr. Garrick did not like the idea of spending a night in a hospital bed, with wires on his chest and head, but he agreed when Dr. Quinn explained that his licence, and perhaps his life, depended on it. The sleep clinic was a quiet room in the east wing, with a bed, a dim lamp, and a camera. A technician named Ms. Adeyemi fixed sensors on his scalp, face, chest and finger. "You do not need to do anything," she said. "Just try to sleep."

The results were ready the following afternoon, and Dr. Quinn invited him to look at the printed summary with her. The central figure was an index, the number of times per hour in which the breathing stopped or became very shallow for at least ten seconds. A healthy adult has fewer than five. Mr. Garrick's was fifty-eight. "It means that, on average, you stopped breathing almost once a minute, all night," she said. "The longest pause was forty-one seconds. In that time, the level of oxygen in your blood fell to eighty-one per cent, which is low. Every time, your brain woke you for a moment, enough to start your breathing again, but not enough for you to remember. You are doing it between four and five hundred times a night."

Mr. Garrick looked at the chart, a series of black spikes down a page. "Four hundred times," he said. "No wonder," and he laughed, in the helpless way of a man who has been vindicated. "It is not that I do not sleep enough. It is that I do not sleep at all."
"The tissue in the throat relaxes when you sleep," said Dr. Quinn, "and, in your case, closes the airway. It is called obstructive sleep apnoea."
ch.clue: four and five hundred times a night
ch.q: What do the results of the sleep study reveal?
o: He slept deeply for eight hours but woke up too early each morning
His breathing was interrupted almost once a minute, which prevented real sleep
His breathing was normal but his heart stopped for some seconds each night
His oxygen level was too high, which kept him awake during the night
His sleep was normal and the cause of his tiredness must be psychological
ch.hint: Uyku çalışmasında solunum duraksama indeksi saatte 58 çıkıyor (normal 5'ten az). Bu rakam gece boyunca ne anlama geliyor ve neden dinlenmemiş uyanıyor?
ch.why: Solunumu neredeyse dakikada bir duruyordu ve beyni her seferinde uyanıp yeniden başlatıyordu; bu yüzden gerçek uyku alamıyordu.

text: The treatment, Dr. Quinn explained, was surprisingly simple and not at all like a medicine. It was a small bedside machine called a CPAP, which blew a gentle, steady stream of air through a soft mask over the nose, enough to keep the airway open all night, like a tent pole holding up a tent. Joe fitted the first one in the clinic, adjusted the straps, and let Mr. Garrick breathe through it for ten minutes in a chair. "It is like putting your head out of a car window," said the driver doubtfully. "A gentle one," said Joe.

There were things to be changed beyond the machine, and Dr. Quinn was frank about them. Mr. Garrick weighed 118 kilograms, and losing even ten per cent would make the airway wider. He should avoid alcohol in the evenings, which relaxes the muscles of the throat. And, until the treatment had been proved to work, he should not drive for more than a short while without rest. She wrote a letter for his employer, saying that he was under treatment and should be reassessed in four weeks.

Six weeks later, he came back for the check, sitting upright and with a lively expression. The machine's memory card showed that he had used it on forty of the forty-two nights, and that his index had fallen to three. "Helen sleeps in our bed again," he said with a grin. "And yesterday I drove for five hours, and did not once have to count the road markings to stay awake." He stood up and held out his hand.
"What I learned," he said, "is that you can be in bed for nine hours and be awake all of them. I never thought it was possible."
ch.clue: like a tent pole holding up a tent
ch.q: How does the treatment help Mr. Garrick?
o: A small operation removes the tissue at the back of his throat completely
A new bed lifts his head so that he stops breathing through the mouth
A diet of vitamins gives him more energy during the daytime
A machine blows gentle air through a mask and keeps his airway open during sleep
A medicine makes his throat muscles stronger so that he can sleep for longer
ch.hint: CPAP cihazı maske aracılığıyla hafif ve sabit bir hava akımı veriyor. Bu hava akımı gece boyunca hava yolunun durumunu nasıl etkiliyor?
ch.why: Cihaz, maskeden verdiği hafif ve sürekli hava akımıyla hava yolunu gece boyunca açık tutuyor ve solunumun durmasını önlüyordu.

outro: Şoförün uykusu, gece boyunca defalarca solunumunun durmasından kaynaklanıyordu; tedavi olarak gece takılan bir solunum cihazı önerildi. Mara şunu yazdı: bazen insanın dinlenememesinin nedeni, yeterince uyumaması değil, uykunun içinde olan şeydir.

title: The Long Delay
hero: Komutan Noor Hale ve mühendis Pip
intro: Mars'a doğru yol alan bir uzay aracında, Dünya ile haberleşme gecikmesi her gün biraz daha artıyor. Mürettebat bunu normal bir mesafe etkisi sanıyor, ama Komutan Noor Hale ile mühendis Pip, rakamların beklenenden daha hızlı arttığını fark ediyor.

text: Eighty-three days after leaving the Earth, the spacecraft Perseverance was cruising towards Mars at a speed of about thirty kilometres a second, and the crew had settled into the quiet routine of a long voyage. In the main cabin, Commander Noor Hale and flight engineer Pip took turns at the communications desk, sending reports to the control centre in Houston and receiving the daily instructions. Because radio signals travel at the speed of light, which is finite, there was always a delay between a message and its reply, and that delay grew as the distance between the ship and the Earth increased.

On the eighty-fourth morning, Pip wrote the figure in the log, as he did every day. The one-way delay was 6 minutes and 40 seconds. "It was 6 minutes 12 yesterday," he said, "and 5 minutes 45 the day before." He did a quick subtraction. "It increases by about twenty-seven seconds a day." Noor looked at the printed flight plan on the wall, which showed the expected delay on each day of the voyage in a long column of numbers.

"The plan says 6 minutes 32 for today," she said. "And 6 minutes 5 for yesterday. The difference between days is expected to be about twenty-seven seconds, and it is. The rate is right, but the figure is eight seconds higher than the plan. Eight seconds of radio signal is about two and a half million kilometres." Pip frowned. "That is a lot of space," he said. "But it is out of a total of two hundred million. It is a small fraction, a matter of one per cent."

"One per cent is not nothing," said Noor. "It is an instrument reading, and I should like to be sure. Check the log of the last twenty days. If a reading is eight seconds high today, it is useful to know whether it was eight seconds high yesterday, too."
ch.clue: eight seconds higher than the plan
ch.q: What does the first comparison between the log and the flight plan show?
o: The delay is exactly the same as that given by the plan on every day
The delay is shorter than expected, so the ship is nearer to the Earth
The delay is growing much more slowly than the plan predicts
The delay is eight seconds longer than planned, though it grows at the expected rate
The delay has been decreasing for the past twenty days
ch.hint: Bugünkü gecikme planlanandan 8 saniye fazla, ama günlük artış hızı (yaklaşık 27 saniye) planla aynı. Bu iki bilgi birlikte neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Gecikme planlananın 8 saniye üstündeydi, ama günlük artış hızı beklenen düzeydeydi.

text: Pip pulled out the log for the previous twenty days, and entered the figures in a spreadsheet on his tablet, along with the expected values from the flight plan. He worked silently for about ten minutes, with his tongue between his teeth, as he always did when concentrating. When he turned the screen to Noor, it showed a table with three columns: the day, the measured delay, and the difference from the plan.

"Look at the third column," he said. On day sixty-four, the difference was 1 second. On day sixty-six, 2 seconds. On day seventy, 3. On day seventy-five, 5. On day eighty, 6.5. On day eighty-four, 8. "It is not constant. It is increasing, slowly. If the instrument were simply reading high by a fixed amount, we would see the same number every day. We see a number that grows."

Noor thought about it. "A fixed error would be a calibration problem, perhaps in the clock or the antenna. A growing error is a different thing. It means that our position is not where the plan says it should be, and that the gap between the two is getting wider with time. Twenty days ago, we were behind the plan by one second of light. Today it is eight."

"Eight seconds in twenty days," said Pip. "A hundred and thirteen thousand kilometres, every day. But that cannot be an error in the radio. It must be in the ship's real distance." He was silent for a moment, and then added in a lower voice: "Or its direction."
Noor nodded slowly. "A ship that is further from the Earth than planned has been flying faster, or in a slightly different direction. Let us ask the navigation computer for its own estimate."
ch.clue: It is not constant. It is increasing, slowly
ch.q: Why does the pattern in the third column matter?
o: A growing difference points to a real change in the ship's path, not a fixed instrument error
A fixed difference would show that the ship is travelling faster than light
A constant difference shows that the radio is working in the correct way
A falling difference shows that the ship is moving back towards the Earth
A growing difference proves that the flight plan was written too carefully
ch.hint: Plan ile gerçek arasındaki fark sabit değil, günden güne büyüyor. Sabit bir fark hangi tür bir hataya, büyüyen bir fark ise hangi tür bir değişime işaret eder?
ch.why: Fark büyüyordu, yani sorun sabit bir cihaz hatası değil, geminin gerçek yolunda zamanla büyüyen bir sapmaydı.

text: The navigation computer, a quiet machine in a cabinet in the lower deck, was designed to compute the ship's position from the stars. It took photographs of a set of reference stars, compared their positions, and calculated, in three dimensions, where the ship was and where it was going. Pip typed the command for a full position report and waited for the printout to appear on the small printer by the door.

When it arrived, he read it aloud, and Noor compared it with the plan, line by line. The ship's position, according to the stars, was 41,000 kilometres ahead of the planned position along the line of flight. Its velocity was also a little different from planned: about 0.4 metres per second faster. And the direction of the velocity differed by 0.0003 degrees, a very small angle, but not zero.

"It agrees with the radio delay," said Pip. "The ship is further along than it should be. If we had been on the planned path, the Earth would be where the plan says. This is a different path, close to the first, and diverging."

"Point four metres per second," said Noor, doing the sum in her head. "In eighty-four days that is about three thousand kilometres. But you say that the position error is forty-one thousand." "The direction also matters," said Pip. "A small angle, kept for many weeks, grows. It is like walking along a path which is a degree off: after a few metres, you do not notice, but after a kilometre, you are standing in another field."

Noor studied the printout for a few seconds. "Where did the difference begin?" she asked. "A speed error of 0.4 metres per second is exactly what the last engine correction should have produced, if it had been a little too long."
ch.clue: a different path, close to the first, and diverging
ch.q: What does the navigation computer's report show?
o: The ship has stopped moving and is standing still in space
The ship is travelling backwards towards the Earth at high speed
The ship is on a path slightly different from the plan, and the gap is widening
The star cameras are broken and give unreliable positions
The ship is exactly where the plan says and the radio delay is false
ch.hint: Yıldızlara göre konum 41.000 km ileride, hız biraz farklı ve yön de çok küçük bir açıyla farklı. Bu üç bilgi gemi hakkında ne söylüyor?
ch.why: Gemi plandakine yakın ama biraz farklı bir yolda ilerliyordu ve iki yol arasındaki fark giderek açılıyordu.

text: Noor and Pip spent the rest of the day with the flight-dynamics team in Houston, in a long series of messages, each of which took thirteen minutes to cross the gap and thirteen to return. The engineers on the ground, led by a calm woman named Dr. Ibarra, repeated the calculation independently. By the evening, they sent their analysis. The last mid-course correction, eleven days before, had lasted nine seconds longer than planned, because of a small valve that opened late. The extra push had changed the ship's speed by 0.4 metres per second, and had altered the direction by a few thousandths of a degree.

"If nothing is done," read the message, "the ship will arrive at Mars 11 hours early and about 190,000 kilometres off the planned point of arrival, which is too far for the landing system to accept. The simple remedy is a second correction burn within the next four days. It will require about eight kilograms of fuel. If it is delayed beyond day ninety, the quantity increases rapidly, and after day one hundred, it would exceed the reserve."

Pip read it over Noor's shoulder. "Four days," he said. "We noticed in time." Noor nodded. "We noticed because we looked at the rate of change, and not only at the figure." She put her hand on the communications panel. "The delay, taken by itself, told us that we were eight seconds from the plan. It was the way in which the eight seconds grew that told us where we were going."
The correction burn took place on the eighty-eighth day, lasted forty seconds, and, in the following week, the third column of Pip's table fell back to zero.
ch.clue: The extra push had changed the ship's speed by 0.4 metres per second
ch.q: What caused the ship's deviation from its planned path?
o: The crew shut down the main engine by mistake on the eightieth day
A meteoroid struck the ship and pushed it off its course
The Earth moved faster in its orbit than the flight plan had predicted
The radio antenna was pointed in the wrong direction for several days
The previous correction burn lasted nine seconds too long because a valve opened late
ch.hint: Houston analizi, on bir gün önceki orta rota düzeltmesinin planlanandan dokuz saniye uzun sürdüğünü gösteriyor. Bu uzun süre neye yol açtı ve neden uzun sürdü?
ch.why: Önceki düzeltme yanması, bir valf geç açıldığı için planlanandan dokuz saniye uzun sürmüştü ve geminin hızını ve yönünü değiştirmişti.

outro: Gecikmenin fazla artması, aracın planlanandan farklı bir yörüngeye girdiğini gösteriyordu; küçük bir seyrüsefer hatası, aylar içinde büyük bir sapmaya dönüşmüştü. Noor şunu yazdı: bir ölçüm tek başına sakin görünebilir; asıl bilgi, değişim hızındadır.

title: The Disputed Border
hero: Tarihçi Dr. Amira Kent ve asistanı Leo
intro: İki köy, yüzyıllardır aralarındaki sınırın nerede olduğu konusunda tartışıyor. Dr. Amira Kent ile Leo, eski haritaları, arazi sözleşmelerini ve taş işaretlerini inceleyerek sınırın tarihsel olarak nereden geçtiğini bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: The villages of Upper Wendle and Lower Wendle lay two miles apart in a green valley, and for as long as anyone could remember, they had disagreed about a meadow. It was a long, flat field of about forty acres between them, rich in hay, with a line of old willows along its eastern edge. Each village believed that the meadow belonged to it, and each had a story to support the belief. The people of Upper Wendle said that their ancestors had mowed it since the Middle Ages. The people of Lower Wendle said that the same was true of theirs.

For many years, the quarrel was no more than a matter of a few rude words at the market. This spring, however, a developer from the city had offered to buy the meadow for a housing estate, and both parish councils had claimed the right to sell. A solicitor had written to both, and the district council had finally decided to ask an independent expert to determine, from the historical record, where the border between the two parishes had originally been drawn.

Dr. Amira Kent accepted the commission, and arrived with Leo in the middle of April, with a car full of boxes. In the village hall of Upper Wendle, they were given tea, a plate of biscuits, and an impressive pile of documents by the chairman of the council, a large man named Mr. Thorne, who said, with great confidence, "You will find that the evidence is clear, Dr. Kent. The border has always been on the river. And the river, as you will see, is on the far side of the meadow."
"We shall see," said Amira, and took the first folder from the top of the pile.
ch.clue: The border has always been on the river
ch.q: What is the main purpose of Amira's work in the valley?
o: To arrange the sale of the meadow to the developer from the city
To make peace between the two parish councils by a compromise
To decide which of the two villages has the better meadow for hay
To find the oldest willow trees on the eastern edge of the field
To determine from historical records where the parish border originally ran
ch.hint: Bölge konseyi bağımsız bir uzman istedi. Amira'nın görevi iki köyün hangisinin haklı olduğuna karar vermek mi, yoksa tarihsel kayıtlardan sınırın aslında nereden geçtiğini bulmak mı?
ch.why: Amira'dan, tarihsel kayıtlara bakarak iki mahalle arasındaki sınırın asıl olarak nereden geçtiğini belirlemesi isteniyordu.

text: The oldest document in Mr. Thorne's pile was a copy of a charter from 1583, in which the lord of the manor granted certain lands to the parish of Upper Wendle. Amira read the Latin carefully, translating aloud for Leo, who took notes. The description of the boundary, which was in English, mixed with some Latin, followed the usual form of such documents: it began at a stone, passed to an oak, and ran "along the midstream of the river called Wend, to the old ford, and thence by the willow row to the lane".

"The river Wend," said Leo. "It flows today on the western side of the meadow, close to Upper Wendle. The ford is marked on the modern map, here, near the bridge. And the willow row, on the east, is right where the document says." He placed the modern ordnance survey sheet on the table, with a pencil mark. "If the boundary ran along the river, then the meadow, which is east of the river, belongs to Lower Wendle."

Mr. Thorne cleared his throat. "That is a misreading," he said. "The border is the river, I grant you. But the river, in those days, ran on the east side of the meadow, not on the west. In our parish tradition, the meadow is on our bank."

Amira raised her eyebrows. "A river does not usually change sides," she said. "But I should like to see the evidence for it." Mr. Thorne produced a second folder, with a smile. "A map," he said, "from 1780. It shows the river on the east. It was drawn by a surveyor, and the lines are very clear."
Amira spread the old map on the table and weighed it down at the corners with the biscuit plate and three heavy books. Leo bent over it with a magnifying glass.
ch.clue: along the midstream of the river called Wend
ch.q: What does the 1583 charter say about the boundary?
o: It is not described and only the area of the parish is given
It runs along the middle of the river Wend, then to the old ford and the willow row
It follows the lane to the church and then returns to the oak tree
It runs along the top of the hills to the east of the meadow
It runs through the middle of the meadow from the ford to the lane
ch.hint: 1583 belgesi sınırı "Wend nehrinin orta çizgisi boyunca" tarif ediyor ve ardından eski geçide ve söğüt sırasına gidiyor. Sınırı belirleyen doğal çizgi nedir?
ch.why: Belge sınırı Wend nehrinin ortasından, eski geçide ve söğüt sırasına doğru izliyordu.

text: The map of 1780 was a large sheet of heavy paper, coloured with delicate washes of green and brown. In the bottom corner, in elaborate lettering, it bore the name of the surveyor, Josiah Pell, the date, and the inscription: A True Survey of the Manor of Wendle. The river was drawn as a double blue line, wiggling across the page from north to south. And as Mr. Thorne had said, it passed on the east of the meadow, near the row of willows, with the village of Upper Wendle on its west side.

"It is a beautiful map," said Leo. "And it seems to agree with Mr. Thorne." But Amira, with her finger on the page, was studying a detail near the middle. The blue line made a wide loop, and, in the loop, the surveyor had written two words in tiny script: Old course. Further north, the line forked into two channels, one thick and one thin. The thin one had been drawn with a broken line, and was labelled: Lately cut.

"Lately cut," said Amira. "A channel that was recently dug, in 1780, or shortly before. The note 'Old course' is on the loop, which lies east of the meadow, close to the willows." She sat back. "So the map shows two rivers: the thick blue line, which is the river as it was in the surveyor's day, and a faded loop which is the river's previous path. And the loop is on the east."
"Which of them is the river of the charter?" asked Leo slowly. "The one that existed in 1583, two hundred years before the survey," said Amira. "The old course. In 1780, the Wend had already moved."
ch.clue: Old course
ch.q: What detail of the map does Amira find important?
o: A note shows that the surveyor had never visited the valley
A note shows that the meadow had been sold to another village
A note shows that the willows were planted after the charter
A note shows that the river's course had recently been changed
A note shows that the ford was destroyed by a flood in 1780
ch.hint: 1780 haritasında nehir eski yatağından yeni bir kanala geçmiş: "Old course" ve "Lately cut" notları var. Bu notlar nehrin rotası hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
