ch.why: Haritadaki notlar, nehrin yatağının yakın zamanda değiştirildiğini ve eski yatağın doğu tarafta, söğütlerin yanında kaldığını gösteriyordu.

text: It took Amira and Leo three more days to be sure, but the conclusion, when it came, was very simple. They found an estate account of 1771, among the papers of the manor, that recorded a payment of eleven pounds to labourers for "cutting a new channel for the Wend, through the lower meadow, to prevent flooding of the mill". They found a letter from the mill's owner, who complained that the old bed, in the east, had silted and stopped, and that the water now ran in a straight cut to the west. They walked along the willow row with a pocket level and found, under the grass, a shallow, long depression, with a flat bottom and gently sloping banks, and, in the soil of its edge, a layer of river gravel.

"That is the bed of the Wend as it was in 1583," said Amira, standing in the dip with her boots in the wet grass. "The charter's 'midstream of the river' ran down this hollow, along the willows. The boundary was set there, and it stayed there, as a line, even after the water left. In 1771, the river was moved a hundred yards to the west, and from that time each village thought that the river, in its new place, was the boundary. For Upper Wendle, the meadow was on their bank. For Lower Wendle, the river was the limit of its land."

Her report, delivered to the district council in May, said that the original boundary ran along the old bed, and that the meadow had been divided at that point: the western two thirds belonged to Upper Wendle, the eastern third to Lower Wendle. Mr. Thorne read the verdict in silence, and then, with an unexpected laugh, said, "Both of us were wrong. And both of us were nearly right."
In the autumn, a stone was set into the grass at each end of the hollow, with a brass plate that read: Old Wend, 1583.
ch.clue: The boundary was set there, and it stayed there, as a line, even after the water left
ch.q: How does Amira explain the dispute?
o: The river had moved in 1771, and each village took the new riverbank for the boundary
The two villages had agreed to share the meadow equally from the beginning
The surveyor of 1780 had drawn the river in the wrong place by mistake
One of the villages had stolen the land from the other village at night
The charter was a forgery which had been written by the parish of Upper Wendle
ch.hint: Dere 1771'de batıya taşınmış, ama sınır eski yatakta kalmış. İki köy de yeni yatağı sınır sanmış. Bu durum anlaşmazlığı nasıl açıklıyor?
ch.why: Nehir 1771'de yatağını değiştirmişti ve her köy yeni yatağı sınır sanmıştı; oysa gerçek sınır eski yatak boyunca uzanıyordu.

outro: Sınır, bir nehrin eski yatağı boyunca uzanıyordu; nehir iki yüz yıl önce yatağını değiştirmişti ve her köy kendi tarafındaki yeni kıyıyı sınır sanmıştı. Amira şunu yazdı: bir haritadaki çizgi, çizildiği günün manzarasına aittir.

title: The Perfect Correlation
hero: Dr. Ilan Voss ve asistanı Dana
intro: Dana, bir tarım deneyinde tarlaya atılan gübre miktarı ile verim arasında neredeyse kusursuz bir ilişki buluyor. Dr. Ilan Voss ise sonuçtan memnun olmak yerine, bu kadar düzgün bir ilişkinin neden şüpheli olduğunu anlatıyor ve verinin nereden geldiğini sorgulatıyor.

text: Dana brought the graph to Dr. Voss's office on a Monday morning, with the pride of a researcher who has, at last, found something clear. She was in the second year of her doctorate, and her project concerned the effect of a new nitrogen fertiliser on the yield of wheat. She had planted forty small plots in the university's experimental farm, applying different amounts of fertiliser to each, from none at all to a very heavy dose, and measured the yield of grain at harvest. Now she laid the result on his desk: a scatter plot, with the fertiliser on the horizontal axis and the yield on the vertical axis, forty dots lying along a smooth, rising line.
"Correlation coefficient, 0.98," she said. "It is almost a straight line. The more fertiliser, the more wheat, in a very regular way. I have never seen anything so clean."

Dr. Voss looked at the graph for a long time. He did not smile, and Dana, who had been waiting for the smile, felt her enthusiasm falter. "It is a beautiful figure," he said at last. "And that is what worries me." He took off his glasses and rubbed the bridge of his nose. "In biology, Dana, nothing is so clean. Wheat plants differ, soils differ from one metre to the next, birds eat some of the seed, a cloud passes over one plot and not another. Forty plots in a field should produce a cloud of dots, with a trend, and plenty of scatter. A line this straight tells me either that you have discovered a law of nature, which I doubt, or that something in the experiment is producing the pattern for you."

"What could that be?" asked Dana, half defensive and half curious. "I do not know yet," said Dr. Voss. "But I shall ask you to tell me everything that was different between the plots, not only the fertiliser."
ch.clue: A line this straight tells me either that you have discovered a law of nature
ch.q: Why does Dr. Voss distrust a correlation of 0.98?
o: Biological data are usually much more scattered, so a perfectly straight line suggests another influence
Wheat always grows better without any fertiliser at all
Dana used too few plots to make any conclusion about wheat
The correlation coefficient can never be greater than zero
The graph was drawn with the wrong scale on the vertical axis
ch.hint: Biyolojik verilerde bitkiler, toprak ve hava durumu yüzünden genellikle çok saçılma olur. Bu kadar düz bir çizgi Dr. Voss'a göre ne anlama gelebilir?
ch.why: Biyolojik verilerde normalde çok sapma olur; bu kadar düz bir çizgi, desene başka bir etkenin neden olduğunu düşündürüyordu.

text: Dana went back to her notebook, and, over the next two days, constructed a list of everything that she could remember about the forty plots. It was longer than she had expected. Each plot was four metres by four, arranged in a long grid of five rows and eight columns. All had been sown on the same day with the same variety of wheat, at the same density, by the same hand. They had received the same amount of rain, because they were in the same field, and the same herbicide in the same week. The fertiliser had been applied by hand, in precise weights, and each plot labelled with a wooden stake.

"Only one thing varies deliberately," she told Dr. Voss, as they sat over the list. "The dose of fertiliser. I assigned the doses in order, from none to the highest, starting at the north-west corner and moving across each row. I thought that it would be simple to keep track."

Dr. Voss put his finger on the last sentence. "In order. From the north-west corner. Plots with no fertiliser at one end of the field, and plots with the highest dose at the other." He drew the grid on a piece of paper, and shaded the squares: light at one corner, dark at the other, in a smooth gradient. "Dana, tell me about the field. Is it perfectly flat? Is the soil the same everywhere?"

Dana looked at the grid. "It slopes slightly to the south-east," she said. "I have heard the farm manager say that the low corner is wetter. And there is an old drainage ditch on the south side, that I had not thought about."
"Then your dose of fertiliser", said Dr. Voss quietly, "is also, very nearly, a map of the field."
ch.clue: is also, very nearly, a map of the field
ch.q: What is the problem with the way Dana assigned the fertiliser doses?
o: The variety of wheat was not the same in each of the plots
The doses were applied by hand instead of by a machine
The doses increase steadily across the field, so they are mixed up with any change in the soil
The doses were not weighed with enough precision
The plots were too small to give any reliable measurement of yield
ch.hint: Dana dozları kuzeybatı köşesinden başlayarak sırayla verdi, tarla ise güneydoğuya doğru eğimli ve bir tarafı daha nemli. Doz sırasının tarlanın haritasıyla örtüşmesi neden sorun?
ch.why: Dozlar tarla boyunca düzenli artıyordu; bu yüzden gübre miktarı, toprağın eğimi ve nemi gibi tarla değişiklikleriyle karışmıştı.

text: They went out to the farm together on Wednesday, with a soil probe borrowed from the geography department, a thin steel rod with a digital display, which measured the water content of the ground. Dana walked along the rows, pushing the probe into each plot in turn, at the same depth, and calling out the number for Dr. Voss to write down. The measurements were taken in the dry spell of the following days, so that rainfall would not confuse them.

When they had finished, he plotted the numbers on a graph at the kitchen table in the farm office. The percentages of soil moisture were low at the north-west corner, about 14 per cent, and rose smoothly across the field to over 30 per cent at the south-east. It was a gradient as regular as the one in the yield. "The soil is three times wetter at one end than at the other," said Dr. Voss. "The south-east corner, where you put the heavy doses, is the lowest part of the field, where the water collects and drains slowly. The north-west is the highest and driest."

Dana stared at the two lines on the page, which now ran together like rails. "And wheat grows better in wetter soil," she said slowly. "In this field, at this time of year, the water is more limiting than the nitrogen. So the plots with more fertiliser also had more water, and I do not know which of them produced the yield."

"The correlation between fertiliser and yield is real, in the sense that the numbers are real," said Dr. Voss. "But it may be an echo of the correlation between water and yield. A third variable which affects both can make two things appear linked, when one of them has no effect at all."
"A confounder," said Dana, writing the word on the first page of a new notebook.
ch.clue: A third variable which affects both can make two things appear linked
ch.q: What does the soil moisture survey reveal?
o: The soil probe gave readings which were too variable to be of any use
The wettest part of the field is the north-west corner, where there was no fertiliser
The soil in the field is too dry for any wheat to grow
The soil is equally wet across the whole of the field
Moisture increases across the field in the same direction as the fertiliser doses
ch.hint: Toprak nemi kuzeybatıda %14, güneydoğuda %30'un üzerinde ve bu eğilim gübre dozlarının sırasıyla aynı yönde. Bu durum, yüksek dozlu parsellerin ayrıca neye sahip olduğunu gösteriyor?
ch.why: Nem, gübre dozlarıyla aynı yönde artıyordu; yani yüksek dozlu parseller aynı zamanda çok daha fazla suya sahipti.

text: The solution that Dr. Voss proposed was an old idea, and Dana had read about it in her first-year course, without grasping how much it mattered. "We must repeat the experiment," he said, "with the doses assigned at random to the plots, so that no pattern in the soil, or in anything else that we have not thought of, can line up with the fertiliser. We put the dose labels into a bag and draw them out one by one, plot by plot. If the soil is wet in the south-east, then some of the high-dose plots will be wet and some dry, and the same for the low doses. The effect of water will average out, and what is left will be the effect of the fertiliser."

Dana added a refinement of her own. She divided the field into five blocks of eight plots, each running from the dry end to the wet end, and assigned each dose once to every block, in random order. In that way, she would be able to estimate the effect of the field's gradient separately.

The results, in the autumn, were less beautiful and a great deal more informative. The dots made a cloud, with a coefficient of 0.54. The fertiliser did increase yield, by about eleven per cent for a medium dose, but only up to a point, after which the heavy doses did no more than the medium. The effect of moisture, estimated from the blocks, was larger than the effect of fertiliser itself.

"It is a smaller result," said Dana, closing her laptop. "And a true one." Dr. Voss smiled for the first time since the day when she had shown him the graph. "A clean line that you cannot explain," he said, "is the thing to be afraid of. A messy cloud that you can explain is the beginning of knowledge."
ch.clue: so that no pattern in the soil, or in anything else that we have not thought of, can line up with the fertiliser
ch.q: Why does Dr. Voss ask Dana to assign the doses at random?
o: So that the wheat will grow faster in the first weeks
So that no hidden pattern in the field can line up with the dose
So that the experiment will use less fertiliser and save money
So that the correlation will be as close to a straight line as possible
So that the highest doses can be given to the best plots
ch.hint: Dr. Voss dozların rastgele dağıtılmasını istiyor. Rastgele atama, tarla eğimi veya nem gibi gizli etkilerin gübre dozuyla aynı hizaya gelmesini nasıl engeller?
ch.why: Rastgele atama, tarladaki gizli bir düzenin (nem gibi) gübre dozlarıyla aynı hizaya gelmesini önlüyor ve gübrenin gerçek etkisini ayırmayı sağlıyordu.

outro: Veri, gerçek ölçümlerden değil, tarladaki toprak nemini düzenleyen bir sulama sistemi üzerinden elde edilmişti; verimi artıran şey, gübre değil, sudaydı. Ilan şunu yazdı: bir ilişki ne kadar düzgünse, ardında gizli bir üçüncü etken olup olmadığını o kadar çok sormalısın.

title: The Leaked Memo
hero: Muhabir Jonas Reid ve fotoğrafçı Ellie
intro: Kingsbridge Daily'ye, belediyenin bir okulu kapatmayı planladığını gösteren bir iç yazışma sızdırılıyor. Jonas Reid ile Ellie, belgenin gerçek olup olmadığını, kimin ve neden sızdırdığını ve yayımlamanın sonuçlarını tartıyor.

text: The envelope was found on the mat in front of the newspaper's door on Thursday morning, with no stamp and no name. Ellie, who arrived first, picked it up and carried it carefully to Jonas's desk, as if it might explode. Inside there were four photocopied pages, stamped Confidential, on the headed paper of Kingsbridge District Council.

Jonas read them slowly, and, by the second page, he had stopped drinking his tea. The document was a memorandum from the director of education, Mr. Ashworth, to the chief executive, dated the third of October. It was entitled School Estate Review: Options for Savings. It began with the council's budget problem, a shortfall of two million pounds, and went on to list the possible ways of reducing the cost of school buildings. On the third page, under the heading Option C, there was a sentence which made Jonas lift his head: Closure of St Anne's Primary School and transfer of its 210 pupils to neighbouring schools would save approximately £340,000 a year.
"St Anne's," said Ellie. "That is the school on Mill Road, where half of the town sends their children. This will cause a riot."

"If it is genuine," said Jonas. He laid the pages on the desk, one beside the other. "Let us be careful. A leaked document is an invitation to be used. Someone has chosen this particular morning to put it under our door, and someone has chosen which pages to photocopy. I want to know three things. Is it real? Who sent it? And what is missing?"

Mrs. Cole, who had come to see what the whispering was about, read the first page and handed it back. "It is the best story we have had all year," she said. "That is exactly why I want you to be certain before we print one word."
ch.clue: someone has chosen which pages to photocopy
ch.q: What three questions does Jonas ask about the leaked document?
o: Whether it is secret, who is angry, and which school is the best
Whether it is genuine, who sent it, and what has been left out
Whether it is legal, who owns it, and how much it would cost
Whether it is funny, who will read it, and where it should be printed
Whether it is long enough, who typed it, and when it was printed
ch.hint: Jonas sızdırılan belgeyle ilgili üç şey bilmek istiyor: gerçek mi, kim gönderdi ve ne eksik. Bu üç soru bir sızıntıyı yayımlamadan önce neden önemlidir?
ch.why: Jonas belgenin gerçek olup olmadığını, kimin gönderdiğini ve neyin çıkarılmış olabileceğini öğrenmek istiyordu.

text: The first question was the simplest to test, and Jonas began with the document itself. The paper was the council's usual letterhead, but that proved nothing, because anyone could copy it. The stamp read Confidential, in a form that the council did use, but it was in a slightly different typeface from the one on the real documents which Jonas had in his files from earlier stories. "It is a photocopy of a photocopy," said Ellie, holding a page up to the window. "You can see the dark edge of another sheet."

He tried a better approach. He made a list of every concrete detail in the memo that could be checked against independent sources. The budget shortfall of two million pounds: the council's published accounts for the previous year showed a gap of exactly that size. The pupils at St Anne's, 210: the Department for Education's school data, which he found online, gave 208 for the year before. The savings estimate: no source. The name of the director, Mr. Ashworth: correct. The date, the third of October, was a Tuesday, and the council's own website confirmed that the directors' meeting had been held that day.

"The details are consistent with a real document," said Jonas, "and some of them would be difficult to invent. But consistency does not make it genuine, because anyone who knows the council could write it." He decided to do what a reporter ought to do, and what the leaker had perhaps hoped that he would not: telephone the council and ask.

The press officer, a polite young woman, listened to a description of the document, said that she would call him back, and did so ten minutes later. "I can confirm," she said, in the careful voice of someone reading from a prepared statement, "that the council has been reviewing options for the school estate, as part of a normal budget process. I cannot comment on any specific document."
Jonas wrote the sentence in his notebook. "It is not a denial," he said to Ellie.
ch.clue: It is not a denial
ch.q: What do Jonas's checks of the details in the memo show?
o: The council has proved that the memo was written by an outsider
The press officer has confirmed that St Anne's will close next year
The numbers in the memo are all wrong and do not match any figures
The details are consistent with a real document, and the council does not deny it
The memo is a forgery because it was written on a different typeface
ch.hint: Jonas bütçe açığı, öğrenci sayısı, müdürün adı ve toplantı tarihi gibi ayrıntıları bağımsız kaynaklarla karşılaştırdı ve belediye belgeyi yalanlamadı. Bu, belgenin gerçekliği hakkında ne söyler?
ch.why: Ayrıntılar gerçek bir belgeyle uyumluydu ve belediye belgeyi yalanlamadı; yine de bu belgenin gerçekliğini kesin kanıtlamıyordu.

text: Establishing the truth of a document is not the same as understanding why it was sent. Jonas had often noticed that the people who leak papers have reasons of their own, and that the reasons shape the parcel. He spread the four pages on his desk once more and, this time, read them as a puzzle. The memo was five pages long, according to its own page numbers, and in the corner of the bottom of the fourth page it said: Page 4 of 5. The fifth page had not been included.

"Someone has copied everything except the last page," said Ellie. "Why not just give us the whole thing?" Jonas ran his finger along the margin. "Because the last page is not helpful to the person who sent it. Think about it. The first four pages are an analysis of the possible ways of saving money, and Option C, the closure of St Anne's, is the most dramatic. If the fifth page, the conclusion, says that the director recommends Option A, a small reduction in the central office budget, then the memo is a list of ideas, not a decision. But a reader of four pages could believe that the school is to be closed."

He had a strong suspicion about the sender's identity, but a suspicion is not a fact, and he did not write it down. Instead, he examined what the sender might gain. A councillor who opposed the budget might want to provoke a public outcry. An employee who disliked the director might want to embarrass him. A parent who had heard a rumour might want to force the council to speak. Each possibility would have led to a different choice of pages.

The telephone on his desk rang, and a quiet voice that he did not know said, "I think you have received something from me. I would be glad if you did not ask me my name. I wanted you to have it. I thought you should see how they really plan things."
"Is there a fifth page?" asked Jonas gently.
ch.clue: Page 4 of 5
ch.q: Why does the missing fifth page matter to Jonas?
o: It may contain the director's recommendation, which would change the meaning of the other pages
It is the page on which the budget figures are explained in detail
It may show that the memo was printed on a different date
It certainly contains the final decision of the council on St Anne's
It probably contains the name and address of the person who sent the memo
ch.hint: Belgenin dördüncü sayfasında "5 sayfanın 4'ü" yazıyor ve beşinci sayfa eksik. Son sayfada müdürün hangi seçeneği önerdiği yazıyorsa, ilk dört sayfanın anlamı nasıl değişir?
ch.why: Beşinci sayfa müdürün asıl önerisini içerebilirdi ve bu, ilk dört sayfanın okunuşunu tamamen değiştirebilirdi.

text: The voice on the telephone hesitated for a long time, and then said, "I will send it to you by post. Not by email." Two days later, a second envelope arrived, with a single sheet, the same size, the same stamp, with a clean copy of the missing page. Jonas read it standing, and Ellie, who read over his shoulder, said, "Oh."

The fifth page was a summary and recommendation. It said, in four short paragraphs, that the director had considered seven options, ranging from small savings in administration to a merger of schools, and that Option C, the closure of St Anne's, was the most efficient financially, but the most damaging socially, because it would force 210 children to travel more than two miles to school, through a dangerous road. The director concluded: I do not recommend Option C. I recommend Options A and E, which together deliver savings of £310,000 with no school closure. The memorandum was to be discussed at a public meeting before any decision.

"So the memo says the opposite of what the first four pages looked like," said Ellie. "Not the opposite," said Jonas. "The council did consider closing the school, and that is a fact worth reporting. But it is one of seven options, and the director opposes it. The story is not 'Council plans to close school'. It is 'Council studied closing school, official advises against'."

He wrote the article that evening, with both facts in the first paragraph. Mrs. Cole read it twice and said, "It will be a smaller sensation. But it will be one that we can defend." The headline said: Council examined closing St Anne's, but director recommends against. Beneath it, he included a paragraph about the way in which the memo had reached the paper, and the fact that its fifth page had been withheld.
On Saturday, two hundred parents attended the public meeting, but nobody shouted.
ch.clue: I do not recommend Option C
ch.q: What does the complete memo show?
o: The memo is a forgery that was written by an unhappy parent
The director wants to close all the schools in the district to save money
The council considered closing the school, but the director recommended against it
The council has already moved all the pupils to the neighbouring schools
The council has decided to close St Anne's at the end of the school year
ch.hint: Beşinci sayfada müdür yedi olasılığı değerlendirdiğini ve C maddesini, yani okul kapatmayı önermediğini yazıyor. Bu, ilk dört sayfadan çıkan izlenimi nasıl değiştiriyor?
ch.why: Belediye okul kapatmayı gerçekten düşünmüştü, ama müdür bunu önermiyordu; kapatma kesin karar değil, yedi olasılıktan biriydi.

outro: Belge gerçekti ama eksikti: okul kapatma, kesinleşmiş bir karar değil, birçok seçenekten biriydi. Gazete haberi bu bağlamla yayımladı. Jonas şunu yazdı: sızdırılan bir belge size gerçeği değil, birinin sizin görmenizi istediği parçayı verir.

title: The Returning Wolves
hero: Park korucusu Wren Calder ve köpeği Bracken
intro: Bir dağ vadisinde kurtların geri döndüğü söyleniyor. Çiftçiler endişeli, doğa severler heyecanlı. Wren Calder ile Bracken, izlere, dışkılara ve kamera kayıtlarına bakarak gerçekte ne olduğunu ve bunun vadi için ne anlama geldiğini anlamaya çalışıyor.

text: The rumour began in the village shop on a Saturday, and by Monday it had travelled round the whole of Glen Aran. A hill farmer named Mr. McLeod had found two of his sheep dead on the upper pasture, torn and partly eaten, and, in the muddy ground near them, large paw prints. "Wolves," said Mr. McLeod at the shop counter, in front of five customers. "They have come back, after three hundred years."

By Tuesday, the local newspaper had telephoned the National Park office, and Ranger Wren Calder found herself in the position, as she put it to Bracken, of being expected to confirm or deny something that she had not yet seen. The mountain-walkers' club said that they were delighted, and had already begun to plan a wolf-watching trail. The farmers' union, on the other hand, held an emergency meeting at which several people said that the wolves would have to be shot.

On Wednesday morning, Wren drove up the track to Mr. McLeod's farm in her old green truck, with Bracken on the seat beside her and a bag of equipment in the back: a camera, a measuring tape, plaster of Paris, a notebook, and a pair of disposable gloves. Mr. McLeod met her at the gate, a tall, weathered man in a waxed jacket, who was angry and upset at the same time.

"They were two of my best ewes," he said. "I have eight hundred sheep, and I am not going to lose them one by one." Wren put her hand on his arm. "I am sorry, Mr. McLeod," she said. "I want to find out what happened, as exactly as I can. Before we say a word about wolves, I should like to see the ground myself, and look at the tracks as they are. It is easy to be sure, and it is easy to be wrong."
"You will see," said Mr. McLeod. He opened the gate.
ch.clue: It is easy to be sure, and it is easy to be wrong
ch.q: What is Wren's attitude when she arrives at the farm?
o: She wants to protect the wolves from the farmers at any cost
She is certain that wolves have returned and is ready to announce it
She wants to examine the evidence carefully before deciding what killed the sheep
She believes that nothing can be learned from the paw prints
She thinks that the farmer is lying about the dead sheep
ch.hint: Wren "kesin olmak kolay, yanılmak da kolay" diyor ve önce izleri kendi gözleriyle görmek istiyor. Bu, olaya yaklaşımı hakkında ne söylüyor?
ch.why: Wren, koyunları neyin öldürdüğüne karar vermeden önce kanıtları dikkatle incelemek istiyordu.

text: The upper pasture was a long, steep field with a stone wall and a stream at its edge. The two ewes had been moved, but the ground where they had lain was marked by dark patches of blood and scattered tufts of wool. At the foot of the wall, in a patch of mud softened by a spring, Mr. McLeod showed Wren the prints that he had found.

Wren crouched, and studied them for several minutes before touching anything. There were four or five clear prints, round and deep, each about nine centimetres long and eight wide. She laid the measuring tape beside the best of them, and took a photograph from directly above, with the tape in the picture. "Four toes," she said. "And a large pad. The claws are visible, quite clearly, in front of the toes." Mr. McLeod nodded with satisfaction. "That is a wolf."

"Let us see," said Wren. She knew that the distinction between the prints of a large dog and a wolf is subtle, and that every amateur gets it wrong at least once. A wolf's print is usually longer than wide, oval in shape, with two forward toes that are placed slightly ahead of the others, and a track that runs in a nearly straight line, because the animal places its hind feet into the prints of the front ones. A dog's print is rounder, with a wider track and a more irregular line, because dogs wander. She followed the track along the foot of the wall for about thirty metres, measuring the distance between prints, and observing that the line was not straight but wavered from side to side, with frequent turns, and in two places, a series of small circles.
"Nine by eight is a round print," she said quietly. "And the track wanders. A wolf on a hunt does not circle and wander."
Mr. McLeod folded his arms. "A dog? On my farm? I would know if there were a dog like that."
ch.clue: A wolf on a hunt does not circle and wander
ch.q: Which features of the prints make Wren doubt that they belong to a wolf?
o: The prints show no claws, which every wolf print would show
The track is very straight and goes directly towards the sheep
The prints appear only in a single place near the stream
The prints are much too small to belong to any large animal
The prints are round rather than oval, and the track wanders instead of running straight
ch.hint: İzler 9'a 8 cm ve yuvarlak, iz çizgisi ise kıvrılıp daireler çiziyor. Kurt izi genellikle oval ve düz bir çizgide ilerler. Wren hangi iki özellikten şüphelenmiş olabilir?
ch.why: İzler oval değil yuvarlaktı ve iz çizgisi düz gitmek yerine sağa sola kıvrılıyordu; bunlar köpek izi özellikleriydi.

text: Wren left a camera trap, a small weatherproof box with a motion sensor, fixed to a fence post in the gorse bushes above the stream. She and Mr. McLeod agreed that it would be checked every morning, and that nothing would be said to the newspapers until they had the result. Bracken, who was not allowed to approach the pasture while the traces were fresh, waited in the truck with a long-suffering expression.

On the fourth morning, Wren climbed the track in the early light, and found the little box intact. She opened it, and, on a small screen, ran through the pictures, most of which showed nothing at all, or a fox, or the white tail of a rabbit. At twenty past three on the night of the previous Saturday, there was a series of nine frames. In the grey infrared light, a group of animals crossed the field in single file, coming up from the stream. There were five. They were large, long-legged and loose-limbed, heavily built, with thick coats. One of them had a white patch on its chest, and one had a drooping, floppy ear.

"Floppy ears," said Wren, in the empty field, aloud. "A wolf's ears are upright." She went through the frames again, slowly. The second animal wore something round its neck: a thin collar, a band of pale material, visible in two of the images. The fourth, in the last frame, was looking straight at the camera, with its tongue out, and its tail curled over its back.

She copied the best three frames on to her phone and sent them to a colleague, a dog specialist in the university, asking one question: What are these? The answer arrived within the hour, in two words. Not wolves.
ch.clue: A wolf's ears are upright
ch.q: What does the camera trap show about the animals?
o: A group of five wolves, all of them with upright ears
A pack of large dogs, some with floppy ears and one with a collar
An empty field, because no animal passed in front of the camera
A group of walkers who were crossing the field at night
A single fox that has been taking sheep from the farm
ch.hint: Kamera, dikilmemiş (sarkık) kulaklı, bir tanesi tasmalı beş büyük hayvan kaydetmiş. Kurtların kulakları dik olur. Bu hayvanlar hangi grubu gösteriyor?
ch.why: Kamera sarkık kulaklı ve birinin boynunda tasma olan, beş büyük köpekten oluşan bir sürüyü kaydetmişti; bunlar kurt değildi.

text: It was not difficult to discover whose dogs they were. Wren showed the three photographs to the local vet, who recognised the one with the white chest immediately. "That is Moss," she said. "A Maremma, a big white and tan sheepdog. They belong to Mr. Fairlie, who lives in the next valley. He has a flock of goats, and he keeps the dogs to protect them. He lost two of them in the spring, I believe. Perhaps the others had gone to look for them."

Wren drove to the next valley that afternoon, with the photographs in a folder on her knees, and found Mr. Fairlie in his yard, a small, red-faced man mending a fence. He looked at the pictures, and the blood left his face. "I have been looking for them for six days," he said. "They got out through the broken gate at the bottom field. I never imagined that they would go so far. Moss and his brothers are as gentle as lambs. But they are big, and, when there are five of them together, they can be frightening."

"They have killed two sheep," said Wren. "I do not think they were hungry. I think that, running together, they behaved like a pack. It happens with dogs." Mr. Fairlie was horrified and offered to pay the damage. Mr. McLeod, who had listened to the story with his mouth open, shook his head slowly. "Dogs," he said. "I was so sure that it was wolves."

"The ground does not lie," said Wren, "but you have to read it carefully." She suggested that the dogs be kept in a secure yard, and that the council be asked to pay for a proper gate. On Friday, the newspaper's front page carried a picture of five dogs behind a fence, under the headline: Not wolves, after all. In the weeks that followed, there were no more losses in Glen Aran, but there was a surprise on Mr. McLeod's gate: a hand-painted sign, thanking the ranger for being right in front of the whole valley.
ch.clue: The ground does not lie
ch.q: What conclusion does the evidence support?
o: The sheep died of a disease and were eaten by foxes afterwards
The sheep were killed by Mr. McLeod's own dogs, and he is lying
The sheep had been killed by hunters who left false prints on the ground
The sheep were killed by a group of dogs that had escaped from a neighbouring farm
The sheep were killed by a pack of wolves from the northern mountains
ch.hint: Veteriner köpeği tanıdı ve Mr. Fairlie beş köpeğinin kırık bir kapıdan kaçtığını söyledi. Koyunları kim öldürmüştü?
ch.why: Koyunları, komşu çiftlikten kaçan bir grup büyük köpek öldürmüştü; kurtlar değil.

outro: İzler kurtlara değil, büyük bir köpek sürüsüne aitti. Bu, çiftçilerin koyunlarına gerçek bir tehdit oluşturuyordu ama kurtlar kadar değil; çözüm de farklıydı. Wren şunu yazdı: bir izin yorumu, onu bırakan hayvanı bilmekten başlar.

title: The Stolen Silence
hero: Küratör Hugo Laurent ve güvenlik görevlisi Mina
intro: Müzenin ses arşivinden, nadir bir halk müziği kaydının orijinal bandı kayboldu. Hiçbir kapı zorlanmadı, alarm çalmadı. Hugo Laurent ile Mina, depo kayıtlarını ve dijital dökümleri inceleyerek bandın nerede ve nasıl kaybolduğunu araştırıyor.

text: The sound archive of the City Museum occupied a long, cool basement room, lined with grey shelves and humming gently with the fans of the air-conditioning. It held about six thousand objects: wax cylinders, shellac discs, magnetic tapes, each in its own labelled box, and each recorded in a catalogue. The most precious of them, according to the curator, was a single reel of quarter-inch tape, recorded in 1958 in a remote mountain village by an ethnomusicologist, and containing the voices of nine elderly singers, six of whom were dead before the end of the decade. It was known as the Hollin Reel, and it was the only recording of its kind.

On a Monday morning in October, the archivist, Ms. Park, opened the box which bore the label HR-1958-04, and found it empty. She searched the shelf, the neighbouring shelves, and the room, and then, with a trembling voice, called Hugo Laurent.

Hugo arrived with Mina, the night guard, who had been asked to come early because she was the last person to have walked through the basement on Sunday night. "The room was locked," said Mina, "and the alarm was set. I did my round at eleven and again at three, and nothing was moved. The log shows that no one came in or out." Hugo looked at the empty box, a plain grey cardboard container with a card on the lid, and, in the dust at the bottom, the faint rectangular outline where the reel had lain.

"Nobody entered the room, and yet the reel is not here," he said slowly. "Either someone has found a way to enter that does not leave a record, or the reel was not in the room when we think it was." He took out his notebook. "Let us start by finding out when it was last seen."
ch.clue: Nobody entered the room, and yet the reel is not here
ch.q: What is the central puzzle of the case?
o: The reel has been damaged by water in the basement of the museum
The catalogue has lost all the information about the Hollin Reel
The box on the shelf is the wrong size for the reel which should be in it
The reel is missing from a locked room with an alarm and no record of anyone entering
The singers' voices on the reel cannot be understood by the archivist
ch.hint: Oda kilitliydi, alarm kuruluydu ve kimse girmemiş görünüyor, ama bant yok. Hugo iki olasılıktan söz ediyor. Bu bilmece neyi içeriyor?
ch.why: Bant, kilitli, alarmlı ve kimsenin girmediği kaydedilmiş bir odadan kaybolmuştu; bu bir bilmeceydi.

ch.t: The Last Time It Was Seen
text: The archive kept a register in which every movement of an object, an exit or an entry, was signed by the archivist. Hugo asked Ms. Park to bring it, and the three of them stood round it in the cool air of the basement, reading the lines for the Hollin Reel. The last entry was dated the fourteenth of September: Removed for digitisation, Unit 2, signed by Ms. Park. The following entry was dated the twentieth of September: Returned from Unit 2. Shelf C-7. Signed: J. Whitfield.

"There," said Hugo. "The reel was taken out on the fourteenth to be copied into digital form, and put back on the twentieth. After that, it should have been on the shelf, in the box." He turned to Ms. Park. "Who is J. Whitfield?" "A technician in the digitisation unit," she said. "A young man. Very careful. He brought back four tapes that day."

"And did you check the box yourself, when he returned it?" asked Hugo. Ms. Park shook her head, embarrassed. "I trusted him. The box was closed, and the shelf number was written in the register. It is not usual to open a box for the purpose of confirming that something is in it. We would be opening every box every time."

Mina, who had been silent, spoke. "So it is possible that the reel was never in the box on the twentieth. That the box was returned empty." Hugo nodded slowly. "The last time that anyone saw the reel was on the fourteenth of September, when Ms. Park handed it over. After that, it passed through the hands of the digitisation unit, and into a box. Between the fourteenth and the twentieth, six days, anything could have happened."
"Unit 2," said Mina. "I think that is where we should look."
ch.clue: Returned from Unit 2
ch.q: What conclusion do Hugo and Mina draw from the register?
o: The reel may have left the shelf on the 14th and never returned, so the search should begin in Unit 2
The reel was stolen on the night of Sunday, when no one was in the basement
The reel was destroyed during the process of digitisation in Unit 2
The reel was never recorded in the register, so no one knows where it was
The reel was returned to the shelf in perfect condition on the 20th
ch.hint: Kayıt defterine göre bant 14 Eylül'de dijitalleştirme için çıkmış ve 20 Eylül'de geri konmuş, ama kutuyu kimse açıp kontrol etmemiş. Bandın en son ne zaman kesin olarak görüldüğü bilindiği için nereye bakmak mantıklı?
ch.why: Bant en son 14 Eylül'de görülmüştü ve kutu geri döndüğünde kimse içini kontrol etmemişti; bu yüzden arama dijitalleştirme biriminden başlamalıydı.

text: The digitisation unit was a bright, noisy room on the second floor, full of machines with spools and dials, where three technicians converted the museum's tapes into digital files. Hugo and Mina found Mr. Whitfield at the third machine, a slight young man with a nervous manner, who stood up quickly when they came in, and who, when asked about the Hollin Reel, turned pale.

"I did the copy on the fifteenth," he said. "It went perfectly. I returned the reel on the twentieth, in the same box. I remember it, because the tape was brittle and I handled it very carefully." Hugo looked at him for a moment, and then, deliberately, asked about the other three tapes that Whitfield had returned that day. "They were from the 1960s," said the technician, "a set of radio recordings. Also in grey boxes. Also labelled by the archive."

Mina went to the shelf where the unit kept the tapes awaiting return, and the finished jobs, a row of grey boxes with numbered labels. She read them aloud, one by one. HR-1958-04 was not among them. But the label next to it, on a box that held a large reel, was HR-1958-O4, a very similar code, with the letter O instead of the numeral zero. She opened it. Inside, unmistakably, was a quarter-inch tape on a metal reel, and a small card, in the hand of the ethnomusicologist: Hollin village, September 1958, nine singers.

"It was in the wrong box," said Mr. Whitfield, in a faint voice. "It has been here the whole time." Hugo put his hand on the reel, which was cool and rather heavy. "Not quite the whole time," he said. "The register said it had been returned to the shelf. This is not the shelf."
ch.q: How did the reel come to be in the wrong place?
o: It was lent to another museum without a note in the register
It was copied and thrown away by mistake when the work was done
It was put in a box with a similar label, which had the letter O in place of a zero
It was hidden by the archivist, who wished to keep it for herself
It was taken from the museum by a technician who wanted to sell it
ch.hint: Mina'nın bulduğu kutunun etiketi "HR-1958-O4" idi (sıfır yerine O harfi). Bu benzerlik bandın kaybolmasında nasıl rol oynamış olabilir?
ch.why: Bant, sıfır yerine O harfi bulunan benzer etiketli bir kutuya konmuştu; bu yüzden asıl kutu boş kalmıştı.

text: The reel was, in fact, safe, and had never left the building. The mistake had been small: a technician, working fast at the end of a long day, had read the label on a box on the shelf, found the right shelf number, and put the box with the wrong label, which looked almost identical, in the right position. The box with the right label, HR-1958-04, which had contained a different, less important tape, had been taken, on the nineteenth, by another technician, who had thought that it was empty and sent it to the central recycling bin for old packaging.

"The box that contained nothing is the one that was on the shelf," said Hugo, laughing for the first time that week, "and the box that contained the reel was the one that nobody was looking for." He took a pencil and wrote a long sentence in his notebook. Mina, who had followed him to the archive again, studied the label on the shelf. "The letter O and the digit zero," she said. "In this typeface, they are almost the same."

By the end of the week, the archive had introduced three new procedures. Every returned object was to be checked against its entry in the register by a second person, opening the box. The catalogue codes were rewritten so that no code contained the letter O or the numeral zero together. And the unit was to hold a short weekly inventory, a quick count of every tape in the building. Ms. Park, who had been very pale all week, regained her colour.

On the following Monday, the Hollin Reel was digitised again, in full, and, for the first time in sixty years, its nine voices were heard by a public audience in the museum's autumn concert. Before the first track, Hugo said a few words. "Sometimes a precious thing disappears," he said. "And it is only waiting for someone to check the label."
ch.clue: The letter O and the digit zero
ch.q: What changes does the archive make after the incident?
o: The technicians are dismissed and replaced by a team of outside experts
The digitisation unit is closed and the work is given to another museum
The catalogue is thrown away and a new one is made with only numbers
All the tapes are locked in a safe and nobody is allowed to listen to them
A second person opens and checks each returned box, and confusing letters are removed from the codes
ch.hint: Arşiv iki yeni önlem alıyor: iade edilen her kutu ikinci bir kişi tarafından açılıp kontrol edilecek ve kodlarda karışabilecek karakterler kaldırılacak. Bu önlemler hangi hatanın tekrarını önlüyor?
ch.why: Arşiv, iade edilen her kutunun ikinci bir kişi tarafından açılıp kontrol edilmesini ve kodlarda karışabilecek karakterlerin kaldırılmasını kararlaştırdı.

outro: Bant çalınmamıştı; müzenin dijitalleştirme biriminde yanlış bir kutuya konmuş ve başka bir kurumun iade sevkiyatına karışmıştı. Hugo şunu yazdı: bir kaybolmanın nedeni her zaman bir hırsız değildir; çoğu zaman bir etikettir.

title: The Chemist's Cabinet
hero: Oyun testçileri Zoe ve Max
intro: Zoe ve Max bu kez eski bir kimyagerin dolabında kilitli kalıyor. Raflarda renkli şişeler, bir terazi ve sayılarla dolu bir defter var. Bulmacalar oran, yoğunluk ve mantık üzerine kurulu. Süre elli beş dakika.

text: The door of the chemist's cabinet closed with a sound like a heavy book, and a brass lamp came on above a long wooden bench. In front of Zoe and Max stood a tall wall of shelves, with rows of glass bottles in every shade of the rainbow, each with a small paper label in faded handwriting. In the centre of the bench was a brass balance with two shallow pans, a set of weights beside it, and, propped against the lamp, an index card.

Max read it aloud. "To open the first drawer, find the heaviest of the four small bottles in the wooden rack, without using any weights, and with no more than two weighings. Place the heaviest bottle's number on the lock." In the rack, four identical glass bottles stood in a row, numbered 1 to 4, each filled with a different coloured liquid. Zoe lifted one and tried its weight in her hand. "I cannot tell by feel," she said. "They look the same size. But one is heavier than the others. We have a balance, and two weighings."

"It sounds simple," said Max, "but let us make sure that we use the weighings wisely. Two weighings and four bottles. If we compare two bottles against two other bottles, we will learn which pair is heavier, but not which bottle in the pair. And then we need a second weighing to decide." He thought about it. "That works. But there is a more careful way, which does not require us to guess at all."

Zoe was already setting bottle 1 on the left pan and bottle 2 on the right pan. "Let us start with the simplest comparison," she said. "One against one." The pans trembled, and then rose and fell until they came to rest. The left pan was lower. On the digital display above the door, the numbers read 54:12.
ch.clue: no more than two weighings
ch.q: What is the task in the first puzzle?
o: To weigh all the bottles and write their weights on a card
To find the bottle that contains the largest amount of liquid
To discover which bottle is the lightest by looking at its colour
To mix the liquids of the four bottles in a single large pan
To find the heaviest of four bottles using the balance in at most two weighings
ch.hint: Kartta dört şişeden en ağırını, ağırlık kullanmadan ve en fazla iki tartımla bulmak isteniyor. Burada hedef ne?
ch.why: Görev, terazi ile en fazla iki tartımda dört şişeden en ağır olanı bulmaktı.

text: "Bottle 1 is heavier than bottle 2," said Max, watching the left pan lie low. "So bottle 2 is not the heaviest. We have eliminated it. We have used one of the two weighings." Zoe set bottle 2 aside. "Three candidates remain: 1, 3 and 4. But we only have one weighing. We must be careful."

"Why not weigh 3 against 4?" asked Max. "Then, whichever is heavier, we compare it..." He stopped. "No. We would not have the third weighing." Zoe sat on the stool and drew a small diagram in the notebook: four circles, one crossed out. "Let us think what a single weighing can tell us. If we weigh bottle 3 against bottle 4, there are three possible results. Either 3 is heavier, or 4 is heavier, or they weigh the same. In the first case, 3 is the heaviest of the remaining three, but bottle 1 is still in competition, because we do not know how it compares with 3. In the second case, the same. In the third case, we know that both 3 and 4 are lighter than bottle 1, because..." She paused. "No. We do not know that."

"We have used our weighings badly," said Max, with a grim smile. "Let us not say that. There is a way, but it begins with a different first step. We should have weighed two bottles against the other two."

Zoe looked at the clock, which was reading 51:40. "We still have a second weighing," she said. "And we have learned that 2 is lighter than 1. Let us put bottle 1 against bottle 3 and see what happens." The balance tilted. This time the right pan, with bottle 3, went down, and the left pan with bottle 1 flew up.
"So 3 is heavier than 1," said Max. "And 1 is heavier than 2. That gives us a chain of three. And bottle 4, which has not been weighed, is the only unknown."
ch.clue: That gives us a chain of three
ch.q: What do the two weighings tell Zoe and Max, and what is still uncertain?
o: Bottle 4 is lighter than all the others and can be put away
Bottle 3 is heavier than 1 and 1 is heavier than 2, but bottle 4 is not yet compared
Bottles 1 and 3 weigh the same and are both heavier than 2
Bottle 2 is the heaviest of all four bottles on the bench
All the bottles weigh the same and there is no difference
ch.hint: İlk tartımda 1, 2'den ağır çıktı; ikincide 3, 1'den ağır çıktı. 4 numaralı şişe hiç tartılmadı. Bu zincir hangi sonucu veriyor ve neresi belirsiz?
ch.why: 3, 1'den ve 1, 2'den ağırdı; ama 4 numaralı şişe hiç tartılmadığı için karşılaştırılmamıştı.

text: Max looked at the little card again, and read the last sentence aloud, with a groan. "The heaviest bottle, with no more than two weighings. We have done both, and we do not know whether it is 3 or 4." Zoe covered her face with her hands. "We have made a mistake. When a puzzle has a limit, we must think of the whole plan before we begin."

They cleared the pans and, in the silence, thought for a while. "What would have worked?" asked Max. Zoe took the pencil again. "Start with two bottles on each pan: 1 and 2 on the left, 3 and 4 on the right. The heavier pair contains the heaviest bottle. That takes one weighing. Then weigh the two bottles in that pair against each other. That takes the second. The heavier of those is the heaviest bottle. Two weighings, and we would be certain."

"A pity that we did not do it that way," said Max. "But the card says nothing about the weighings being independent, and we have not broken the rule: we have used two weighings, and we know something. It is only that we do not know enough." He stared at the four bottles. "Do we have any additional information?"

Zoe picked up bottle 4, held it in her palm, and turned it slowly. On the glass base, in tiny letters, she read the number 380, and on the base of bottle 3, 350, and on the other two, 320 and 305. "They are labelled with their mass in grams," she said. "The manufacturer's mark. I should have looked at the bottom of the bottle at the beginning." She put down bottle 4, and read the number on the display above the door, which said 47:55.
"The heaviest is 4," said Max. "We wasted a weighing."
ch.clue: The manufacturer's mark
ch.q: Which bottle is the heaviest, and how do Zoe and Max find out?
o: Bottle 1, because it was heavier than bottle 2 on the balance
Bottle 2, because it is the smallest of the four in size
It cannot be known without a third weighing
Bottle 4, by reading the mass printed on the base of each bottle
Bottle 3, because it was heavier than bottle 1 on the balance
ch.hint: Zoe şişelerin altında gram cinsinden kütle yazdığını fark ediyor: 380, 350, 320 ve 305. En büyük sayı hangi şişede ve bu bilgiye nasıl ulaştılar?
ch.why: 4 numaralı şişe en ağırdı; Zoe bunu her şişenin tabanında basılı olan gram değerlerini okuyarak buldu.

text: The label on the second drawer, which sprang open when Max entered the number 4, was written in a tiny hand: A solution is made of 20% acid. How much pure water must be added to 100 ml of it so that the acid is 5% of the mixture? Write the volume of water, in millilitres, on the slate. Beside it lay a small blackboard and a piece of chalk.

"Aha," said Zoe, "a proportion problem. Let us see." She wrote on the slate: 100 ml of solution, 20% acid, so there are 20 ml of pure acid. When we add water, the amount of acid does not change: it is still 20 ml. But the total volume increases, and the acid must be only 5% of the new total. Then 20 ml is 5% of the total, and therefore the total is 20 divided by 0.05, which is 400 ml.

"Four hundred millilitres in all," said Max, nodding. "We started with 100, so we must have added three hundred." He held the chalk over the slate. "But wait. We should check it. Twenty millilitres of acid in 400 millilitres of mixture is a twentieth, which is five per cent. Correct. And we have added 400 minus 100, three hundred of water."

Zoe took the chalk and, in large figures, wrote 300 on the slate. A small bell rang somewhere in the wall, and the back of the cabinet shifted with a deep scraping sound. A narrow door, painted the same brown as the bench, had been hiding in the panelling, and it now stood a hand's width open. On the digital display above the entrance, the numbers showed 33:07. "We have half an hour," said Zoe. "And I think that the last puzzle is behind that door."
ch.clue: the amount of acid does not change
ch.q: How much water must be added to the solution?
o: 300 millilitres
400 millilitres
80 millilitres
20 millilitres
100 millilitres
ch.hint: 100 ml çözeltide 20 ml saf asit var ve su eklenince asit miktarı değişmiyor. Asit toplam karışımın %5'i olacaksa toplam hacim kaç ml olmalı ve ne kadar su eklenmeli?
ch.why: 20 ml asit toplamın %5'i olunca toplam 400 ml gerekiyordu; 100 ml zaten vardı, yani 300 ml su eklenmeliydi.

outro: Son şişe doğru sıraya girdiğinde dolabın arka duvarı kaydı ve oyunun çıkışı göründü. Oyunun yaratıcısı, bulmacaların hiçbirinin gerçek kimya bilgisi gerektirmediğini, ama hepsinin dikkatli okuma istediğini söyledi.

title: The Lost Connection
hero: Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ve stajyer Sam
intro: Bir grup turist, aktarma yaptıkları havalimanında bagajlarının bir sonraki uçağa yüklenmediğini söylüyor. Dara Mills ile Sam, bagaj etiketlerini, uçuş saatlerini ve sistem kayıtlarını inceleyerek bagajların nerede olduğunu ve neden yanlış gittiğini araştırıyor.

text: At twenty past two on a drowsy Wednesday afternoon, a group of six travellers arrived at the baggage services desk of Heathfield Airport, with a small girl asleep on the shoulder of one of them. They were a family: three adults, two teenagers and a child. They had flown from Lisbon, changed planes at Heathfield, and were due to fly on to Dublin on a connecting flight that had left, according to the board, at one o'clock.

"We arrived in Dublin at three," said the father, a patient, bespectacled man named Mr. Caldeira, "and found that our suitcases had not arrived. The staff in Dublin told us that the cases had not been loaded on the connecting flight at Heathfield. We took a later flight, which has just landed, and we have come to the desk to ask for help." He laid six baggage tags on the desk. "Here are the tags. Each is marked for Dublin."

Dara Mills, who had come on duty at noon, looked at the tags. They bore the airline's usual information: the name, the flight number of the first flight, TP 482, from Lisbon to Heathfield, and the second, EI 321, from Heathfield to Dublin. "Let me see what the system says," she said, and turned to her screen. She typed the bag numbers, one by one. Sam, her trainee, leaned over her shoulder.

"Six bags, all with the same history," she read slowly. "Checked in at Lisbon at 8:05. Arrived at Heathfield on TP 482, at 11:15. Status: transferred to EI 321. Transfer time: forty-five minutes. Loaded: No."

"Forty-five minutes?" Sam frowned. "It is a standard transfer time. But the bags did not make it." Dara said nothing for a moment. Then she took a pencil and wrote the times beside the status: 11:15 arrival, 1:00 departure.
"Tell me, Sam," she said, "how many minutes are there between 11:15 and 1:00?"
ch.clue: Transfer time: forty-five minutes
ch.q: What is the first puzzle that Dara notices in the record?
o: The system says the transfer was forty-five minutes, but the times suggest a longer gap
The system says that the flight from Lisbon arrived late at Heathfield
The system says that the bags were loaded, but they were not in Dublin
The system shows that the family had no bags to transfer at all
The system says that the bags were never checked in at Lisbon
ch.hint: Kayıt "aktarma süresi 45 dakika" diyor, ama varış saati 11:15 ve kalkış saati 1:00. Bu iki saat arasındaki gerçek süre nedir ve Dara neden bunu soruyor?
ch.why: Sistem aktarma süresini 45 dakika olarak gösteriyordu, ama 11:15 ile 1:00 arasındaki fark farklıydı; Dara bu tutarsızlığı fark etti.

text: "One hour and forty-five minutes," said Sam, counting on his fingers. "From 11:15 to 1:00 is an hour and three quarters, not forty-five minutes. Either the system has made a mistake, or the times mean something that we have not understood." Dara nodded slowly. "When two times in the same record disagree, the first suspect is always the clock. Different airports sometimes use different time zones, and a computer that subtracts without converting will produce nonsense."

She opened the airline's operational log, the technical messages that an aircraft sends when its wheels touch the ground and when its brakes are released, which are always stamped in universal time, UTC. "These are the facts," she said. "TP 482 touched down at Heathfield at 10:15 UTC. EI 321 pushed back at 12:00 UTC. Britain is on summer time, one hour ahead of UTC, so the local times were 11:15 and 13:00, exactly the times on the schedule." She wrote the numbers on a sheet. "Lisbon, Heathfield and Dublin are all on the same clock at this time of year, so there is nothing to convert."

"So the clock is innocent," said Sam. "The gap between the aircraft really was one hour and forty-five minutes. That is a comfortable margin for six bags, with a terminal change." He frowned at the screen. "But the system recorded forty-five. It did not measure that figure from the times. It is a number which came from somewhere else."

Dara looked at the line again: Transfer time: 45 min. There was a small grey symbol beside it, which she had never noticed, a tiny letter M. She moved the cursor over it, and a note appeared, in pale text: Value from MCT table.
ch.clue: Value from MCT table
ch.q: What does Dara's check of the aircraft log show?
o: The bags were checked in at Lisbon later than the passengers
The two aircraft used clocks which showed different times at Heathfield
The flights really were separated by one hour forty-five, and no time-zone error explains the figure
The flight from Lisbon landed after the flight to Dublin had taken off
The flight to Dublin left forty-five minutes after the arrival of the first flight
ch.hint: Uçakların UTC kayıtlarına göre Lizbon uçağı 10:15'te indi, Dublin uçağı 12:00'de kalktı. Üç şehir de aynı saati kullanıyor. Bu kayıt saat dilimi karışıklığı konusunda ne gösteriyor?
ch.why: Uçak kayıtları iki uçuş arasındaki gerçek sürenin bir saat kırk beş dakika olduğunu gösteriyordu; saat dilimi hatası yoktu, yani 45 dakika başka bir yerden gelmişti.

text: "MCT," said Sam. "It stands for minimum connection time." Dara had known it for years, and she explained it patiently. "Every airport has a table, a list of the shortest times in which a passenger and his bags can safely change from one flight to another. The numbers are fixed, based on the distance between the gates and the time it takes to move a suitcase by belt from one aircraft to the next. The system does not look at the real times. If the real gap is longer than the minimum in the table, it assumes that all is well, and routes the bags by the standard method."

She opened the table for Heathfield, a grid of numbers, with the arrival terminal down the side and the departure terminal across the top. At the intersection of Terminal 1 and Terminal 1, the number was 45. At the intersection of Terminal 2 and Terminal 2, also 45. But at the points where the arrival terminal and the departure terminal were different, the number was 90. "Forty-five minutes is the time for a connection inside the same terminal," she said. "Ninety is for a connection between two terminals, where the bags must be driven across the airfield."

"And the record says forty-five," said Sam. "So the system treated the connection as one inside a single terminal." Dara said nothing for a moment. She selected the two flights again and, in a small window on the right side of the screen, read the arrival and departure positions of the aircraft. Her mouth tightened.
"TP 482 arrived at stand 14, Terminal 2," she said. "And EI 321 departed from stand 6, in Terminal 1."
ch.clue: Forty-five minutes is the time for a connection inside the same terminal
ch.q: What is the meaning of the figure of forty-five minutes in the record?
o: It is the delay that the airline added to the flight because of a fault
It is the length of the flight between the cities of Heathfield and Dublin
It is the real time that the bags spent travelling between the two aircraft
It is the time of the family's last meal before they left the airport
It is a fixed minimum from a table, and it applies to connections inside one terminal
ch.hint: Sam MCT'nin asgari aktarma süresi tablosu olduğunu söylüyor. Tablo aynı terminal için 45, farklı terminaller için 90 dakika veriyor. Kayıttaki 45 dakika neyi ifade ediyor?
ch.why: Kırk beş dakika, gerçek ölçülen süre değil, tablodan gelen sabit bir değerdi ve aynı terminal içindeki aktarmalar için geçerliydi.

text: The answer, when Dara found it, was a little banal, and she sat back in her chair with a sigh. The cause of the error was a single wrong entry in the record of the flight. "The aircraft arrived in Terminal 2 and the connection left from Terminal 1," she said to Sam, who was following her finger on the screen. "Different terminals. The table should have said ninety minutes, and then the system would have routed the bags through the long transfer belt. Instead, it applied the forty-five minute value, as though they had been in the same terminal, and sent the bags through the short route, to a belt which, at that hour, was closed for maintenance. They sat in a bay until the afternoon."
"So the real gap was long enough," said Sam, "but the bags took the wrong door." "Exactly," said Dara. "It was not the clock. It was the terminal."

She sent the report to the operations office, with a request that the terminal code in the table for the flight be corrected, and went herself to the bay, where six suitcases stood in a neat row under a yellow light. By six o'clock, they were on a flight to Dublin. Mr. Caldeira, receiving the news on the telephone, said something in Portuguese which Sam did not need to have translated.
That evening, Sam wrote a note on the office whiteboard: Check the terminal before the clock.
ch.clue: It was not the clock. It was the terminal
ch.q: What really caused the bags to miss the flight?
o: The time zones were confused and the flight times were wrong in the system
The system applied the short transfer route for the same terminal, although the flights used different terminals
The family had not checked in their bags at the airport in Lisbon
The aircraft from Lisbon landed after the Dublin flight had left
The bags were left at the airport in Lisbon by mistake
ch.hint: Bagaj sistemi minimum bağlantı süresi tablosunu kullanıyor: aynı terminal için 45, farklı terminal için 90 dakika. Uçaklar farklı terminallerdeydi ama sistem 45'i uygulamış. Bu hata bagajları nasıl etkiledi?
ch.why: Uçuşlar farklı terminallerdeydi ama sistem aynı terminal için olan kısa aktarma rotasını uyguladı ve bagajlar o saatte kapalı olan banda gitti.

outro: Bagajlar, aktarma süresi çok kısa olduğu için yeni uçağa yetişememişti; sistem bu süreyi 'yeterli' saymıştı çünkü iki uçuşun saati farklı saat dilimlerine göre kaydedilmişti. Dara şunu söyledi: bir saat farkı, saatin kendisine değil, kimin saatine baktığınıza bağlıdır.

title: The Inheritance Letters
hero: Dedektif Edmund Crane ve asistanı Tess
intro: Yaşlı bir hanımefendinin ölümünden sonra, vasiyeti iki farklı sürümle ortaya çıkıyor ve iki yeğen, birbirine zıt belgeler gösteriyor. Edmund Crane ile Tess, mektupların kâğıdını, mürekkebini ve tarihlerini karşılaştırarak hangisinin gerçek olduğunu bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: Miss Eleanor Pritchard died in her sleep on a wet Tuesday in March, at the age of eighty-seven, in the large, cold house on the hill where she had lived alone for thirty years. The first thing that her solicitor, Mr. Lloyd, did on hearing the news was to open his safe. The second was to receive a telephone call from the elder of her two nephews, Mr. Julian Pritchard, who said that he had found a will in the dead woman's writing desk.

Within three days, there were two wills on the table of Mr. Lloyd's office. The first, which had been in his own safe for six years, was dated the fourth of June of that year and left the house and most of the money to a small animal sanctuary, with a modest sum to each of the nephews. The second, which Julian had brought, was dated the ninth of February, only five weeks before the death, and left everything, house, savings and furniture, to Julian himself.

Edmund Crane, who had been asked by the sanctuary's trustees to examine the case, sat across the table from the solicitor, with Tess at his side, and read both wills twice. They were short, and each was signed Eleanor M. Pritchard, in a shaky, careful hand, and witnessed by two signatures. "The second is the later one, and therefore, if genuine, it replaces the first," said Mr. Lloyd, with a sigh. "The law is simple. The question is whether it is genuine."

"The signatures look the same to me," said Tess. "To mine, too," said Edmund. "Which is exactly why I shall not look at the signatures at all, for the moment. A will is two things: a signature, and what is written above it. Let us examine the second."
ch.clue: A will is two things: a signature, and what is written above it
ch.q: What is the dispute at the beginning of the case?
o: The animal sanctuary wishes to buy the house from the nephews
Two wills exist, and the later one gives everything to one nephew
The solicitor has refused to read either will to the family
Both nephews claim the same will, which names them equally
A will has been lost and the solicitor cannot find a copy
ch.hint: Mr. Lloyd'un kasasındaki ilk vasiyet hayvan barınağına, Julian'ın getirdiği ikincisi ise her şeyi Julian'a bırakıyor ve daha yeni tarihli. Anlaşmazlık neyle ilgili?
ch.why: İki vasiyet vardı ve daha yeni tarihli olanı her şeyi tek bir yeğene, Julian'a bırakıyordu.

text: Edmund borrowed the second will for two days, and took it to a laboratory run by an old friend, a forensic document examiner named Dr. Mbeki, whose white coat was always covered with a fine layer of pale dust. She placed the page under a microscope and examined it in different kinds of light. "It is a single sheet of good cream paper," she said, "of a type sold in stationery shops for the last twenty years. There is a watermark, which gives the maker's name, and a year code in the corner, in tiny numbers. That tells us when the paper was made."

She tilted the sheet against a bright lamp. "The year code is 2011," she said. "So the paper cannot be older than 2011, which is not a problem, since the will is dated this year. But look at the ink." She put the sample under a second lens. "The signature is in blue-black ink from a fountain pen, which has soaked well into the fibres of the paper. The text above it, the body of the will, is printed in black by a laser printer. And between them there is a remarkable thing. The signature lies below the printing in some places, and above it in others."

Tess leaned closer. "What does that mean?" "In a normal document," said Dr. Mbeki, "the text is printed first, and then the person signs underneath. The ink of the signature would lie on top of the printed letters, where they cross. Here, in the places where the signature touches the lines, the toner of the printing lies on top of the ink. The signature was there first."
Edmund took off his glasses very slowly. "The printing was added after the signature," he said. "And that is a thing which Miss Pritchard could never have done."
ch.clue: The signature was there first
ch.q: What does Dr. Mbeki discover about the second will?
o: The ink of the signature was made only a few days before the will was found
The watermark shows that the will was made by the animal sanctuary
The paper of the will is more than a hundred years old and has faded
The signature lies beneath the printed text, so it was on the paper before the text was printed
The printed text was written by hand by a person who copied the style of a printer
ch.hint: Imzanın mürekkebi, yazıcı tonerinin altında kalıyor: imza metinden önce kâğıtta. Bir vasiyette normalde sıra ne olurdu ve burada neden farklı?
ch.why: İmza, yazıcıyla basılmış metnin altında kalıyordu; yani imza kâğıtta daha önce vardı ve metin sonradan basılmıştı.

text: "A signature below the printing," said Tess in the car on the way back. "Which means that the sheet was signed when it was blank." Edmund watched the grey hills go by. "Or when it had other writing on it, which was later covered. I have often noticed that a lie, when it is built on top of a truth, uses the truth as a foundation. If Miss Pritchard signed a blank sheet, it was for a reason. Old people do that, sometimes, when they are asked to sign documents which they trust somebody else to fill. A letter to the bank, an authorisation."

He telephoned the solicitor that night, and asked the question that Mr. Lloyd had not thought to ask: had Miss Pritchard, in recent years, ever signed a blank form for her nephews? The solicitor was silent for a moment. "Not to my knowledge," he said, "but there is the matter of the power of attorney. Four years ago, when she began to find the stairs difficult, she asked her nephew Julian to manage her bank affairs. I remember that I was surprised, because she had never trusted him. She signed some papers at the bank, and, I think, a number of blank authorisation sheets."

"So Julian had, in his possession, one or more sheets with the real signature of his aunt on the bottom," said Edmund. "And at some time after the date of the first will, he printed a will above one of them, and gave it the date of the ninth of February."

"Can we prove it?" asked Tess. "Printers," said Edmund. "A printer leaves a signature, too. Little yellow dots, invisible to the eye, which encode the date and the serial number of the machine. Dr. Mbeki is looking for them at this moment."
ch.clue: Four years ago
ch.q: Why does Edmund suspect that Julian had a signed blank sheet?
o: Julian managed his aunt's bank affairs and may have received blank sheets with her signature
Miss Pritchard wrote a letter to the bank which Julian later kept
Julian was the only person in the family who knew how to use a printer
The solicitor told the police that the sheets were never signed at the bank
Julian had stolen the second will from the solicitor's safe
ch.hint: Dört yıl önce Julian halanın banka işlerini yönetmeye başlamış ve hala bankada boş yetki kâğıtları da imzalamış. Bu bilgi imzalı bir boş kâğıdın nasıl Julian'ın eline geçmiş olabileceğini nasıl açıklıyor?
ch.why: Julian halasının banka işlerini yönetiyordu ve hala yetki için boş kâğıtlar imzalamış olabilirdi; bu da Julian'a imzalı boş bir kâğıt vermiş olabilirdi.

text: Dr. Mbeki's report arrived on the following Friday, in a neat blue folder. She had examined the second will under infrared and blue light, and found that the page carried the faint pattern of tiny yellow dots which laser printers of a certain make add to everything that they print. The dots, once decoded with the manufacturer's key, gave two facts. The serial number of the printer, and the date and time of printing: the twenty-ninth of March, at 16:42.

"The twenty-ninth of March," said Tess. "That is five days after Miss Pritchard died. The will bears the date of the ninth of February, and the signature of a woman who had been in her grave since the twenty-fourth." Edmund nodded. "The serial number is more interesting. The manufacturer has given us the name of the shop which sold the printer, and the shop has told us the name of the purchaser. It was bought in January. By a Mr. Julian Pritchard."

On the following Monday, Edmund and Tess accompanied Mr. Lloyd to Julian's house. Julian opened the door with his usual smile, which disappeared as he looked at the folder in Edmund's hands. "It is a very careful forgery," said Edmund. "You were right to use her real signature, and a sheet from a drawer that was her own. A printer is a more careless witness."

"I only did what she intended," Julian began, and then stopped. "She would have wanted me to have the house." Mr. Lloyd, who had known the old woman for forty years, said nothing at all. The first will was accepted by the court, in June, and, at the opening of the sanctuary's new wing, a plaque was fixed by the door with the name of Miss Eleanor Pritchard.
ch.clue: five days after Miss Pritchard died
ch.q: How is the forgery finally proved?
o: The handwriting expert says that the signature is a poor imitation
A witness saw Julian printing the will on the night before her death
The hidden yellow dots show that the will was printed five days after her death
The sanctuary finds a letter from Miss Pritchard which names Julian as a thief
The solicitor remembers that he never saw the will before the funeral
ch.hint: Yazıcının görünmeyen sarı noktaları, belgenin Miss Pritchard'ın ölümünden beş gün sonra basıldığını gösteriyor. Bu, ikinci vasiyet hakkında neyi kanıtlıyor?
ch.why: Gizli sarı noktalar, vasiyetin yazıcıdan Miss Pritchard öldükten beş gün sonra çıktığını gösteriyordu; yani 9 Şubat tarihi sahteydi.

outro: Gerçek vasiyet, daha eski tarihli olandı; öteki, hanımın ölümünden birkaç gün önce, yeğenlerden biri tarafından, yaşlı hanımın yıllar önce imzaladığı boş bir kâğıdın üzerine yazılmıştı. Edmund şunu söyledi: bir imza yalnızca imzalanmış bir kâğıdın var olduğunu kanıtlar, üstündeki yazının ne zaman yazıldığını değil.

title: The Confident Student
hero: Dr. Mara Quinn ve hemşire Joe
intro: Bir tıp öğrencisi, bir hastada nadir görülen bir hastalığı teşhis ettiğinden çok emin. Dr. Mara Quinn ile hemşire Joe, hastanın bulgularını yeniden değerlendirerek, öğrencinin hangi olasılığı gözden kaçırdığını ve neden bu kadar kendinden emin olduğunu inceliyor.

text: Daniel Reeve, in the fourth year of his medical degree, was the kind of student whom the teachers like and the other students slightly resent. He was clever, quick, and extremely well-read, and his reports were beautifully written. On the morning that Dr. Mara Quinn took a group of five students round the medical ward, he was standing a little ahead of the others, with a file in his hand and the air of a man who has found something interesting.

"Mr. Okafor, bed seven," he said, as they reached the bay. "Forty-one years old. Three months of weight loss, tremor of the hands, palpitations, heat intolerance, and a general restlessness. His heart rate is 118, his appetite is large, and he cannot sleep." He took a breath. "I believe that this is a phaeochromocytoma, a rare tumour of the adrenal gland, which releases adrenaline in bursts and produces exactly this picture. I have read three case reports, and the symptoms are identical."

Nurse Joe, who stood at the back with the observation chart, raised his eyebrows very slightly. Dr. Quinn waited, with her hands in her coat pockets. "It is a thoughtful hypothesis, Daniel," she said. "A phaeochromocytoma is a famous cause of palpitations and sweating. How common is it?"

"About one in a hundred thousand people each year," said Daniel promptly. "It is rare, which is why it is so often missed. I thought it would be a good moment to demonstrate that we should look for the unusual." A student at the side smiled, and Dr. Quinn, who had noticed, gave her a quiet glance.
"We shall go and talk to Mr. Okafor," she said. "And I would like you to ask him some questions that you have not yet asked."
ch.clue: I have read three case reports
ch.q: What diagnosis does Daniel propose, and what is Dr. Quinn's first comment?
o: A severe allergy, and she asks him to take a blood sample
A heart attack, and she asks how it is treated
A rare adrenal tumour, and she asks him how common it is
A common cold, and she asks him to prescribe medicine
A broken rib, and she asks him to examine the chest
ch.hint: Daniel nadir bir adrenal tümör (feokromositoma) öneriyor ve Dr. Quinn "ne kadar yaygın?" diye soruyor. Soru neden önemli: nadirlik bir tanıyı nasıl etkilemeli?
ch.why: Daniel nadir bir adrenal bez tümörü öneriyordu ve Dr. Quinn bunun ne kadar yaygın olduğunu sordu; çünkü nadirlik bir tanının olasılığını etkiler.

text: Mr. Okafor was a thin, sandy-haired man in a hospital gown, propped up with two pillows. He had pale blue eyes and a faint tremor of the hands, which he kept in his lap. His wife sat beside him with a bag of knitting, and, when the group approached, she sat up with an expression of hope. Dr. Quinn introduced the students and asked Daniel to continue.

Daniel asked about the symptoms, which Mr. Okafor repeated in the same words that he had used the day before. Dr. Quinn then asked, gently, whether she might put some questions of her own. "Mr. Okafor, how would you describe your mood in these three months?" "Irritable," said the patient at once. "I have been snapping at everyone. Helen says that I am impossible." "And your skin?" "Hot and damp," he said, "always. I have been wearing a T-shirt in January." His wife added, "And his eyes. I think that they look larger."

"Have you noticed any swelling in the neck?" asked Dr. Quinn. He hesitated. "My collar has been tight. I put it down to weight, but I have lost weight." Joe, who had stepped forward, moved the patient's chin up with two fingers, and looked at the front of the neck. "There is a fullness here," he said quietly, "on both sides of the windpipe."

The students looked at the neck. Daniel, who had been writing furiously, stopped. "A goitre," said a young woman called Priya, in a small voice. "An enlarged thyroid gland." Dr. Quinn nodded, and turned to the group. "The patient has described a restless, hot, thin man with a fast heart, with a swelling at the front of his neck, and with eyes which seem to protrude. Daniel, you have the symptoms right. Tell me, what else produces them?"
Daniel did not answer immediately.
ch.clue: I have been wearing a T-shirt in January
ch.q: Which new information changes the picture of Mr. Okafor's illness?
o: He has been working in a hot room with chemicals for three months
He has a recent history of a fever and an infection of the chest
He has stopped eating and drinks very little water each day
He has a family member who suffered from a similar tumour
