He has a fullness at the front of his neck and eyes that look larger
ch.hint: Hastanın boynunda sağlı sollu bir dolgunluk, gözlerinde de öne çıkma var; ayrıca hep terli ve sinirli. Bu yeni bulgular hangi organa dikkat çekiyor?
ch.why: Boynun ön tarafındaki dolgunluk ve büyümüş görünen gözler, sorunun adrenal bezden çok boyundaki tiroid bezi olabileceğini düşündürüyordu.

text: "Thyroid," said Daniel at last. "An overactive thyroid. Hyperthyroidism." He said it softly, and his face had reddened. Dr. Quinn waited until the silence was complete. "Why did you not consider it?" she asked, without reproach. "Because it is common," said Daniel. "I assumed that somebody would have excluded it."

"Somebody has not," said Dr. Quinn. "Mr. Okafor was admitted two days ago by a night doctor who wrote 'palpitations, ?anxiety'. The thyroid blood test was not ordered. Let me teach you something, and I hope that you will remember it long after you have forgotten my name. There is an old saying in medicine: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras. A zebra is the rare and beautiful animal that you read about. A horse is what is usually in the field. Hyperthyroidism affects about two people in a hundred, a thousand times more commonly than the tumour that you have described. Before the zebra, we must exclude the horse."

"But the zebras exist," said Daniel stubbornly. "They do," said Dr. Quinn, "and sometimes they are the answer. But a hundred cases of palpitations in a hospital will contain, on average, ninety-nine for whom the cause is common, and one who has something unusual. The best doctors do not stop looking for zebras. They look for horses first, and have a plan for when the horse does not fit."

Joe had already taken the blood form from the clipboard. "Thyroid function," he read out, ticking the box, "and a heart tracing. I will take the sample now." Mr. Okafor rolled up his sleeve, and his wife put down her knitting.
ch.clue: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras
ch.q: What lesson does Dr. Quinn teach Daniel?
o: A doctor should avoid reading case reports of unusual illnesses
Common causes should be excluded before rare ones are considered
A diagnosis must be confirmed by three students before it is accepted
Rare diseases should always be tested before any common disease
Students should never offer an opinion in front of a patient
ch.hint: Dr. Quinn "nal sesi duyunca at düşün, zebra değil" atasözünü anlatıyor. Bir doktor ilk hangi tür nedenleri dışlamalı?
ch.why: Dr. Quinn'e göre bir hekim, nadir bir hastalığı düşünmeden önce yaygın nedenleri dışlamalıydı.

text: The blood results came back by four o'clock, and Dr. Quinn invited the students to gather round the screen in the ward office. Mr. Okafor's thyroid stimulating hormone, which in a healthy person is between 0.4 and 4, was below 0.01, so low that the laboratory had marked it with a red flag. The level of thyroid hormone itself, which should have been in the middle of the normal range, was almost three times the upper limit. And the heart tracing showed a rapid but regular rhythm, which fell, in the doctor's words, "within the family of a thyroid heart".

An ultrasound of the neck, performed the following morning, confirmed an enlarged gland with a uniform pattern. A second test, for the antibodies that, in this disease, stimulate the thyroid by mistake, was positive. "Graves' disease," said Dr. Quinn, "an autoimmune condition. The body's defences attack, not to destroy, but to over-stimulate. It also explains the eyes, because the same antibodies affect the tissue behind them."

Mr. Okafor was treated with a tablet that reduced the production of the hormone and a second that slowed his heart, and within three weeks he was sleeping again, with a heart rate of seventy-eight. The tumour that Daniel had suspected was never needed. He took the news with grace, and, a few days later, brought Dr. Quinn a short summary of the disease, written in his usual elegant style, with a final paragraph which she kept.

Next time, he wrote, I will start with the horse. But I shall remember that the zebra is somewhere in the field. Dr. Quinn smiled, and put the summary in the teaching folder, with a note: Share with next year's students.
ch.clue: an autoimmune condition
ch.q: What was Mr. Okafor's real diagnosis?
o: A rare tumour of the adrenal gland that releases adrenaline
An anxiety disorder with no physical cause
A reaction to a medicine that he had taken during the winter
Graves' disease, an overactive thyroid caused by antibodies
A chronic infection of the heart which required an operation
ch.hint: Tetkikler çok düşük TSH, yüksek tiroid hormonu ve pozitif antikor gösterdi. Bu sonuçlar hangi hastalığı işaret ediyor?
ch.why: Hastada tiroid bezini aşırı uyaran antikorların neden olduğu Graves hastalığı (aşırı çalışan tiroid) vardı; nadir tümör gerekmedi.

outro: Hastanın şikâyetleri nadir bir hastalıktan değil, çok daha yaygın bir sorun olan tiroid fazlalığından kaynaklanıyordu. Mara şunu yazdı: bir hekimin ilk öğrendiği şey, nadir bir hastalığı aramadan önce yaygın olanı dışlamaktır.

title: The Water Budget
hero: Komutan Noor Hale ve mühendis Pip
intro: Ay üssündeki su depolarında, beklenenden daha hızlı bir azalma var. Komutan Noor Hale ile mühendis Pip, su geri dönüşüm sistemini, mürettebatın tüketimini ve olası sızıntıları inceleyerek açığın nerede olduğunu bulmaya çalışıyor.

text: On Moonbase Selene, water was the most precious thing, and every drop of it was counted. It was brought from Earth at huge expense, or extracted from the frozen ice in the permanent shadow of a nearby crater, and then used, cleaned, and used again. The crew of six drank it, washed in it, cooked with it, and grew lettuce in it, and, through a complicated recycling system, recovered about ninety-five per cent of everything that they used. The remaining five per cent, the water that left the system and had to be replaced, was calculated to the last litre.

On the twentieth day of the mission's second quarter, Pip came to Commander Noor Hale's cabin with a tablet in his hand, and an expression that she knew. "The inventory," he said. "The tanks are lower than the budget says they should be. According to the plan, we should have 4,180 litres. The sensors report 4,020. We are missing a hundred and sixty."

Noor sat up. "A hundred and sixty litres is a lot," she said. "How long has it been going on?" "I checked the weekly figures," said Pip, "and the difference has grown by about forty litres every week, for the last four weeks. The pattern is steady, almost exactly the same each time." Noor studied the graph. A leak would be steady, but a leak would also show on the pressure sensors, and the base's atmosphere had not changed. "Make a list of everything that could account for a loss of forty litres a week," she said. "Both real and unreal."

Pip took a pen and, in an old habit, wrote on the back of his hand. "A leak. A crew member using more than we think. An error in the recycling process. And a sensor that is reading wrongly." He looked up. "I shall begin with the tanks."
ch.clue: Both real and unreal
ch.q: What is the problem that Pip reports?
o: The recycling system has stopped working completely for four weeks
The sensors have stopped working and cannot measure the water
The crew members have been using water without recording it
The water tanks hold 160 litres less than the budget says, and the gap grows every week
The water from the crater is frozen and cannot be used
ch.hint: Bütçeye göre 4.180 litre olması gerekirken sensörler 4.020 litre gösteriyor ve fark her hafta yaklaşık 40 litre artıyor. Pip'in bildirdiği sorun nedir?
ch.why: Su depoları bütçede olması gerekenden 160 litre az gösteriyordu ve fark her hafta yaklaşık 40 litre artıyordu.

text: The first possibility to test was that of a real leak, because it was the worst. Pip and Noor spent the following morning in the water plant, a long, cramped module filled with pipes, pumps and filters, with a torch, a dry cloth and a pressure gauge. They examined every joint and valve, and the whole length of the pipework, looking for drops, stains, or the white crust that dried water leaves on metal. They found nothing. A dry cloth, pressed against each coupling for a full minute, came away dry.

They tried another method. By closing the valves, they isolated each tank and the pipe that fed it, and watched the pressure for two hours. A leak would have produced a slow fall, and the gauge would have marked it. In every section, the line on the screen was flat. "Nothing is escaping," said Pip. "At least not from the tanks or the pipes. If we are losing forty litres a week, it is not going into the lunar dust." Noor turned to the second possibility. "The crew. If someone is using more water than is recorded, the total would drop."

The consumption records were kept by a flow meter in each module, and checked against a daily log that every crew member signed. Noor went through six weeks of entries. The daily average was 38 litres per person, which was within the target and almost exactly the same, week after week. The numbers did not match the pattern of the missing water. "The loss is steady," said Pip. "Always forty litres a week. Human use fluctuates. Somebody has a long shower, somebody is on a spacewalk and uses less. The numbers are too regular, even for us."
Noor put down the log. "A regular loss without a physical leak," she said. "That is a measurement, not a movement." She looked at the tablet. "Show me the calibration record of the tank sensors."
ch.clue: The numbers are too regular, even for us
ch.q: What do the tests of the pipes and the crew's records indicate?
o: No physical leak exists and human use is too steady to explain the loss, so a measurement error is likely
The pipes are leaking in a place that cannot be reached with a torch
The pressure gauge is broken and gives the same reading in every section
The crew has been wasting water at night while the others are asleep
The recycled water is being used faster by the lettuce plants
ch.hint: Borular kuru ve basınç düşmüyor. Mürettebatın günlük tüketimi de hep aynı. Kayıp ise her hafta 40 litre ile çok düzenli. Bu düzenlilik fiziksel bir sızıntıdan çok neyi düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Fiziksel sızıntı yoktu ve insan kullanımı kaybı açıklayamayacak kadar düzenliydi; bu bir ölçüm hatasını düşündürüyordu.

text: The sensors in the tanks were of an unusual type. They did not measure the depth of the water directly. Instead, a small pressure cell at the bottom of each tank measured the weight of the water above it, and a computer turned the pressure into a volume, using a calibration constant: a number, measured at the factory, which says how many litres correspond to each unit of pressure. On Earth, where the gravity is constant, such a constant is the same everywhere. But on the Moon, the gravity is about one sixth of that on Earth, and the calibration must be adjusted accordingly.

Pip opened the maintenance log and began to read it, line by line. The tanks' sensors had been installed eight months earlier, and calibrated for lunar gravity by the engineers on Earth. In the log of the previous quarter, however, he found an entry that made him stop. A software update, installed six weeks earlier, had replaced the calibration file. The update note said: Calibration constants refreshed from the factory master. Lunar adjustment to be applied in the next release.

"Six weeks ago," said Noor, reading over his shoulder. "And the gap began four weeks ago." Pip tapped the screen. "The update installed the factory constants for Earth gravity. The sensor now believes that the pressure from a litre of water on the Moon corresponds to a lower volume than it really does. It is reading a little less than the real amount. And because the water level in each tank decreases slowly through use, the error is proportional, and grows in step with the consumption."

"So the water is not missing," said Noor. "It is simply being counted by a ruler that is the wrong length." She looked at the two numbers on the tablet, 4,180 and 4,020. "We should test it with a known amount."
ch.clue: Lunar adjustment to be applied in the next release
ch.q: What is the most probable explanation for the missing 160 litres?
o: The tanks have been damaged by a series of small meteorite impacts
The crew has been given extra water for their gardens without a record
A software update installed Earth calibration constants, so the sensors under-read the real volume
The recycling plant is losing five per cent of the water instead of one
A pipe is leaking slowly into the lunar soil under the base
ch.hint: Yazılım güncellemesi tank sensörlerinin kalibrasyon sabitini fabrikadaki Dünya değerleriyle değiştirmiş ve Ay yerçekimi ayarı yapılmamış. Bu, sensörlerin okumasına ne yapar?
ch.why: Güncelleme Dünya yerçekimine ait kalibrasyon sabitlerini yüklemişti; bu yüzden sensörler gerçek hacimden daha az gösteriyordu.

text: The test was simple, and Pip designed it with relish. They took a calibrated container, a sealed steel tank of exactly fifty litres, filled it from the main supply, and pumped the water into an empty tank, number three, whose sensor had been showing the largest error. If the reading rose by fifty litres, the sensor was correct. If it rose by a smaller amount, then the sensor was under-reading, and, from the ratio, they could calculate the true constant.

It took an hour. When the last litre had been pumped, Noor read the display of tank three. "Forty-seven point one," she said. Pip did the division: 47.1 over 50 was 0.942. "The sensor is reading 94 per cent of the real value," he said. "A shortfall of six per cent. If that applies to all of the six tanks, which hold about 2,800 litres in total at present, the missing amount would be six per cent of the 2,800, which is a hundred and sixty-eight litres. It matches, within the margin of error, the gap that we found."

"The water has been here all the time," said Noor. She wrote a short message to the engineers on Earth, with the numbers, and the request that the lunar calibration be re-applied. The corrected file arrived on the next data link, and Pip, with a smile, installed it on the second day. The inventory climbed from 4,020 to 4,181 litres in a single moment, and the missing hundred and sixty returned to the budget.

"What did we learn?" asked Noor, as they sat in the cramped plant, drinking a cup of recycled tea. "That before looking for a leak," said Pip, "we should check that we are counting correctly. Water does not hide. But a number can."
ch.clue: The water has been here all the time
ch.q: How do Noor and Pip confirm their explanation?
o: They receive a message from Earth saying that the budget was wrong
They find a small hole in the pipe and seal it with a patch
They take away the sensors and measure the tanks with a long stick
They ask the crew to use less water for a period of three weeks
They pump a known 50 litres into a tank and find that the sensor reads only 47.1
ch.hint: 50 litrelik bilinen su miktarı tanka pompalandığında sensör yalnızca 47,1 litre gösteriyor. Bu sonuç sensör hakkında neyi doğruluyor?
ch.why: Bilinen 50 litre su pompalandığında sensör 47,1 litre gösterdi; bu, sensörün gerçek hacmi eksik okuduğunu kanıtlıyordu.

outro: Su, bir sızıntıdan değil, bir sensörün hatalı kalibrasyonundan 'kaybolmuştu'; depodaki gerçek miktar ölçülenden daha fazlaydı. Noor şunu yazdı: bir bütçe açığı, para eksik olduğundan değil, birinin yanlış saydığından da çıkabilir.

title: The Famous Letter
hero: Tarihçi Dr. Amira Kent ve asistanı Leo
intro: Ünlü bir tarihî mektubun, tarihçiler tarafından yüz yıldır aynı biçimde yorumlandığı biliniyor. Dr. Amira Kent ile Leo, yeni bulunan bir kopyayı, orijinal metinle karşılaştırarak ünlü bir cümlenin eksik bir kelimesi yüzünden yanlış anlaşılıp anlaşılmadığını araştırıyor.

text: Every school child in the county of Harrowdale learned the sentence by heart. It came from a letter written in 1745 by Lord Edmund Thorne, the commander of the local militia, to the mayor of the town, on the eve of a battle that, in the end, never took place. In the version printed in the school textbooks, the sentence reads: I shall defend the bridge to the last man, and surrender it only when the river runs dry. It had been engraved on the statue in the market square, and printed on tea towels, and quoted by three prime ministers.

Dr. Amira Kent had never had occasion to doubt it, until a Thursday in October, when the county record office telephoned her with a surprising piece of news. While clearing a damp store, a volunteer had found a bundle of papers belonging to the mayor of the time. Among them was a handwritten letter, apparently dated the same day, and signed by Lord Thorne. It was only a draft, or a copy, and it was in poor condition, but its first lines looked familiar.

Amira and Leo drove over the same afternoon. In the reading room, under a grey light from the high window, the fragile sheet lay on a foam support. Amira read the first paragraph, and her expression changed. "It is the letter," she said. "At least, it is a version of it." She pointed at the middle of the second line. "And here is the famous sentence. But it is not quite the same."
Leo leaned over the page. He read the line twice, with his lips moving. Then he took a pencil, and wrote the two versions one beneath the other in his notebook, and looked at them for a long time.
"It has a word that the textbook does not have," he said. "A very small word."
ch.clue: A very small word
ch.q: What do Amira and Leo find in the newly discovered letter?
o: The letter has no connection with the one that is known
The letter is a modern forgery made by the record office
The letter is written in a language that they cannot read
The sentence is missing from the letter entirely
The famous sentence appears with a small difference from the version in the textbooks
ch.hint: Yeni bulunan mektupta meşhur cümle var, ama ders kitaplarındakinden küçük bir farkla. Leo "çok küçük bir kelime" diyor. Bu keşif neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Yeni mektuptaki cümle, ders kitaplarındaki sürümden küçük bir kelime farkıyla ayrılıyordu.

text: The word was not. In the new letter, the sentence read: I shall not defend the bridge to the last man, and I shall surrender it when the river runs dry. Amira copied it out in full, with the spelling of the eighteenth century, which differed from the modern form in the doubling of letters and the generous use of capitals. She laid her own transcription beside the printed text of the textbook and the statue.

"The two sentences are almost identical," said Leo. "But the meanings are not. The statue says that Lord Thorne will defend the bridge to the last man. The letter says that he will not." He rubbed his forehead. "That is not a small matter. It would mean that the hero of Harrowdale, the man on the pedestal in the square, was announcing that he would not fight."

"Do not hurry," said Amira. "We have a draft, in poor condition, in an unknown hand. A single word could be an error. A copyist, working quickly, may write a word that is not in the original, as easily as he may leave out one that is." She spread the original paper under the lamp and looked at the line again, at the shape of the letters. "In this version, the word is written in the same ink and the same hand as the rest. It was not added afterwards. If it is a mistake, the mistake was made at the time. But if it is a copy, the copyist may have made it."

"So we have two texts, with a difference of one word," said Leo, "and no way of knowing which is right." Amira picked up the telephone on the desk, and asked for the head of the record office. "I should like to know," she said, "how the textbook version came to be printed. And in particular, whose copy it comes from."
ch.clue: A copyist, working quickly, may write a word that is not in the original
ch.q: Why does Amira not immediately accept the new letter as the correct version?
o: The textbook version has been proved to be correct by three historians
It may be a copy in which the copyist added or omitted a word by mistake
The letter is too short to give any reliable information
The paper of the new letter is much older than the date of the battle
Leo has written down the wrong sentence in his notebook
ch.hint: Amira, kopyacıların kelime ekleyip çıkarabileceğini söylüyor. İki sürüm arasındaki fark neden hemen doğru olanı göstermiyor?
ch.why: Yeni mektup bir kopya olabilirdi ve kopyacı bir kelimeyi yanlışlıkla eklemiş ya da düşürmüş olabilirdi; bu yüzden iki metinden hangisinin doğru olduğu bilinmiyordu.

text: The head of the record office, Mrs. Abney, was a calm woman with a large bunch of keys on her belt, and she led Amira and Leo to a steel cabinet in the basement. "The textbook version," she said, "comes ultimately from a book published in 1820, The History of Harrowdale, by a local clergyman, the Reverend Mr. Hollis. He printed the letter in full, in a long appendix. I believe that he copied it from the manuscript, in the possession, at that time, of the mayor's family."

She laid a thick volume on the table, and, on page 211, they found the sentence, as in the textbooks: I shall defend the bridge to the last man. Mrs. Abney turned the page and showed them a footnote in small type. The Reverend explained, in a modest tone: The original, I regret to say, is much damaged, and in some places the copyist, who prepared it for me, was obliged to supply from conjecture words which time had obscured.

"Words which time had obscured," said Amira slowly. "So the Reverend admits that part of his version is a reconstruction. And a copyist is the unnamed person in the middle." She counted on her fingers. "The original letter of 1745 is lost. The Reverend's copyist made a copy, in the early nineteenth century, from a damaged original. The Reverend printed it in 1820. The textbooks have copied the printed book. And our little draft, which is in a hand of the eighteenth century, is a different, older line of transmission, a copy made at the time."

"So the draft is nearer to the original," said Leo, "by a hundred years." "Nearer," said Amira, "but not necessarily right. We need a third witness. If I were a mayor in 1745, to whom would I send a copy of this letter?"
ch.clue: supply from conjecture words which time had obscured
ch.q: What does the footnote in the Reverend's book reveal?
o: The Reverend wrote the whole letter himself to make the town famous
The mayor's family had kept the letter secret for a hundred years
The original letter was destroyed by the Reverend after he had printed it
Part of the printed letter was reconstructed by a copyist from a damaged original
The copyist was a soldier who had been present at the battle
ch.hint: Papaz dipnotta orijinalin hasarlı olduğunu ve kopyacının kayıp kelimeleri tahminle tamamladığını söylüyor. Bu itiraf, basılı metnin güvenilirliği hakkında ne gösteriyor?
ch.why: Papaz, orijinal mektubun hasarlı olduğunu ve kopyacının bazı kelimeleri tahminle tamamlamak zorunda kaldığını belirtiyordu; yani basılı metnin bir kısmı yeniden oluşturulmuştu.

text: A mayor receives letters, and, if he is prudent, he forwards them. Amira searched the records of the neighbouring town of Eastbridge, where, in 1745, the mayor was a cousin of the mayor of Harrowdale, and a regular correspondent. In the town archive, in a box of "letters regarding the rebellion", she found a small bundle tied with a faded ribbon, and, among them, a fair copy of Lord Thorne's letter, made at the time by the Eastbridge town clerk, and endorsed: Received 14 Sept. 1745, being a copy of my Lord Thorne's letter to Harrowdale.

The sentence in the clerk's version was clear and unambiguous, in a bold, careful hand, with no damage at all. It read: I shall not defend the bridge to the last man, and I shall surrender it when the river runs dry. The same words, in the same order, as in the little draft. The clerk had even underlined the word not, with the small flourish that scribes of the time used for emphasis.

"Two independent copies, made at the time, agree," said Leo, "and the one that differs is the later one, printed after the original had been damaged." Amira nodded. "The Reverend's copyist, working with a damaged paper, would have seen the word 'not' as a smudge, and would have supposed that a hero would not write it. He supplied the sentence that he expected. It is a very human error."

In the spring, the museum added a new panel next to the statue in the market square, with the two sentences, side by side. Lord Thorne, the new text explained, had been a prudent man. He had not wished to lose the lives of his men, and had written, in a moment of honesty, that he would not die for a bridge. The statue stayed. The children of Harrowdale, who had learned the old sentence at school, learned the new one the following autumn, and, in their opinion, it was a great deal more interesting.
ch.clue: I shall not defend the bridge to the last man
ch.q: What does the third copy show?
o: Two copies made at the time agree on the word 'not', so the textbook version was a reconstruction error
The word 'not' was added to the letter in the nineteenth century by a vicar
The third copy disagrees with both and gives a different sentence
The letter was written by the clerk and not by Lord Thorne at all
The statue in the square was built to honour a different commander
ch.hint: Eastbridge kâtibinin 1745'te yaptığı kopya, küçük taslakla aynı: "not" kelimesi var. Bu iki bağımsız ve dönemin kopyası, basılı sürümün kaynağı hakkında ne gösteriyor?
ch.why: Dönemin iki bağımsız kopyası "not" kelimesinde birleşiyordu; basılı sürümdeki farkın, hasarlı orijinalden yapılan bir yeniden kurma hatası olduğu anlaşıldı.

outro: Cümlede 'not' kelimesi, kopyacının dikkatsizliği yüzünden düşmüştü; yani yüz yıldır okunan anlam tamamen tersiydi. Amira şunu yazdı: tarih, çoğu zaman bir kelimenin, bir virgülün ve bir kopyacının yorgunluğunun üzerine kuruludur.

title: The Contaminated Sample
hero: Dr. Ilan Voss ve asistanı Dana
intro: Dr. Voss'un laboratuvarında bir bakteri kültürü, üç ardışık deneyde aynı beklenmedik sonucu veriyor. Dana kültürün kirlendiğinden şüpheleniyor, Ilan ise bunun gerçek bir bulgu olup olmadığını sınamak istiyor. İkisi, kirlenmeyi ve gerçek bir etkiyi ayırt edecek bir deney tasarlıyor.

text: Dana was the first person in the laboratory every morning, and the first to look at the plates. On the Tuesday morning that began this story, she opened the incubator at half past seven and took out a tray of Petri dishes, each filled with a thin layer of pink jelly and a spreading film of bacteria. She read the plates as she had read them every morning for a month, running her finger along the rows, and then she stopped, and read the third row again.

The experiment was a simple one. Dr. Voss's team was testing whether a new antibiotic, a compound called AX-9, slowed the growth of a common bacterium called Escherichia coli. On each plate, there were two zones: one treated with the drug, one with plain water as a control. The expectation was clear. Where the drug was present, the colony should be smaller.

On the third row, the drug zone was smaller, as expected, by about a third. But the control zone, the water, was strange. In the middle of each colony, a fine ring of tiny, pale, almost transparent dots was visible, like a necklace around a bright disc. She had not seen it in any previous experiment. "It is the third time," she said aloud to the empty laboratory. "Monday, last Thursday, and now."

When Dr. Voss came in, she showed him the plates. He looked at them for a long time, with his hands behind his back. "An interesting ring," he said. "Either it is a contamination, which is the likeliest thing, because a laboratory is full of invisible organisms and they love a warm plate. Or it is something new." He paused. "It is a very old and very good rule in science that when you see a surprising result three times, you do not announce a discovery. You try, as hard as you can, to prove that it is wrong."
ch.clue: You try, as hard as you can, to prove that it is wrong
ch.q: What strategy does Dr. Voss recommend for a surprising result?
o: To try as hard as possible to show that it is a mistake before announcing it
To ignore it because the expected result was already obtained
To throw away all the plates and start a completely new experiment
To publish it immediately because it has appeared three times
To ask the other laboratories to confirm it without checking it first
ch.hint: Üç kez gördüğü sürpriz sonuç için Dr. Voss yeni bir keşif ilan etmeyi değil, ne yapmayı öneriyor? Bilimsel şüphecilik hangi yönde çalışır?
ch.why: Dr. Voss, sonucu açıklamadan önce yanlış olduğunu kanıtlamaya olabildiğince çalışmayı öneriyordu.

text: Over coffee, in the small kitchen at the end of the corridor, Dr. Voss and Dana drew up two columns. In one, they wrote the reasons for suspecting a contamination. The ring was small, uniform, and located in the control zone, where nothing special had been added. It appeared in three experiments, but only in the dishes from one incubator, the old one on the left, which had been giving trouble with its door. The bacterium that they used grew as a smooth, round colony, and a ring of dots was a different shape, which suggested a second organism.

In the second column, the reasons for suspecting something real. "Three times is not an accident," said Dana, a little defensively. "The same pattern, the same ring, in the same position. A contaminant would be scattered and random. A real effect would be reproducible." Dr. Voss smiled. "It is a good argument, and it is also the argument of everyone who has ever mistaken a contamination for a discovery. A contaminant that lives in an incubator will find the same plates every time, because the plates all sit in the same place, at the same temperature, with the same humidity. It is reproducible, in the sense that it recurs. That tells us nothing about whether it is real."

He stood up and took a marker from the pocket of his coat. On the whiteboard, he drew a small diagram. "We need an experiment that makes the two hypotheses predict different things. If it is a real effect of the bacteria, it should appear whenever we grow them, in any incubator, from any stock. If it is a contaminant, it should depend on the incubator or the batch of medium, and not on the bacteria."
Dana looked at the diagram. "Four conditions," she said slowly. "Two incubators, and two stocks of the bacterium." She was already reaching for her pencil.
ch.clue: A contaminant that lives in an incubator will find the same plates every time
ch.q: Why is the repetition of the ring not proof that it is a real effect?
o: The ring is only visible in the plates that are treated with the drug
The bacteria change colour whenever the temperature is raised
A contaminant in the same incubator can recur every time under the same conditions
A real effect can never appear more than once in an experiment
Dr. Voss is certain that the ring has been drawn by a student
ch.hint: Dr. Voss, bir bulaşıcı organizmanın aynı kuluçka makinesindeki aynı plakalarda her seferinde tekrar edebileceğini söylüyor. Tekrarlanma neden gerçek bir etkinin kanıtı olmayabilir?
ch.why: Aynı kuluçka makinesinde yaşayan bir kirletici, aynı koşullarda her seferinde tekrar edebilirdi; tekrarlanma tek başına gerçekliği göstermezdi.

text: They grew the bacteria in the following way. Two stocks: the usual one, from the freezer, and a fresh culture, obtained from a different supplier. Two incubators: the old one on the left, and a new one that the department had bought in the spring, installed in another room. Each combination of stock and incubator was represented by six plates, and the plates were labelled with codes that Dana had not been told, so that her reading would not be influenced by what she expected to see. Dr. Voss had asked a postdoctoral colleague, Dr. Yilmaz, to arrange the codes.

The plates stayed in the warmth for twenty-four hours, and, when they were taken out, Dana read each one in turn, with a hand lens, recording the presence or absence of the ring on a sheet. Only when she had finished did Dr. Yilmaz open the sealed envelope with the key.

The result was as clear as a diagram. In the old incubator, the ring was present on every one of the twelve plates, whatever the stock. In the new incubator, it was absent from all twelve. It did not depend on the bacterium, which was the same in each case, and it did not depend on the drug. It depended on the machine.

"It is the incubator," said Dana, looking at the table. Her voice was steady, but her face showed disappointment, which she did not try to hide. "There was never a discovery." Dr. Voss laid a hand on her shoulder. "There was something better," he said. "A question, and an answer, produced in three days. And now we have a reason to look inside that incubator."
ch.clue: It depended on the machine
ch.q: What does the four-condition experiment show?
o: The ring does not appear in any of the plates in the experiment
The ring appears only on plates treated with the new antibiotic
The ring appears with one bacterial stock and not with the other
The ring appears in all the incubators and with all the stocks
The ring appears only in the old incubator, whichever bacterium is used
ch.hint: Eski kuluçka makinesindeki on iki plakanın hepsinde halka var, yenisindeki on iki plakanın hiçbirinde yok. Bu sonuç halkanın kaynağı hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Halka yalnızca eski kuluçka makinesinde görülüyordu ve bakteri stokundan bağımsızdı; yani sorun makineydi.

text: The next morning, Dana and Dr. Yilmaz took the old incubator apart. They switched it off, removed the shelves, and wiped the walls with a swab, which they spread on a plate of nutrient jelly and left to grow for two days. At the back of the chamber, behind the fan, in a corner that had not been cleaned for years, they found a damp patch. The seal around the door, a rubber strip, had cracked in one place, and a little condensation had collected along the lower edge.

The plate from the swab grew, within forty-eight hours, a furry grey-green colony, easy to recognise even without a microscope. "A mould," said Dr. Yilmaz, tapping the lid. "Penicillium, or something very close to it. It is one of the commonest moulds in the world, and it reproduces by tiny spores, which float in the air. They would have drifted out of the damp corner whenever the door was opened, settled on the plates, and produced the pale ring of small colonies that you saw." Under the microscope, the dots in the ring were a mixture of bacterial and fungal cells.

Dr. Voss ordered the incubator to be cleaned and its seal replaced. He asked Dana to write a short report on the whole story, for the laboratory's notebook, with the title: A ring that was not a discovery. "It will be one of the most useful pages in the book," he said. "Every young scientist will meet a result that is too interesting to be true. It is good to see how one is dismantled."

That afternoon, Dana ran the original experiment again, in the new incubator, with the drug and the control. The colonies were round and smooth, and there was no ring. The drug zone was smaller by a third, as before. The antibiotic, in other words, worked, and was the only discovery that the week had produced.
ch.clue: a damp patch
ch.q: What caused the ring on the plates?
o: A chemical reaction between the jelly and the water in the control zone
A mould growing in a damp corner of the old incubator, whose spores settled on the plates
A fault in the lens that Dana used to read the plates
A new kind of bacterium that appeared only when the antibiotic was used
A mistake in the labelling of the plates by Dr. Yilmaz
ch.hint: Eski kuluçka makinesinin arkasındaki nemli köşede küf bulundu ve sporlar plakalara yayılmış. Halka neyin sonucuydu?
ch.why: Halkayı, eski kuluçka makinesinin nemli köşesinde büyüyen bir küfün sporları yapmıştı; sporlar kapak açıldıkça plakalara konuyordu.

outro: Kirlenme gerçekti: kültür kabının kapağındaki küçük bir hatadan bir küf mantarı girmişti ve sonuçları o bozmuştu. Ilan şunu yazdı: beklenmedik bir sonuç, her zaman bir keşif değildir; ama her zaman bir soruyu hak eder.

title: The Viral Photograph
hero: Muhabir Jonas Reid ve fotoğrafçı Ellie
intro: Sosyal medyada hızla yayılan bir fotoğraf, Kingsbridge'de bir sel sırasında yardım çalışması yapan 'kahraman bir itfaiyeci'yi gösteriyor. Jonas Reid ile Ellie, fotoğrafın ne zaman, nerede ve kim tarafından çekildiğini doğrulamaya çalışırken şaşırtıcı bir gerçekle karşılaşıyor.

text: By Friday morning, the photograph had been shared eleven thousand times. It showed a firefighter in a yellow jacket and a white helmet, standing waist-deep in brown, rushing water, with a small child in his arms, and, behind him, a half-submerged street of terraced houses with a church tower in the distance. The caption read: Our hero. A firefighter from Kingsbridge rescues a child in the floods. Please share so that he gets the recognition he deserves.

The town had been flooded the previous weekend, it was true, when the river Wend had burst its banks and covered some of the low-lying streets. Three hundred people had been evacuated, and the local fire brigade had worked day and night. The image seemed to capture the whole story. The mayor had shared it with a warm comment. Two councillors had suggested a medal. The local radio had asked its listeners to help to identify the man.

Mrs. Cole read the shared post at the morning meeting, and then looked round the table. "I should like to know who he is," she said. "A hero deserves a name. Jonas, will you find him? Ellie, you were on the Mill Road all weekend. Do you recognise the picture?" Ellie took the telephone, enlarged the image, and studied it for a full minute, frowning. "I photographed that stretch for two days," she said slowly. "And I do not recognise it. I do not remember a church tower like that, nor houses with those chimneys."

"It could be a different street," said Jonas. "Kingsbridge has forty." "It could," said Ellie. "But I know them, and there is something wrong with this one. I cannot say what. Give me an hour with the original file."
ch.clue: I do not remember a church tower like that
ch.q: Why is Ellie uneasy about the photograph?
o: She has seen the same firefighter on the television news the day before
She does not recognise the buildings or the church tower from her own photographs of the floods
She knows that the fire brigade did not take part in the rescue
She thinks the child in the picture is too young to be rescued
She believes the photograph was taken by someone who wanted to be famous
ch.hint: Ellie iki gün boyunca sel bölgesini fotoğrafladığını ama resimdeki kilise kulesini ve evleri hatırlamadığını söylüyor. Bu rahatsızlık hangi ihtimali düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Ellie selin olduğu sokakları iyi biliyordu ve resimdeki kilise kulesi ile evleri hatırlamıyordu; bu, fotoğrafın başka bir yerden olabileceğini düşündürüyordu.

text: Ellie sat at her computer for an hour, with a large cup of tea, and examined the photograph as a detective examines a room. She began with what could be read in the picture itself. The firefighter's jacket was yellow, with reflective stripes and a badge on the left shoulder, too small to read at the size of the shared post. The helmet was white. "The Kingsbridge brigade wear red helmets," she said. "I have photographed them for ten years."

Next, she studied the street. The houses were of red brick, terraced, with small front gardens, and with a distinctive feature that she had noticed at once: a row of shutters on the upper windows, painted in pale blue. "Shutters," she said. "No houses in Kingsbridge have shutters. It is not a local style." She enlarged the church tower in the background. It was square, with a pointed roof of green copper, and a clock whose face was visible. "There is no clock tower in the town with a green roof."

She tried to find the picture's origin with a reverse image search, a tool that finds copies of a picture across the web. The search returned forty results, sorted by date. The latest were all from this week, all with the caption about the Kingsbridge hero. But the earliest, at the bottom of the list, was dated three years ago, and it came from a news agency's website, with a different caption, in a different language.

"Jonas," she called, and he came across the room. "Look at this. It is the same picture, but with a different story." She turned the screen. He read the line beneath, which was in Dutch, and took out his phone to translate. "A firefighter carries a child through the floodwater in a village on the river Maas," he read slowly. "Dated July. Three years ago."
ch.clue: Shutters
ch.q: What does Ellie's reverse image search reveal?
o: The picture has been edited so that the firefighter looks like a Kingsbridge man
The picture was posted for the first time by the mayor of Kingsbridge
The picture is a painting that was copied from a news photograph
The earliest copy of the picture is three years old and has a caption from another country
The picture was taken by a famous photographer working for a national newspaper
ch.hint: Ters görsel arama, fotoğrafın en eski kopyasının üç yıl önce, başka bir dilde bir ajans sitesinde yayımlandığını gösteriyor. Bu tarih ve altyazı fotoğrafın kaynağı hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Fotoğrafın bilinen en eski kopyası üç yıl önceye ve başka bir ülkenin haber sitesine aitti; yani Kingsbridge'de bu hafta çekilmemişti.

text: Jonas did not take the Dutch caption on trust. A single article, even from a news agency, could be wrong, or might itself have borrowed the picture from somewhere else. He wrote down the details: the name of the agency, the date, the name of the photographer, and the location. Then he began, in the way that he had learned as a young reporter, to check each of them against another source.

The agency's name was Beeldbank Zuid, a regional picture library in the south of the Netherlands. Its website carried a page for the photographer, a freelance named Marit de Wit, with a short biography and a gallery of the floods that had covered the Limburg province in the summer, three years before. In the gallery, he found the picture, number nine of forty, with the caption that the search had found. He telephoned the library, where a helpful woman confirmed that the photograph had been taken in the village of Itteren, on the fifteenth of July.

"Is there any way to be sure that it is the same picture?" he asked. "Of course," said the woman. "I will send you the original file." It arrived within ten minutes. Jonas opened it next to the shared version, and, with the help of Ellie, compared the details: the shape of the helmet, the angle of the child's arm, the tilt of the church tower. Every curve and shadow was identical, down to a small bird, which was perched on a wire in the upper right corner. "It is the same picture," said Ellie. "It has been cropped, and the colour a little brightened. But it is the same."
"So we have two sources and a file," said Jonas. "A photographer, an agency, and the village of Itteren, in Limburg. This was not taken in Kingsbridge."
ch.clue: Every curve and shadow was identical
ch.q: How does Jonas confirm the origin of the photograph?
o: He contacts the picture library and compares the original file with the shared picture
He relies on the caption, which says that the picture was taken in the Netherlands
He asks the mayor of Kingsbridge to explain where the photograph came from
He finds the firefighter in the picture and asks him in person
He uses a computer programme which draws the firefighter's face
ch.hint: Jonas ajansı arıyor, orijinal dosyayı alıyor ve paylaşılan görselle ayrıntı ayrıntı karşılaştırıyor. Bu yöntem tek bir altyazıya güvenmekten neden daha sağlam?
ch.why: Jonas, resim kütüphanesinden orijinal dosyayı istedi ve paylaşılan resimle ayrıntı ayrıntı karşılaştırarak aynı fotoğraf olduğunu doğruladı.

text: It would have been easy to ignore the matter. The photograph had already been shared eleven thousand times, the mayor had praised it, and, in a sense, nobody had been harmed. But Mrs. Cole, when Jonas laid the evidence on her desk, shook her head. "The town is looking for a hero who does not exist," she said. "If we say nothing, some poor man will be pointed out in the street as the firefighter in the picture. And somebody has probably collected money." Jonas had found a fundraising page, launched on Thursday, with the title: A reward for our Kingsbridge hero, which had already collected four thousand pounds.

The story that appeared on the front page on Monday was a calm one, without a trace of triumph. The headline read: Flood photo shared by thousands was taken in the Netherlands three years ago. Beneath it, Jonas explained how the check had been made, in plain steps that readers could repeat: the shutters, the helmet, the reverse search, the original file. A second article, by Ellie, gave a different view of the same week. It was entitled: The real heroes of Mill Road, and it was a gallery of her own pictures of the actual rescue, with the names of twelve volunteers and firefighters.

The reaction was immediate and, for the most part, generous. The mayor posted a short apology, and the fundraising page was redirected to the fire brigade's own charity, with a note of thanks to the donors. Some readers wrote angry letters accusing the paper of spoiling a lovely story. One, from an old man in the town, said: I would rather have the true heroes than a false one. Jonas pinned it to the wall above his desk. In the afternoon, he wrote a rule for the newsroom on a card: A picture is not a witness until we know when and where it was taken.
ch.clue: A picture is not a witness until we know when and where it was taken
ch.q: What is the main lesson of the case?
o: A newspaper should never print photographs which come from social media
The mayor of a town must be told about any mistake before it is published
A photograph must be checked for the time and place at which it was taken before it is believed
Picture libraries are always more accurate than a reporter's own eyes
Local heroes are more reliable than people from other countries
ch.hint: Jonas'ın gazete odasına astığı kural: "Fotoğraf, ne zaman ve nerede çekildiği bilinene kadar bir tanık değildir." Bu olaydan çıkan temel ders nedir?
ch.why: Bir fotoğrafa inanmadan önce ne zaman ve nerede çekildiği doğrulanmalıdır.

outro: Fotoğraf gerçekti ama Kingsbridge'de ve bu yıl çekilmemişti; üç yıl önce başka bir ülkede yaşanmış bir selin görüntüsüydü. Jonas şunu yazdı: bir fotoğraf yalan söylemez, ama hangi zamana ve hangi yere ait olduğunu söyleyen etiket yalan söyleyebilir.

title: The Salt Marsh
hero: Park korucusu Wren Calder ve köpeği Bracken
intro: Kıyıdaki tuzlu bataklıkta, her yıl kışı geçiren göçmen kuşlar bu yıl çok daha az sayıda. Wren Calder ile Bracken, su düzeyini, bitki örtüsünü ve besin kaynaklarını inceleyerek kuşların neden uzaklaştığını araştırıyor.

text: The salt marsh at Penhallow Bay was a wide, flat expanse of mud, reeds and silver creeks, where the land of the valley met the sea. It lay behind a low sea wall, and was cut by a network of channels through which, twice a day, the tide came in and went out. In winter, it was one of the finest bird sites on the western coast: thousands of waders, such as dunlin, curlew, redshank and knot, arrived from the Arctic in October and stayed until March, feeding in the mud at low tide, in flocks that rose together into the sky like smoke.

Ranger Wren Calder had counted them for twelve years. On the first Sunday of every month, she walked the sea wall at low tide with a telescope and a clicker, and wrote the totals in a notebook that she kept in a plastic bag. Last winter, in December, she had counted just over nine thousand. This December, with Bracken sitting patiently on the wall, she counted for two hours and reached the figure of 2,140.

She counted again, to be sure. Then she walked the full length of the marsh, almost three kilometres, and made a map of where the birds were and where they were not. The map surprised her more than the figure. The flocks, which usually spread over the whole of the lower marsh, were now concentrated in a small area at the far end, near the river mouth, a hundred metres wide. The rest of the mud, which stretched to the sea wall, was empty.
"They have not left," she said to Bracken. "Not all of them. They have concentrated." She wrote a note in her book: The birds avoid most of the marsh. Why? And underneath: Food, safety, or water?
ch.clue: The birds avoid most of the marsh
ch.q: What does Wren's map of the birds show?
o: The birds are spread evenly across the whole of the marsh
The birds have moved from the river mouth to the middle of the marsh
The birds have gathered in a small area and avoid most of the marsh
The birds have all flown away and none remain in the area
The birds are sitting only on the sea wall and not on the mud
ch.hint: Wren'in haritasında kuşlar bataklığın büyük bölümünü terk etmiş ve nehir ağzındaki küçük bir alanda toplanmış. Bu dağılım hangi soruyu doğuruyor: yiyecek, güvenlik ya da su?
ch.why: Kuşlar bataklığın çoğundan kaçınıyor ve nehir ağzındaki küçük bir alanda toplanıyordu.

text: Wren began with safety. A flock of waders is easily frightened, and a single disturbance, a dog, a drone, a person walking on the mud, can make it leave a feeding ground for days. She checked the visitor counters on the paths, which showed no increase. She asked the neighbouring farms about dogs, and found that the number was unchanged. She spent two mornings in the hide at the far end, scanning the sky with her binoculars for birds of prey, which could also drive the waders away. In forty hours, she saw two sparrowhawks and one peregrine, which was normal for the season. "Nothing here," she said. "The place is as quiet as ever."

She turned to the water. The marsh depended on the tide, and she measured the height of the water in the channels at high and low tide, with a graduated pole that she had used for years. The readings were in line with the tide tables for the area. The water had come in and out as it should. "The water is right," she said. Bracken, who had been in the creek, shook himself, covering her in mud.

That left food. She walked out on the flats at low tide, with a metal tube a few centimetres across, and took cores of the mud, to see what lived in it. In the cores from the end of the marsh, where the flocks had gathered, the mud was dark and thick, and teeming with small creatures: tiny snails, worms, and shrimps, about a thousand to a square metre. She repeated the sampling at six places on the empty side. The cores were light grey, dry, and crumbly. Many contained no animals at all. In two, she found three or four dead snails.
She put the cores in a row on the wall in the winter sun, and looked at them for a long time. "They are not afraid," she said at last. "They are hungry. The food is in one place, and not in another."
ch.clue: They are hungry
ch.q: What does Wren discover about the empty parts of the marsh?
o: The birds of prey hunt there every day from the nearby hills
The mud there is full of food, but it is covered by a thin layer of oil
The tide there is so high that the birds cannot stand on the mud
The area is full of dogs and people who frighten the birds away
The mud there is dry and almost without the small creatures on which the birds feed
ch.hint: Wren, kuşların bulunmadığı kısımdaki çamuru örnekledi: kuru, ufalanıyor ve neredeyse hiç küçük canlı yok. Kuşlar neden oradan kaçınıyor?
ch.why: Boş bölümlerdeki çamur kuru ve neredeyse hiç küçük canlı içermiyordu; kuşların yiyeceği orada yoktu.

text: A marsh is not naturally dry. The mud that she had found was cracked and pale, like the bed of a drying pond, and a sample, when shaken in a jar of water, floated a thin white crust. Wren recognised it. "Salt," she said. "But too much, or too little?" The salinity meter, which she had in her truck, read the water from the creeks on the empty side: seven parts per thousand, which is very low, a fifth of the salinity of sea water.

"Fresh water in a salt marsh," she said to Bracken. "That is wrong." The small animals that lived in the mud, the snails and shrimps, were adapted to a particular balance. They needed the sea water that came in with every tide to keep the mud moist and salty. If the salt water did not arrive, the mud dried out, and the animals died, or were replaced by species that waders do not eat.

She followed the creeks inland, tracing the line on her map from the far end, where the sea entered through a gap in the sea wall. The tide, she realised, entered the marsh in a single channel, and then spread out through the smaller creeks. But in the middle of the marsh, a creek that should have been open was dry. At the point where it joined the main channel, there was a small concrete structure with a metal flap, a tidal gate, designed to let the sea in and prevent water from draining out, so that the lower marsh stayed wet at low tide.

The gate was open, with its flap lying on the ground at an angle, caught on something. She bent to look. A large log, brought down by the winter storms, was jammed in the gap between the gate and its frame, holding the flap open. "It is not closing," she said slowly. "It lets the water out at low tide, and nothing is holding it in."
ch.clue: A large log, brought down by the winter storms, was jammed in the gap
ch.q: What is wrong with the tidal gate?
o: The gate is too small to let enough water out of the marsh
A log has jammed the gate open, so the water drains from the lower marsh and the mud dries
The gate has been removed by the council to make the marsh larger
The gate is locked closed and does not let any sea water into the marsh
The gate is covered with salt and cannot be seen from the sea wall
ch.hint: Gelgit kapağının menteşesi bir kütükle sıkışmış ve kapak açık kalmış. Alçak gelgitte su dışarı akıyor ve içeri tutulamıyor. Bu durum alt bataklığı nasıl etkiliyor?
ch.why: Kütük kapağı açık tutuyordu; alçak gelgitte su akıp gidiyor, çamur kuruyor ve küçük canlılar ölüyordu.

text: Wren photographed the gate from three angles, marked its position on her map, and telephoned the manager of the Environment Agency's flood team, a brisk man named Mr. Doyle, who sent a technician, with a winch and a crowbar, the next morning. It took them an hour to free the log, which weighed more than two hundred kilograms. When it was dragged away, the flap fell back with a deep metallic clang, and, as the tide came in that afternoon, the water filled the lower channels and, for the first time in months, stayed.

"It will take time," said Wren, as she and Mr. Doyle stood on the wall in the evening light. "The animals that live in the mud do not return in a week. We must wait for the marsh to recover, and the snails to come back. In the end it depends on the larvae brought in by the tide." Mr. Doyle, who had expected a more dramatic report, nodded slowly. "I shall have the gate inspected every month," he said. "A log may be a small thing, but I see what it did."

By the end of January, the cores that Wren took from the lower marsh were dark, damp and full of small snails again, and, in the second week of February, the first flocks of dunlin settled on the mud, a little cautiously, in groups of fifty and a hundred. In March, on the last count of the winter, she reached 6,300, still short of the usual nine thousand, but climbing. Bracken, who had been left in the truck, was allowed on the wall to watch.

At the end of the season, Wren added a paragraph to the report. The empty marsh was not a mystery, she wrote. It was a map of something which had been missing, and the birds had read it before we did.
ch.clue: the birds had read it before we did
ch.q: What results from freeing the gate?
o: The tide stops entering the marsh and the mud becomes very dry
The Environment Agency decides to remove the gate completely
The birds leave the marsh for good and find a new home on the coast
The lower marsh becomes wet again, the small animals return, and the birds come back in large numbers
The snails die because the sea water is too salty for them to live in
ch.hint: Kütük çıkarılıp kapak kapanınca su alt kanallarda kaldı, çamurda küçük salyangozlar geri geldi ve martıların yerine dunlin sürüleri döndü. Kapak onarımının sonucu neydi?
ch.why: Alt bataklık yeniden ıslandı, küçük canlılar geri döndü ve kuşlar yeniden büyük sayılarda gelmeye başladı.

outro: Bataklığın alt kısmındaki bir kapakçığın bozulması, tuzlu suyun içeri girmesini engellemişti; böceklerin ve küçük kabukluların yaşadığı çamur kurumuş, kuşlar yiyecek bulamamıştı. Wren şunu yazdı: bir ekosistemde en önemli şey çoğu zaman gözle görünen şey değil, ayağımızın altındaki çamurdur.

title: The Lost Provenance
hero: Küratör Hugo Laurent ve güvenlik görevlisi Mina
intro: Müzeye bağışlanan bir heykelin geçmişi (provenansı) kayıtlarda eksik. Hugo Laurent ile Mina, bir yasa dışı kaçakçılık şüphesini göz önünde bulundurarak heykelin nereden geldiğini belgelere, müzayede kayıtlarına ve fotoğraflara bakarak araştırıyor.

text: The bronze head arrived at the City Museum in a wooden crate, as a gift from the estate of a retired businessman, Mr. Everett Marsh, who had died in the spring. It was a beautiful thing: the head of a young man, about thirty centimetres high, with curled hair, a straight nose, and eyes that had once been inlaid with glass and now, empty, seemed to look at something far away. The catalogue of the estate described it as Roman, first or second century, and the museum's own expert, Dr. Osei, had agreed that it was almost certainly genuine.

But, before accepting any gift of antiquity, the museum was obliged to establish its provenance, the history of its ownership, from its discovery to the present day. In the case of an object from the ancient Mediterranean, the law of most countries required that it had left its country of origin legally, and a museum that accepted an object without a clear history risked becoming an unwitting receiver of stolen goods. Hugo Laurent, as curator, took the responsibility seriously.

He asked the solicitor of the estate for all the documents. The folder that arrived contained three items: a receipt from a London dealer, dated 1987, for the sum of eight thousand pounds, with the description "Roman bronze portrait head"; a photograph, showing the head on a mantelpiece, dated 1991; and a letter of 1964, from an earlier owner, a Captain Wallace, to the dealer, offering the object for sale. Before 1964, there was nothing.

"Sixty years of history," said Mina, who was helping him to read the papers, "and before that, a hole. Where did Captain Wallace get it?" Hugo took off his glasses. "That is the question. In a case like this, a silence is not evidence of a crime. But it is a reason to ask."
ch.clue: a silence is not evidence of a crime
ch.q: What is the problem with the bronze head?
o: The head has been damaged and the eyes are missing from it
The museum has already paid eight thousand pounds for the head
Dr. Osei believes that the head is a modern copy made from plastic
Its history cannot be traced before 1964, so it is unclear whether it was legally exported
The estate has refused to give any documents about the head
ch.hint: Başın geçmişi 1964'ten öncesi için belgelenmemiş. Bir müze, yasa dışı yoldan çıkmış bir eseri istemeden kabul etmemek için neyi bilmek zorunda?
ch.why: Başın geçmişi 1964'ten önce izlenemiyordu; bu yüzden eserin ülkesinden yasal yoldan çıkıp çıkmadığı belli değildi.

text: Hugo began with the only name in the file. Captain Wallace, according to a note on the letter, was a retired army officer, and had lived in Bristol. A search of the local newspapers and the county records produced his obituary, dated 1979, in which a brief life was described: born 1894, served in the First World War in the Near East, as an officer in a unit stationed in the Levant between 1917 and 1920, and, after the war, in the administration of a mandate territory. He retired in 1946.

"The Levant," said Mina. "That is where the head might have come from?" "It is one of the possibilities," said Hugo. "Bronze portraits of this kind were found in many parts of the eastern Mediterranean. If the Captain served there, he might have obtained it, but the question is how. An officer in a time of war may have bought it from a local dealer, or been given it as a gift, or, in a less happy case, taken it from a site." He read the obituary again, to the end. "He is said to have 'formed a modest collection of antiquities, which he kept in his Bristol house'. Which suggests that he collected over many years."

He wrote to the university in Bristol, where Captain Wallace's papers might have been deposited, and received, ten days later, a polite reply from the archivist. The Wallace papers, she wrote, were in the possession of his granddaughter, Mrs. Fenwick, who lived in Somerset, and who was known to be helpful. Hugo telephoned her that afternoon, introduced himself, and explained as simply as he could what he needed.
"My grandfather kept a lot of notebooks," said Mrs. Fenwick, in a warm, hesitant voice. "They are in two tin trunks in my attic. I have never read them. Would you like to come on Saturday?"
ch.clue: formed a modest collection of antiquities
ch.q: What does Hugo learn about Captain Wallace?
o: He served in the Levant after the First World War and later collected antiquities in Bristol
He was a museum curator who donated the head to the estate of Mr. Marsh
He was a thief who was arrested for the theft of the bronze head
He was a dealer who sold bronze heads in London during the 1980s
He was a politician who bought the head from the government of Rome
ch.hint: Kaptan Wallace'ın ölüm ilanı, Birinci Dünya Savaşı sonrasında Levant'ta görev yaptığını ve Bristol'de bir eski eser koleksiyonu oluşturduğunu söylüyor. Bu bilgiler başın kökeni için neyi düşündürüyor?
ch.why: Kaptan Wallace Birinci Dünya Savaşı sonrası Levant'ta görev yapmış ve daha sonra Bristol'de eski eser toplamıştı; baş oradan gelmiş olabilirdi.

text: On Saturday afternoon, Hugo and Mina sat on the floor of a low attic in a Somerset farmhouse, with a flask of tea between them, and two battered tin trunks open in front of them. They contained a lifetime of papers: diaries, ledgers, pressed flowers, a few photographs of dusty roads and white-robed men on camels. Mrs. Fenwick, who had brought a blanket for her knees, sat in an armchair and watched with a mixture of curiosity and guilt.

It took them three hours to find what they needed. In a small black ledger marked Acquisitions, in the Captain's clear hand, was a list of thirty-two items, with the date, the source and the price paid. Item 14, dated the third of June 1921, read: Bronze head, Roman, young man, purchased from M. Haddad, antiquarian, Beirut, for £40, with export licence no. 218 from the Department of Antiquities of the Mandate. The ledger had a pocket at the back, and, in it, a folded paper, brown at the edges. Hugo unfolded it carefully. It was an official document, in French and English, with a stamp and a signature: a licence to export one bronze head, issued to Captain R. Wallace on the twelfth of June 1921, number 218.

"An export licence," said Mina, reading over his shoulder. "From a government that was in charge of the territory at the time." Hugo held it up to the light. "The licence is genuine as far as I can tell, and the number matches the entry. It means that the head left the country in 1921, with the permission of the authorities of the time, and with a receipt. That is not a complete history, because we do not know where M. Haddad found it. But it is a start, and a significant one."
Mrs. Fenwick put her hand to her mouth. "I did not know that he kept all of it," she said. "I thought it was only old paper."
ch.clue: export licence no. 218
ch.q: What do the ledger and the licence show?
o: The licence is a forgery which was made by the Captain's granddaughter
The head was made in Bristol and sold to a dealer in the Levant
The head was bought in Beirut in 1921 and exported with an official licence
The head was stolen from a museum in Beirut by Captain Wallace
The head was never in the possession of Captain Wallace at all
ch.hint: Defterde 1921'de Beyrut'tan satın alınan Roma dönemi bir bronz baş ve 218 numaralı ihracat lisansı kayıtlı. Bu belgeler başın çıkışı hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
ch.why: Baş 1921'de Beyrut'ta satın alınmış ve resmî bir ihracat lisansıyla ülkeden çıkarılmıştı; yani çıkışı yasaldı.

text: Hugo wrote his report in the evening, and, as was his custom, began with a short, honest paragraph about what had been established and what had not. The head had left the Levant in 1921 with a valid export licence, which was a fact, documented by the Captain's ledger and the licence itself. It had been in Britain since then, in the Captain's collection, then, after 1964, in the hands of a London dealer, and finally, from 1987, in the collection of Mr. Marsh, who had kept it on his mantelpiece. Every link in the chain was supported by a document.

What was not known was the earlier history. M. Haddad, the dealer in Beirut, had not recorded where the head had been found, and it was very possible that no one now could say. The museum had also asked the national authorities of the country concerned, to see whether any claim had been made, and had received a negative reply. "We cannot say where it was dug up," wrote Hugo. "We can say that it was not exported illegally, that its journey was documented, and that no authority has claimed it. This is the standard of proof that the profession demands, and in my judgement, the head can be accepted."

Mina, who had read the draft, wrote one comment in pencil in the margin. "Why do you say 'in my judgement'?" she asked. "Because a provenance is never complete," said Hugo. "Every object has a history before the first document, and we can only be honest about the part we can see. I would rather put in the report what we do not know than pretend that there is no gap."

The head was accepted by the museum's board, and, when it was displayed in the spring, the label did not give only the date and the material. It told the whole story, including the line: Before 1921, unknown. Visitors, Mina noticed, always read that line twice.
ch.clue: Before 1921, unknown
ch.q: Why does Hugo include what is not known in his report?
o: He is sure that the head was stolen and wants to warn the board
He has not been able to read most of the Captain's notebooks
The museum wants to refuse the gift and needs an excuse
The law demands that every report should contain a list of mistakes
A provenance is never complete, and honesty requires that the gaps are stated
ch.hint: Hugo raporun yargısına "bana göre" ifadesini koyuyor ve bilinmeyenleri de yazıyor. Bir menşe (provenans) belgesi neden hiçbir zaman tamamlanmış olmaz ve dürüstlük burada neyi gerektirir?
ch.why: Provenans hiçbir zaman tam olamazdı ve dürüstlük, boşlukların açıkça belirtilmesini gerektiriyordu.

outro: Heykel yasa dışı bir kazıdan değil, 1920'lerde yasal olarak ihraç edilmiş bir koleksiyondan geliyordu; ama kayıtlardaki boşluk, bir savaşta kaybolan bir arşivden kaynaklanıyordu. Hugo şunu yazdı: bir belge eksikse bu, suçun kanıtı değil, sorunun işaretidir; ama o sorunu çözmek de müzenin görevidir.

title: The Archivist's Vault
hero: Oyun testçileri Zoe ve Max
intro: Zoe ve Max bu kez bir arşiv kasasında kilitli. Raflarda numaralı klasörler, bir dizin kartı ve şifre bulmacaları var. Her bulmaca bir sonraki klasörü gösteriyor. Süre altmış dakika.

text: The vault door shut behind Zoe and Max with the heavy, soundless closing of a safe. It was a long, narrow room lined from floor to ceiling with grey metal shelves, each filled with box files, numbered in black paint. At the far end stood a small desk, with a lamp, a card index in a wooden drawer, and a ring of keys. Above the door, the clock began to count down from sixty minutes.

On the desk, a typed note lay on a stack of blank cards. Max read it aloud. "To leave the vault, you must find the file marked with the correct number. The number is the answer to a question. The question is on card 1." He took the first card from the index and read it. "How many files in this room bear a number which is a multiple of 7, but not a multiple of 14?" Below the question, in smaller type, a note: The files are numbered consecutively from 1 to 100.

"So we have to count," said Zoe. "From 1 to 100, how many are multiples of 7, but not of 14?" She was already writing in her notebook. "The multiples of 7 up to 100 are: 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42, 49, 56, 63, 70, 77, 84, 91, 98. There are fourteen of them. Of these, the multiples of 14 are the even ones: 14, 28, 42, 56, 70, 84 and 98. There are seven."

Max smiled. "So the odd multiples of 7 are the ones we want: 7, 21, 35, 49, 63, 77 and 91." He counted them on his fingers. "Seven of them." Zoe stared at the notebook. "But the question asks how many, and the answer is a number, and the file that opens the next drawer must have that number." She looked up at the shelves, where, at the level of her eyes, the box files stood in a long row. "File number seven," she said. "The first one on the left."
ch.clue: The files are numbered consecutively from 1 to 100
ch.q: What is the answer to the question on card 1?
ch.hint: 1'den 100'e kadar 7'nin katları 14 tane. Bunlardan 14'ün katı olanlar çift olanlar. 7'nin katı olup 14'ün katı olmayanların sayısı kaç?
ch.why: 7'nin 14 katı var ve bunların yedisi (çift olanlar) 14'ün de katıdır; geriye 14 − 7 = 7 sayı kalır.

text: Max pulled out file seven, a battered cardboard box tied with a faded red ribbon, and placed it on the desk under the lamp. Inside there was a single sheet, typed on yellowing paper, and a small card marked with the number 2. The sheet carried a short message, and below it, a line of numbers: 3 1 20 1 12 15 7 21 5.

The message said: Every file in this vault is described in one word. Find that word, count its letters, and open the file that bears the same number. Zoe looked at the line of numbers for a long moment. "They are letters," she said. "One is A, two is B, and so on up to twenty-six for Z. It is the oldest cipher there is, and the archivist must have loved it." She wrote the alphabet in a row in her notebook, with the numbers under it, and began to translate, tapping her pencil on each figure.

"Three is C," she said. "One is A. Twenty is T. One is A again. Twelve is L. Fifteen is O. Seven is G. Twenty-one is U. Five is E." She wrote the letters as she found them, and, when she had finished, she held the notebook up to Max, with the nine letters in a neat row. He read them aloud, slowly. The clock above the door showed 49:30.

"It is a word that I have seen on the label of every box in the room," said Max. "And the instruction says that we must count its letters, and open the file with that number. We shall have to count them carefully. I would not like to open the wrong file." He turned to look along the shelves, where the numbered files stood in long grey rows, and then at the little card in his hand, which said: One file is the key. The others are not.
ch.clue: Every file in this vault is described in one word
ch.q: Which word do the numbers spell?
o: CORRIDOR
CATALOGUE
DOCUMENT
CABINET
ARCHIVES
ch.hint: Sayıları alfabedeki sıraya göre harfe çevir: 3 = C, 1 = A, 20 = T, 1 = A, 12 = L, 15 = O, 7 = G, 21 = U, 5 = E. Hangi kelime çıkıyor?
ch.why: Sayılar sırayla C, A, T, A, L, O, G, U, E harflerini veriyor ve CATALOGUE kelimesini oluşturuyordu.

text: "Catalogue," said Max, writing the letters one under another in a column. "C, A, T, A, L, O, G, U, E. Nine letters. The file we need is number nine." They found it on the same shelf, a thin grey box between file eight and file ten, with a brass catch and a card in the slot on the front. Zoe opened it and took out a single page, covered in a small, neat typewriter hand.

The page said: You have opened file seven, and now you open file nine. A vault has many files, but only one holds the key. The number of that file is the product of the two file numbers that you have opened, and no other. Do not add them. Do not subtract them. Multiply them.

Zoe put the page on the desk, beside the card from the first drawer, and looked at the two numbers that she had written on the cover of her notebook: seven and nine. "A product is the result of a multiplication," she said. "It is what you get when you take one number as many times as the other says. Seven nines, or nine sevens. I cannot remember which one the archivist meant, but it makes no difference to the result."

"There is a catch," said Max, leaning on the shelves. "The vault holds a hundred files, and we must be sure that the product is not more than a hundred. Otherwise there would be no such file." Zoe was already writing. She looked up at the clock, which showed 47:10, and then at the long corridor of shelves, with all the numbers that were hiding in the dim light.
ch.clue: The number of that file is the product of the two file numbers that you have opened
ch.q: Which file holds the key?
o: File 16
File 79
File 72
File 63
File 54
ch.hint: Anahtarın bulunduğu dosyanın numarası, açılan iki dosyanın numaralarının çarpımı: 7 ile 9. Yedi kere dokuz kaç eder?
ch.why: Açılan dosyaların numaraları 7 ve 9'du ve çarpımları 7 × 9 = 63 yapıyordu.

text: File sixty-three stood on the lowest shelf of the third row, behind a box of old receipts which had been pushed in front of it. Max had to kneel on the floor and take out the receipts, one by one, before he could reach it. It was a heavy file, bound in black cloth, with the number painted on the spine in white. When he laid it on the desk, it fell open at once, as if somebody had read it a thousand times.

Inside there was a single card of thick cream paper, and a key of dark brass. The card was printed in an elegant italic hand: Congratulations. You have read the archive correctly. The key opens the door of the vault. But the best archivists know that the answer is always in the catalogue, and the catalogue was in front of you from the beginning. Zoe read the last sentence aloud, twice.

"The answer was in the catalogue," she said. "The heading of the sheet in file seven, the word that we decoded, the number that it gave us, and the number from the first card. We needed each of them to arrive here. But I do not see how they were in front of us from the beginning." Max laughed softly, turning the heavy key in his fingers. "The first card asked about the numbers from 1 to 100. Seven, then nine, then sixty-three. It was one chain, and each link was a thing that we had already found."

He put the key in the lock of the vault door. The mechanism turned with a deep, smooth click, and the door swung open on a bright corridor. On the screen above it, the numbers showed 41:55. "We were nearly twenty minutes early," said Zoe. "I think that the archivist would have been proud."
ch.clue: You have read the archive correctly
ch.q: How do Zoe and Max find the key that opens the vault door?
o: They open file 63, whose number is the product of 7 and 9, the two files that they had already opened
They find the key under the lamp on the desk at the end of the room
They open file 100, because it is the last file in the vault
They ask the archivist, who gives them the key through the door
They open file 16, whose number is the sum of 7 and 9
ch.hint: Zoe ve Max anahtarı hangi dosyada buldu ve o dosyanın numarası nasıl ortaya çıktı? Zinciri hatırla: ilk bulmaca 7'yi, kelime 9'u verdi.
ch.why: Anahtar, daha önce açtıkları 7 ve 9 numaralı dosyaların çarpımı olan 63 numaralı dosyadaydı.

outro: Son klasörün içindeki kart kasanın kapısını açtı ve Zoe ile Max koridora çıktı. Oyunun yaratıcısı, en güzel bulmacanın, cevabın zaten gözünüzün önünde olan ama sizin okumadığınız olduğunu söyledi.

title: The Customs Declaration
hero: Havalimanı görevlisi Dara Mills ve stajyer Sam
intro: Bir yolcu, gümrükte bir tablo getirdiğini ve değerinin çok düşük olduğunu söylüyor. Dara Mills ile Sam, belgeleri, fotoğrafları ve sanat piyasası kayıtlarını karşılaştırarak tablonun gerçek değerini ve yolcunun beyanının neden eksik olduğunu araştırıyor.

text: The woman at the customs desk was elderly, round-faced and cheerful, with a bag of shopping on her arm and a large flat package wrapped in brown paper and string at her feet. She introduced herself as Mrs. Alder, a retired schoolteacher from Kent, returning from a week's holiday in France. Dara Mills, who was on duty at the red channel, asked her whether she had anything to declare.

"Only this," said Mrs. Alder, with a delighted smile. "A little picture that I bought at a flea market in Normandy. It cost fifteen euros, and I think that it is very pretty. I understand that I must tell you about anything that I buy abroad. It is a very small sum." Sam, standing a pace behind Dara, with the trainee's earnest expression, wrote the figure in the register: Painting, purchased 15 euros, flea market. Dara asked her permission to see it.

Mrs. Alder unwrapped the package with the care of a woman who loved the thing. It was an oil painting, about fifty centimetres wide, in a plain wooden frame, showing a harbour in the early morning, with fishing boats, a pale sky and a few figures on a quay. The brushstrokes were quick and bold, and the light, a warm yellow, seemed to rise from the water. It was signed in the lower right corner with a single, large initial: R.

Dara looked at it for a while without speaking. She was not an art expert, and had no pretension to be, but she had been working in the airport for twelve years, and she had learned that people who brought paintings to the customs desk sometimes had no idea what they had in their hands. "It is lovely, Mrs. Alder," she said. "May I ask you to wait a few minutes? I should like a colleague to look at it."
ch.clue: R
ch.q: Why does Dara ask Mrs. Alder to wait?
o: She wants a colleague to look at the painting because it may be worth more than the declared price
She has to ask the customs for permission to open the package
She cannot find the register in which the purchase must be recorded
She wants to give the painting back to the owner of the flea market
She suspects that Mrs. Alder has stolen the painting from a museum
ch.hint: Dara sanat uzmanı değil ama on iki yıllık deneyiminden bazı insanların ellerindeki eserin değerini bilmediğini biliyor. Neden bir meslektaşından bakmasını istiyor?
ch.why: Dara, tablonun beyan edilen fiyattan çok daha değerli olabileceğini düşündü ve bir meslektaşının da bakmasını istedi.

text: The airport had a small team of specialists, some of whom were part-time, who could be called to examine unusual items. The one who came to the desk was a thin, grey-haired man in a cardigan named Mr. Brandt, who worked for a London auction house two days a week and was, by coincidence, at Heathfield that afternoon to collect a parcel. Dara explained the situation briefly. He put on a pair of glasses, bent over the picture, and did not speak for about a minute.
