"May I take it out of the frame?" he asked, and Mrs. Alder, who was by now a little anxious, agreed. Using a small screwdriver from his pocket, he removed four pins and lifted the painting out. He turned it over. On the back of the canvas, there were several marks: a faded paper label, with a number written in ink, and a stencilled stamp, partly rubbed, in the shape of a small crown. "It is a collector's mark," he said. "And the number is an inventory number. This picture has been in a collection, a good one, and has been catalogued."

He turned it to the light and studied the signature. "R," he said softly. "A single initial. That was how a certain painter signed his early harbour scenes, in the 1890s, before he was famous. I do not wish to alarm you, Mrs. Alder, because I am not certain. But I should be very surprised if this were a copy."

"It cost fifteen euros," said Mrs. Alder faintly. "It was in a box of old frames, under a heap of postcards." Mr. Brandt straightened his back. "I should like to take photographs," he said, "and compare it with some images from the catalogue of a painter whose name I shall not say before I am sure. Would you give me an hour?" Sam looked at Dara. Dara, who had thought of a hundred possible endings to the afternoon, and had not included this one, nodded slowly.
ch.clue: I should be very surprised if this were a copy
ch.q: What does Mr. Brandt notice on the back of the canvas?
o: A date which shows that the painting was made last year in France
A price tag from the flea market which says that it is a copy
A collector's stamp and an inventory number, which suggest that the painting belonged to a catalogued collection
A note from Mrs. Alder saying that the painting was made by herself
A message from the customs office asking the owner to declare it

ch.why: Arkadaki koleksiyoncu damgası ve envanter numarası, tablonun kayıtlı bir koleksiyona ait olduğunu düşündürüyordu.

text: It took Mr. Brandt less than an hour. In the corner of the customs office, with a laptop and a photograph on the screen, he searched the online catalogue of a major art library, and then a second database, which lists works that have been recorded as missing or stolen. Dara, who had known many people who stared into computers, had rarely seen anybody who looked so alive. At ten past four, he stood up and closed the lid with great care.

"I have found it," he said. "I am almost completely sure. The picture is called Morning at the Quay, and it was painted in 1893 by a painter whom I may now name. His signature at that period was a single initial. It was exhibited in Paris in 1894, bought by a collector in Rouen, and recorded in the catalogue raisonné of the artist's works, number 117. In 1943, during the war, the collection was evacuated from the city, and the picture disappeared. It has not been seen since. The auction houses have had it on a list of missing works for eighty years."

Mrs. Alder sat down on the nearest chair. "I thought it was pretty," she said. "I had no idea." Dara, who had put aside her notebook, spoke gently. "Mrs. Alder, I must tell you what happens next. You did nothing wrong, and you declared the picture in good faith. The law, however, requires that a work which is believed to have been lost in the war must be reported, and its history investigated. The customs service will keep the picture safely while that is done, and you will have a receipt."

"It will be a long process," said Mr. Brandt. "The heirs of the Rouen collector may have a claim. But in the end, it is common in such cases for the finder, and for the family, to come to an agreement." Mrs. Alder looked at the empty frame on the desk. "It was only a harbour," she said. "But it did make me happy, in my kitchen."
ch.clue: The auction houses have had it on a list of missing works for eighty years
ch.q: What does Mr. Brandt discover about the painting?
o: It is a picture stolen from the airport yesterday
It is a modern copy which a French shop made last year
It is a work by Mrs. Alder, which she painted as a child
It is a worthless print on canvas, as the flea market said
It is a lost work of a famous painter, missing since the Second World War
ch.hint: Mr. Brandt kataloglarda tabloyu buluyor: 1893'te boyanmış, 1894'te sergilenmiş ve 1943'te savaş sırasında kaybolmuş. Bu bilgi tablo hakkında ne gösteriyor?
ch.why: Tablo, ünlü bir ressamın Dünya Savaşı sırasında kaybolmuş eseriydi.

text: The weeks that followed were long and, for Mrs. Alder, rather bewildering. The customs service placed the painting in the care of a national gallery, where specialists examined it, took samples of the paint, and compared the canvas and the stretcher with the records of the collection in Rouen. By the end of the month, a report confirmed that it was the missing Morning at the Quay. The French authorities were informed, and the heirs of the collector, three grandchildren who lived in different countries, were traced by a team of lawyers.

Dara kept in touch with Mrs. Alder by telephone, and, one Friday in November, learned the result. After three meetings, the heirs and the finder had agreed that the painting would be sold at auction, and that the proceeds would be divided: a fixed share to the heirs, and a smaller, but still generous, share to Mrs. Alder, for her good faith, and for the fact that, without her honest declaration, the picture might never have been recognised. "I shall buy a new roof for the house," said Mrs. Alder cheerfully, "and perhaps a trip to Normandy. To look for another box of frames."

In the office, Sam wrote the closing line of the report in his careful hand, and showed it to Dara. "What did you notice that day?" he asked. "I did not notice anything special," said Dara. "I noticed that she was honest. The declaration was a very small sum, and she had written it down with a smile. People who hide things look at the desk. People who have nothing to hide look at the thing they love." She stamped the file.
"The first rule of the customs," she said, "is to look at what is declared. The second is to look at what the person does not know."
ch.clue: The first rule of the customs
ch.q: How is the case resolved?

The painting is given to the airport as a gift from the customs service
The painting is returned to Mrs. Alder, who hangs it in her kitchen

outro: Yolcu tabloyu gerçekten bir bit pazarında on beş poundluk bir kopya sanarak satın almıştı; ancak yapılan inceleme, tablonun bilinen bir ressamın kayıp eseri olduğunu gösterdi. Dara şunu söyledi: bir beyan, yalnızca beyan eden kişinin bildiğini yansıtır; gümrüğün işi, bilinmeyeni sormaktır.
